courses/coe-328/ch01-number-systems-and-.title: Ch 1: Number Systems and Digital Waveforms
courses/coe-328/ch01-number-systems-and-.content:
Overview


                  
                  Readings Lectures: Introduction to Digital Waveform and Lecture 1: Binary Numbering System · weeks 1–2 · Floyd, Digital Fundamentals ch. 1–2
                  
                

Digital circuits only know two voltage levels, HIGH and LOW, which stand for the bits 1 and 0. This chapter covers how those levels show up as waveforms (and how to read them off an oscilloscope), then how numbers are written with bits: binary, hexadecimal, BCD, and the 1’s and 2’s complements used for negative numbers.
Notes
Logic levels
A digital signal is either HIGH or LOW. Each level is a range of voltages, not one exact value, with a gap in between that’s invalid:





















Range (5 V logic)Meaning2\ \text{V} to 5\ \text{V}HIGH, binary 10.8\ \text{V} to 2\ \text{V}Invalid (only passed through during a transition)0\ \text{V} to 0.8\ \text{V}LOW, binary 0
A single binary digit is a bit. Using HIGH = 1 and LOW = 0 is called positive logic, and it’s what this course uses.
Digital waveforms
A digital waveform switches back and forth between LOW and HIGH. One trip up and back down is a pulse:

Positive-going pulse: normally LOW, goes HIGH, then back to LOW.
Negative-going pulse: normally HIGH, goes LOW, then back to HIGH.
The first edge of a pulse is the leading edge, the second is the trailing edge. On a positive-going pulse, the leading edge is the rising edge and the trailing edge is the falling edge.

A waveform is periodic if its pulses repeat at a fixed interval, and non-periodic otherwise (like a data signal). A periodic waveform is described by:

Figure 1.1: The parts of a periodic pulse waveform.



































QuantitySymbolMeaningPeriodTTime for one full cycle (one HIGH part + one LOW part)FrequencyfCycles per second (Hz). f = 1/TPulse widtht_WTime the pulse spends HIGHDuty cycle—Fraction of the period spent HIGH, as a %AmplitudeAVoltage from LOW to HIGH (V_{pp}, peak-to-peak)
A square wave is the special case with a 50% duty cycle.
Waveforms carry binary data
When a waveform carries data, each bit gets an equal slice of time called the bit time. The waveform is HIGH during a bit time for a 1 and LOW for a 0. All the waveforms in a system are lined up with a periodic clock signal, whose period equals one bit time. To read the bits off a waveform, look at its level during each clock period.
Reading an oscilloscope
A scope screen is a grid of divisions. The two knobs tell you how much each division is worth:

Vertical (V/div): voltage per division. Amplitude = (number of divisions tall) × V/div.
Horizontal (time/div): time per division. Period = (number of divisions per cycle) × time/div.

Going the other way, to sketch a waveform you divide: divisions = value ÷ (value per division).
Try it: set a frequency, duty cycle, and amplitude, then change the scope settings and see how many divisions each part takes up.
Interactive oscilloscope (open this page on the site to use it).
Decimal and binary numbers
Both decimal and binary are positional (weighted) number systems: each digit is multiplied by a weight that depends on its position, and the results are added.

Decimal (base 10): weights are powers of 10. 568.23 = 5 \times 10^2 + 6 \times 10^1 + 8 \times 10^0 + 2 \times 10^{-1} + 3 \times 10^{-2}
Binary (base 2): weights are powers of 2, so each bit is worth double the one to its right.




























Position… 2^32^22^12^0.2^{-1}2^{-2}2^{-3} …Weight8421.0.50.250.125

The rightmost whole-number bit is the LSB (least significant bit), weight 2^0 = 1.
The leftmost bit is the MSB (most significant bit).
Bits right of the binary point have fractional weights 2^{-1}, 2^{-2}, \ldots

Counting in binary: with n bits you can count from 0 up to 2^n - 1 (e.g. 4 bits count 0 to 15).












































n123456789102^n2481632641282565121024Largest number, 2^n - 11371531631272555111023
Converting between binary and decimal
Binary → decimal: add up the weights of every bit that’s a 1.
1101101_2 = 64 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 109_{10}
Decimal → binary, two ways:

Sum of weights: find binary weights that add up to the number, then put a 1 in those positions. 25 = 16 + 8 + 1 \Rightarrow 11001_2
Repeated division by 2: keep dividing by 2 until the quotient is 0. The remainders are the bits, first remainder = LSB, last remainder = MSB.



















































DivisionQuotientRemainder156 \div 2780 (LSB)78 \div 239039 \div 219119 \div 2919 \div 2414 \div 2202 \div 2101 \div 201 (MSB)
Reading the remainders bottom to top: 156_{10} = 10011100_2.
Binary addition and subtraction









































AdditionResultSubtractionResult0 + 000 - 000 + 111 - 011 + 011 - 101 + 110 (sum 0, carry 1)10 - 11 (0 − 1 with a borrow)1 + 1 + 111 (sum 1, carry 1)
A borrow is only needed when subtracting a 1 from a 0. It takes 1 from the next column to the left, which is worth 2 in the current column.
1’s and 2’s complement
These are how computers represent negative numbers (more on this in Ch 5).

1’s complement: flip every bit (0 → 1, 1 → 0). In hardware this is just an inverter on each bit.
2’s complement: the 1’s complement plus 1.

\begin{aligned}
\text{number:} &\quad 10110010 \\
\text{1's complement:} &\quad 01001101 \\
\text{2's complement:} &\quad 01001110
\end{aligned}
Shortcut for 2’s complement: starting at the LSB, copy the bits up to and including the first 1, then flip all the bits after it.
10111\underline{000} \;\rightarrow\; \text{copy } \underline{1000}, \text{ flip } 1011 \;\rightarrow\; 01001000
Why it means negative: in n bits, the 2’s complement of x is 2^n - x. In 4 bits, 3 = 0011 and its 2’s complement is 1101, which is 13 as an unsigned number, but 13 = 16 - 3, so it stands for -3.
Hexadecimal
Hex (base 16) is shorthand for binary: each hex digit is exactly 4 bits. Digits are 0–9, then A–F for 10–15.






























































Hex0123456789ABCDEFBinary0000000100100011010001010110011110001001101010111100110111101111Decimal0123456789101112131415

Binary → hex: split into groups of 4 starting from the right (pad the leftmost group with 0s), then replace each group. 1001111011110011100 \rightarrow 0100\ 1111\ 0111\ 1001\ 1100 = 4F79C_{16}
Hex → binary: replace each hex digit with its 4 bits. 6BD3_{16} = 0110\ 1011\ 1101\ 0011
Hex → decimal: multiply each digit by its weight (16^0, 16^1, 16^2, \ldots) and add, or go through binary.
Decimal → hex: go through binary, or divide repeatedly by 16 (remainders are the hex digits, first = least significant).

Counting continues past F the same way as decimal: …, E, F, 10, 11, …, 1F, 20, … Two hex digits reach FF_{16} = 255, three reach FFF_{16} = 4095, four reach FFFF_{16} = 65\,535.
Binary coded decimal (BCD)
BCD (the 8421 code) writes each decimal digit as its own 4-bit group, with weights 8, 4, 2, 1. It’s used where people meet hardware: keypads and digital displays.

Decimal → BCD: replace each decimal digit with 4 bits. 2469 = 0010\ 0100\ 0110\ 1001
BCD → decimal: split into 4-bit groups from the right and read each as a digit. 1000\ 0010\ 0010\ 0111\ 0110 = 82276
Only 0000–1001 (0–9) are used. The six codes 1010 to 1111 are invalid in BCD.



                  
                  BCD is not the same as binary. 35_{10} in binary is 100011, but in BCD it's 0011\ 0101.
                  
                

Try it: click the bits to build a number and see it in every form from this chapter. (The signed rows come back in Ch 5.)
Interactive number converter (open this page on the site to use it).
Key formulas
Waveforms
f = \frac{1}{T}, \qquad T = \frac{1}{f} \tag{1.1}
\text{Duty cycle} = \frac{t_W}{T} \times 100\% \tag{1.2}

f: frequency, in hertz (Hz)
T: period, the time for one full cycle, in seconds
t_W: pulse width, the time spent HIGH in each cycle

Reading a scope
\text{value} = (\text{number of divisions}) \times (\text{value per division}) \tag{1.3}

Use V/div for amplitudes and time/div for T and t_W.

Binary numbers
V = \sum_{i} b_i \, 2^i \tag{1.4}

V: the decimal value
b_i: the bit in position i (0 or 1). i = 0 is the LSB, and i < 0 are the bits right of the binary point.

\text{Largest } n\text{-bit number} = 2^n - 1, \qquad \text{number of combinations} = 2^n \tag{1.5}

n: number of bits

Complements (of an n-bit number P)
K_1 = (2^n - 1) - P, \qquad K_2 = 2^n - P = K_1 + 1 \tag{1.6}

K_1: 1’s complement of P (flip every bit)
K_2: 2’s complement of P (flip every bit, then add 1)

Examples
These follow the lecture examples, with different numbers.
Example 1: Reading a scope screen

Like the waveform lecture’s scope examples

A square wave on a scope is 4 divisions tall and one cycle spans 5 divisions, of which the HIGH part takes 2. The scope is set to 0.5 V/div and 20 µs/div. Find V_{pp}, T, f, t_W, and the duty cycle.

Amplitude: V_{pp} = 4 \times 0.5\ \text{V} = 2\ \text{V}
Period and frequency:
T = 5 \times 20\ \mu\text{s} = 100\ \mu\text{s}, \qquad f = \frac{1}{100\ \mu\text{s}} = 10\ \text{kHz}
Pulse width and duty cycle:
t_W = 2 \times 20\ \mu\text{s} = 40\ \mu\text{s}, \qquad \text{Duty} = \frac{40}{100} \times 100\% = 40\%



                  
                  With a 40% duty cycle this isn't a "square" wave, even though it looks like one. Square means 50%. 
                  
                

Example 2: Sketching a waveform on a scope

Like the waveform lecture’s sketching examples

Sketch a pulse waveform with f = 25\ \text{MHz}, V_{pp} = 2\ \text{V}, and a 60% duty cycle, on a scope set to 500 mV/div and 10 ns/div. How many divisions does each part take?

Period: T = \frac{1}{25\ \text{MHz}} = 40\ \text{ns}, so one cycle spans \frac{40\ \text{ns}}{10\ \text{ns/div}} = 4 divisions.
Amplitude: \frac{2\ \text{V}}{0.5\ \text{V/div}} = 4 divisions tall.
Pulse width: t_W = 0.60 \times 40\ \text{ns} = 24\ \text{ns}, so the HIGH part spans \frac{24}{10} = 2.4 divisions and the LOW part the other 1.6.

Check it with the oscilloscope above: set 25 MHz, 60%, 2 V, 500 mV/div, 10 ns/div.
Example 3: Range of an n-bit number

Like Lecture 1, counting examples

What range of numbers can 7 bits count? How many bits are needed to count up to 300?

7 bits: 2^7 - 1 = 127, so 0 to 127 (128 different values).
Up to 300: 8 bits only reach 2^8 - 1 = 255, which is too small. 9 bits reach 2^9 - 1 = 511, so 9 bits are needed.

Example 4: Binary to decimal

Like Lecture 1, Exercises 4–5

Convert 1011011_2 and 110.101_2 to decimal.

1011011_2: the 1s sit at weights 64, 16, 8, 2, 1.
64 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 91
110.101_2: the whole part is 4 + 2 = 6. The fraction has 1s at 2^{-1} and 2^{-3}:
6 + 0.5 + 0.125 = 6.625

Example 5: Decimal to binary

Like Lecture 1, Exercises 6–7

Convert 74 using sum of weights, and 173 using repeated division by 2.
Sum of weights: the largest weight that fits in 74 is 64, leaving 10 = 8 + 2.
74 = 64 + 8 + 2 = 2^6 + 2^3 + 2^1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 1001010_2
Repeated division:


















































DivisionQuotientRemainder173 \div 2861 (LSB)86 \div 243043 \div 221121 \div 210110 \div 2505 \div 2212 \div 2101 \div 201 (MSB)
Reading bottom to top: 173 = 10101101_2. Check: 128 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 173 ✓
Example 6: Binary addition and subtraction

Like Lecture 1, Example 11

Find (a) 1011 + 0110 and (b) 1100 - 0101.
(a) Work right to left, carrying when a column adds to 2 or more:

Column 0: 1 + 0 = 1
Column 1: 1 + 1 = 10, write 0, carry 1
Column 2: 0 + 1 + 1 = 10, write 0, carry 1
Column 3: 1 + 0 + 1 = 10, write 0, carry 1 into a new column

\begin{array}{r}
1011\\
+\;0110\\ \hline
10001
\end{array}
Check: 11 + 6 = 17 = 10001_2 ✓
(b) Borrow when subtracting 1 from 0:

Column 0: 0 - 1 needs a borrow. The column-1 bit is also 0, so the borrow comes from column 2, leaving column 2 = 0 and column 1 = 1. Column 0 becomes 10 - 1 = 1.
Column 1: 1 - 0 = 1
Column 2: 0 - 1 needs a borrow from column 3, giving 10 - 1 = 1 and column 3 = 0.
Column 3: 0 - 0 = 0

1100 - 0101 = 0111
Check: 12 - 5 = 7 ✓
Example 7: 1’s and 2’s complements

Like Lecture 1, Examples 12–15

Find the 1’s and 2’s complements of 10110100.

1’s complement: flip every bit: 01001011
2’s complement: add 1: 01001011 + 1 = 01001100
Check with the shortcut: copy up to the first 1 from the right (100), flip the rest (10110 \rightarrow 01001): 01001\,100 ✓

Example 8: Binary and hexadecimal

Like Lecture 1, Examples 16–17

Convert 1101011100101_2 to hex, and 3A7_{16} to binary.

Group by 4 from the right, padding the left group: 0001\ 1010\ 1110\ 0101 = 1AE5_{16}
Replace each hex digit: 3A7_{16} = 0011\ 1010\ 0111_2

Example 9: Hex and decimal

Like Lecture 1, Examples 18–19

Convert 2C7_{16} to decimal and 500_{10} to hex.


Hex → decimal: C = 12, so
2C7_{16} = 2 \times 256 + 12 \times 16 + 7 \times 1 = 512 + 192 + 7 = 711


Decimal → hex by dividing by 16:

500 \div 16 = 31 remainder 4
31 \div 16 = 1 remainder 15 = F
1 \div 16 = 0 remainder 1

Reading the remainders last to first: 500_{10} = 1F4_{16}. Check: 256 + 240 + 4 = 500 ✓


Example 10: BCD

Like Lecture 1, Examples 20–22

(a) Write 4073 in BCD. (b) Convert the BCD code 011010010010 to decimal. (c) Is 0101\ 1011 a valid BCD number?

(a) One 4-bit group per digit: 4073 = 0100\ 0000\ 0111\ 0011
(b) Group from the right: 0110\ 1001\ 0010 = 692
(c) No. 1011 is 11, which isn’t a decimal digit, so it’s one of the six invalid codes.

Common mistakes

Reading the remainders of repeated division top to bottom. The first remainder is the LSB.
Grouping binary into 4s for hex from the left. Always group from the right (the binary point) and pad on the left.
Mixing up BCD and binary: BCD encodes each decimal digit separately.
Forgetting the +1 for the 2’s complement, or doing the shortcut from the wrong end (it starts at the LSB).
Calling any 0/1 waveform a “square wave”. It’s only square at a 50% duty cycle.
Using the total number of scope divisions instead of the number for one cycle when finding T.

courses/coe-328/ch02-intro-to-logic-circ.title: Ch 2: Introduction to Logic Circuits
courses/coe-328/ch02-intro-to-logic-circ.content:
Overview


                  
                  Readings Brown & Vranesic §2.1–2.10 · Lectures 2–4 (Logic Gates, Boolean Algebra, NAND and NOR Logic Networks) · weeks 2–4
                  
                

Logic gates are the building blocks of every digital circuit, and Boolean algebra is the math that describes them. This chapter covers each gate, how to read a circuit as a Boolean expression (and back), the rules for simplifying expressions, the two standard forms (SOP and POS), how to build anything out of just NAND or just NOR gates, and the basic design process: specification → truth table → expression → circuit.
Notes
The basic gates
Every gate has one output and (except NOT) two or more inputs. A gate with n inputs has 2^n input combinations, so its truth table has 2^n rows.













































GateExpressionOutput is 1 when…NOT (inverter)X = \overline{A}the input is 0 (it flips the input)ANDX = ABall inputs are 1ORX = A + Bat least one input is 1NANDX = \overline{AB}at least one input is 0 (AND, then NOT)NORX = \overline{A + B}all inputs are 0 (OR, then NOT)XORX = A \oplus B = A\overline{B} + \overline{A}Bthe inputs are differentXNORX = \overline{A \oplus B} = AB + \overline{A}\,\overline{B}the inputs are the same























































ABANDORNANDNORXORXNOR00001101010110101001101011110001
Try it: pick a gate, then click the inputs (on the diagram or the buttons) to flip them. The matching row of the truth table lights up.
Interactive logic gates (open this page on the site to use it).
Notes on each gate

NOT: also called complementation. The small circle (bubble) on its output is the negation indicator: anywhere a bubble appears, the signal is inverted.
AND: called logical multiplication (A \cdot B or just AB). Useful as an enable gate: with one input at 1 the other passes through, with one input at 0 the output is stuck at 0.
OR: called logical addition. Unlike binary addition there’s no carry: 1 + 1 = 1.
NAND / NOR: the universal gates. Either one alone can build NOT, AND, and OR, so it can build any circuit (see NAND and NOR logic).
XOR: exactly two inputs. Its output is the sum bit of adding two bits (1 + 1 = 10, sum 0), so it’s a 1-bit modulo-2 adder, and it detects when two signals disagree.
XNOR: the opposite of XOR, so it’s a 1-bit equality detector.

Active-HIGH and active-LOW
The bubble also tells you what level is active (asserted):

No bubble: the input/output is active-HIGH: it “does its thing” when it’s 1.
Bubble: the input/output is active-LOW: it “does its thing” when it’s 0.

This leads to a second way to read NAND and NOR gates:

Figure 2.1: The NAND gate is also a negative-OR gate, and the NOR gate is also a negative-AND gate.

NAND as negative-OR: output is 1 when A is 0 OR B is 0. Use this view when you’re detecting “any input LOW”.
NOR as negative-AND: output is 1 when A is 0 AND B is 0. Use this view when you’re detecting “all inputs LOW”.

Both are the same physical gate; DeMorgan’s theorems (DeMorgan’s theorems) prove the two symbols are equal.
Timing diagrams
In real circuits the inputs are waveforms, not fixed levels. A timing diagram lines up the waveforms on the same time axis. To find a gate’s output waveform:

Draw a vertical line at every edge of every input.
In each interval between lines, the inputs are constant, so apply the truth table.
Draw the output level for each interval.

Try it: click any time slot of A or B to flip it and watch the output. Switch gates with the buttons.
Interactive timing diagram (open this page on the site to use it).
Boolean algebra basics

A variable (A, B, …) is 0 or 1. Its complement \overline{A} (“not A”, “A bar”, or A') is the opposite value. A variable or its complement is a literal.
A sum term is literals ORed together (A + \overline{B} + C). It’s 0 only when every literal is 0.
A product term is literals ANDed together (A\overline{B}C). It’s 1 only when every literal is 1.

Laws

























LawAddition (OR)Multiplication (AND)CommutativeA + B = B + AAB = BAAssociativeA + (B + C) = (A + B) + CA(BC) = (AB)CDistributiveA(B + C) = AB + AC
The 12 rules






































































#RuleWhy1A + 0 = AOR with 0 passes A through2A + 1 = 1OR with 1 is always 13A \cdot 0 = 0AND with 0 is always 04A \cdot 1 = AAND with 1 passes A through5A + A = A0 + 0 = 0, 1 + 1 = 16A + \overline{A} = 1one of them is always 17A \cdot A = A0 \cdot 0 = 0, 1 \cdot 1 = 18A \cdot \overline{A} = 0one of them is always 09\overline{\overline{A}} = Ainverting twice gets you back10A + AB = AA(1 + B) = A \cdot 111A + \overline{A}B = A + Bproved below12(A + B)(A + C) = A + BCproved below
Rules 1–9 come straight from the gate truth tables. Rules 10–12 are derived from them:
\begin{aligned}
A + \overline{A}B &= (A + AB) + \overline{A}B &&\text{Rule 10} \\
&= AA + AB + A\overline{A} + \overline{A}B &&\text{Rules 7, 8} \\
&= (A + \overline{A})(A + B) &&\text{factor} \\
&= A + B &&\text{Rules 6, 4}
\end{aligned}
\begin{aligned}
(A + B)(A + C) &= AA + AC + AB + BC &&\text{distribute} \\
&= A(1 + C + B) + BC &&\text{Rule 7, factor} \\
&= A + BC &&\text{Rules 2, 4}
\end{aligned}


                  
                  Rule 12 is the distributive law "the other way": OR distributes over AND too, which ordinary algebra doesn't allow. 
                  
                

DeMorgan’s theorems
\overline{XY} = \overline{X} + \overline{Y} \qquad\qquad \overline{X + Y} = \overline{X}\,\overline{Y}
In words: break the bar, change the sign. Splitting a bar over a product turns the AND into an OR, and splitting a bar over a sum turns the OR into an AND. They work for any number of variables:
\overline{WXYZ} = \overline{W} + \overline{X} + \overline{Y} + \overline{Z} \qquad \overline{W + X + Y + Z} = \overline{W}\,\overline{X}\,\overline{Y}\,\overline{Z}
Procedure for a big expression (e.g. \overline{\overline{A + B\overline{C}} + D(\overline{E + \overline{F}})}):

Treat each term under the longest bar as a single variable (X = \overline{A + B\overline{C}}, Y = D(\overline{E + \overline{F}})).
Apply DeMorgan to the longest bar: \overline{X + Y} = \overline{X}\,\overline{Y}.
Cancel any double bars (Rule 9).
Repeat on the remaining bars until every bar sits over a single variable.

\overline{\overline{A + B\overline{C}} + D(\overline{E + \overline{F}})} = (A + B\overline{C})(\overline{D} + E + \overline{F})
From circuit to expression to truth table
Circuit → expression: start at the inputs and write the expression at each gate output, working toward the final output.
Expression → truth table:

List all 2^n input combinations (count in binary).
Find which combinations make the expression 1 (or work out every intermediate column).
Fill in the output column.

For example, A(B + CD) is 1 only when A = 1 and B + CD = 1, i.e. when A = 1, B = 1 (any C, D), or A = 1, C = 1, D = 1 (any B).
Simplifying with Boolean algebra
A simpler expression means fewer gates for the same function: fewer chips, less power, and less material to make them. The usual moves:

Factor out a common literal: AB + A\overline{B} = A(B + \overline{B}) = A
Absorb with Rule 10: A + AB = A
Remove a complemented literal with Rule 11: A + \overline{A}B = A + B
Duplicate a term you need twice (Rule 5: X = X + X)



                  
                  Lecture example: AB + A(B + C) + B(B + C)
                  
                

\begin{aligned}
&= AB + AB + AC + BB + BC &&\text{distribute} \\
&= AB + AC + B + BC &&\text{Rules 5, 7} \\
&= AB + AC + B &&\text{Rule 10 } (B + BC = B) \\
&= B + AC &&\text{Rule 10 } (B + AB = B)
\end{aligned}
Five gates become two (one AND, one OR).


Algebra works, but it’s easy to miss a step. Ch 4 gives a systematic method (the Karnaugh map).
Standard forms: SOP and POS
Any expression can be rewritten in one of two standard forms:




















FormLooks likeBuilt withSum of products (SOP)AB + \overline{A}C + B\overline{C}DAND gates feeding one OR gate (AND-OR)Product of sums (POS)(A + B)(\overline{A} + C)(B + \overline{C} + D)OR gates feeding one AND gate (OR-AND)
In both forms a bar can only cover one variable: \overline{A}\,\overline{B} is allowed, \overline{AB} is not.

To get SOP from a general expression, distribute: A(B + CD) = AB + ACD.
The domain is the set of all variables in the expression. A standard (canonical) SOP or POS has every variable of the domain in every term.

Converting to standard SOP: multiply each product term by (X + \overline{X}) for each missing variable X (that’s multiplying by 1), and expand. Each missing variable doubles the number of terms.
A\overline{B} \;\text{(domain } A, B, C) = A\overline{B}(C + \overline{C}) = A\overline{B}C + A\overline{B}\,\overline{C}
Converting to standard POS: add X\overline{X} for each missing variable (that’s adding 0), then use Rule 12 to split.
A + \overline{B} = A + \overline{B} + C\overline{C} = (A + \overline{B} + C)(A + \overline{B} + \overline{C})
Minterms and maxterms
Each row of a truth table has one standard product term that’s 1 only on that row, and one standard sum term that’s 0 only on that row:

Minterm m_i: product term that’s 1 only on row i. A 1 in the row becomes the variable, a 0 becomes its complement.
Maxterm M_i: sum term that’s 0 only on row i. A 0 in the row becomes the variable, a 1 becomes its complement.




























































Row iA\,B\,CMinterm m_iMaxterm M_i00 0 0\overline{A}\,\overline{B}\,\overline{C}A + B + C10 0 1\overline{A}\,\overline{B}CA + B + \overline{C}20 1 0\overline{A}B\overline{C}A + \overline{B} + C30 1 1\overline{A}BCA + \overline{B} + \overline{C}41 0 0A\overline{B}\,\overline{C}\overline{A} + B + C51 0 1A\overline{B}C\overline{A} + B + \overline{C}61 1 0AB\overline{C}\overline{A} + \overline{B} + C71 1 1ABC\overline{A} + \overline{B} + \overline{C}
So from any truth table:

Standard SOP = OR of the minterms for the rows where the output is 1. Shorthand: f = \sum m(\ldots).
Standard POS = AND of the maxterms for the rows where the output is 0. Shorthand: f = \prod M(\ldots).

The two lists are complements of each other: every row number is in exactly one of them.


                  
                  The lecture slides (Floyd) describe this as the "binary value" of a term: A\overline{B}C\overline{D} has binary value 1010 because that's the one input that makes it 1, and A + \overline{B} + C + \overline{D} has binary value 0101 because that's the one input that makes it 0. Same idea as m_{10} and M_5.
                  
                

NAND and NOR logic
NAND and NOR are universal: each one alone can make every other gate.



































To getWith NAND onlyWith NOR onlyNOTtie the inputs together: \overline{AA} = \overline{A}tie the inputs together: \overline{A + A} = \overline{A}ANDNAND, then a NAND inverterinvert both inputs, then NOR: \overline{\overline{A} + \overline{B}} = ABORinvert both inputs, then NAND: \overline{\overline{A}\,\overline{B}} = A + BNOR, then a NOR inverterNOROR (above), then a NAND inverter—NAND—AND (above), then a NOR inverter
Two-level NAND = SOP. An AND-OR circuit becomes NAND-NAND just by swapping every gate for a NAND, because the bubbles cancel in pairs:
X = \overline{\overline{AB}\;\overline{CD}} = \overline{\overline{AB}} + \overline{\overline{CD}} = AB + CD
Two-level NOR = POS. In the same way, an OR-AND circuit becomes NOR-NOR:
X = \overline{\overline{A + B} + \overline{C + D}} = (A + B)(C + D)
Dual symbols. To read a NAND or NOR circuit quickly, redraw it so every connection is bubble-to-bubble or plain-to-plain. Bubbles that meet cancel (they’re a double inversion), so you can read the gates as plain AND/OR:

In NAND logic, draw gates as NAND and negative-OR symbols, alternating by level, with the output gate as a negative-OR.
In NOR logic, draw gates as NOR and negative-AND symbols, with the output gate as a negative-AND.
If a bubble meets a plain input, that variable picks up a bar.

Design process
The textbook’s three steps (§2.8):

Specify exactly what the circuit should do.
Synthesize: specification → truth table → Boolean expression → circuit.
Test: apply every input combination and check the output.

Design example: three-way light control. A room has three doors, each with a switch (x_1, x_2, x_3) for the same light f. Flipping any one switch must change the light. Start with the light off when all switches are open (000). Then flipping one switch turns it on, flipping a second turns it off, and so on: the light is on when an odd number of switches are closed.



























x_1\,x_2\,x_3000001010011100101110111f01101001
f = \sum m(1, 2, 4, 7) = \overline{x_1}\,\overline{x_2}\,x_3 + \overline{x_1}\,x_2\,\overline{x_3} + x_1\,\overline{x_2}\,\overline{x_3} + x_1 x_2 x_3
f = \prod M(0, 3, 5, 6) = (x_1 + x_2 + x_3)(x_1 + \overline{x_2} + \overline{x_3})(\overline{x_1} + x_2 + \overline{x_3})(\overline{x_1} + \overline{x_2} + x_3)
Both are correct implementations (NOT → AND → OR for SOP, NOT → OR → AND for POS). This function is also just f = x_1 \oplus x_2 \oplus x_3.
Design example: 2-to-1 multiplexer. A multiplexer (MUX) is a data selector: a select input s picks which data input reaches the output. If s = 0 then f = x_1; if s = 1 then f = x_2.



























s\,x_1\,x_2000001010011100101110111f00110101
\begin{aligned}
f &= \overline{s}\,x_1\overline{x_2} + \overline{s}\,x_1 x_2 + s\,\overline{x_1}\,x_2 + s\,x_1 x_2 \\
&= \overline{s}\,x_1(\overline{x_2} + x_2) + s\,x_2(\overline{x_1} + x_1) \\
&= \overline{s}\,x_1 + s\,x_2
\end{aligned}
Multiplexers with more inputs are in Ch 6.
Key formulas
Number of input combinations
N = 2^n \tag{2.1}

N: rows in the truth table
n: number of input variables

XOR and XNOR
A \oplus B = A\overline{B} + \overline{A}B, \qquad \overline{A \oplus B} = AB + \overline{A}\,\overline{B} \tag{2.2}
Useful rules
A + AB = A, \qquad A + \overline{A}B = A + B, \qquad (A + B)(A + C) = A + BC \tag{2.3}
DeMorgan’s theorems
\overline{XY} = \overline{X} + \overline{Y}, \qquad \overline{X + Y} = \overline{X}\,\overline{Y} \tag{2.4}

X, Y: any variables or sub-expressions

Standard forms from a truth table
f = \sum m(\text{rows where } f = 1) = \prod M(\text{rows where } f = 0) \tag{2.5}

m_i: minterm, the product term that’s 1 only on row i
M_i: maxterm, the sum term that’s 0 only on row i

2-to-1 multiplexer
f = \overline{s}\,x_1 + s\,x_2 \tag{2.6}

s: select input
x_1: data input passed through when s = 0
x_2: data input passed through when s = 1

Examples
These follow the lecture examples, with different numbers and circuits.
Example 1: Truth table for a multi-input gate

Like Lecture 2, Example 2

(a) Write the truth table for a 3-input NOR gate. (b) How many input combinations does a 5-input NAND gate have?
(a) A NOR output is 1 only when all inputs are 0, so only the first row is 1:



























A\,B\,C000001010011100101110111X10000000
(b) N = 2^5 = 32 combinations.
Example 2: Choosing a gate from active-LOW sensors

Like Lecture 2, Examples 10–11 and 14–15

A press has two safety guards. Each guard’s sensor outputs LOW when the guard is closed and HIGH when it’s open. (a) Pick one gate whose output is HIGH (enabling the press) only when both guards are closed. (b) Pick one gate whose output is HIGH (a warning light) when at least one guard is open.
(a) “Both inputs LOW → output HIGH” is a negative-AND, which is a NOR gate: X = \overline{A + B} = \overline{A}\,\overline{B}.
(b) “At least one input HIGH → output HIGH” is a plain OR gate: X = A + B.


                  
                  When a question describes inputs that are active-LOW, think in terms of negative-OR (NAND) and negative-AND (NOR). 
                  
                

Example 3: DeMorgan with several variables

Like Lecture 3, Examples 3–5

Apply DeMorgan’s theorems to (a) \overline{(A + \overline{B})C} and (b) \overline{A\overline{B}C + \overline{D}E}.
(a) Treat A + \overline{B} as one variable. The bar is over a product, so it becomes a sum:
\overline{(A + \overline{B})C} = \overline{A + \overline{B}} + \overline{C} = \overline{A}B + \overline{C}
(b) The bar is over a sum, so it becomes a product of the two complemented terms, then each of those is split:
\overline{A\overline{B}C + \overline{D}E} = (\overline{A\overline{B}C})(\overline{\overline{D}E}) = (\overline{A} + B + \overline{C})(D + \overline{E})
Example 4: Expression with nested bars

Like Lecture 3, “Applying DeMorgan’s Theorems”

Simplify \overline{(\overline{A} + B)\,\overline{CD}} so that bars only sit over single variables.

Longest bar first. It covers a product of two terms, so it becomes a sum:
\overline{(\overline{A} + B)\,\overline{CD}} = \overline{\overline{A} + B} + \overline{\overline{CD}}
Second term: double bar cancels, \overline{\overline{CD}} = CD.
First term: DeMorgan again, \overline{\overline{A} + B} = A\overline{B}.

\Rightarrow\quad A\overline{B} + CD
Example 5: From a circuit to a truth table

Like Lecture 3, “Boolean Expression for a Logic Circuit”

Find the expression and the truth table for the circuit in Figure 2.2.

Figure 2.2: Circuit for Example 5.

G1 is an OR: A + B. G2 is a NOT: \overline{C}.
G3 ANDs them: X = (A + B)\,\overline{C}
Truth table: X = 1 needs \overline{C} = 1 (so C = 0) and A + B = 1 (so A or B is 1).




























A\,B\,C000001010011100101110111X00101010
Example 6: Simplifying with Boolean algebra

Like Lecture 3, Examples 7–8

Simplify (a) AB + A\overline{B} + \overline{A}B and (b) ABC + A\overline{B}(\overline{A} + C).
(a)
\begin{aligned}
AB + A\overline{B} + \overline{A}B &= A(B + \overline{B}) + \overline{A}B &&\text{factor} \\
&= A + \overline{A}B &&\text{Rules 6, 4} \\
&= A + B &&\text{Rule 11}
\end{aligned}
(b)
\begin{aligned}
ABC + A\overline{B}(\overline{A} + C) &= ABC + A\overline{A}\,\overline{B} + A\overline{B}C &&\text{distribute} \\
&= ABC + A\overline{B}C &&\text{Rule 8: } A\overline{A} = 0 \\
&= AC(B + \overline{B}) = AC &&\text{factor, Rule 6}
\end{aligned}
Example 7: Nonstandard SOP to standard SOP

Like Lecture 3, Examples 10–11 and 14

Convert X = A\overline{B} + B\overline{C} (domain A, B, C) to standard SOP, then write its truth table.

Each term is missing one variable, so multiply by (\text{missing} + \overline{\text{missing}}):
A\overline{B}(C + \overline{C}) + B\overline{C}(A + \overline{A}) = A\overline{B}C + A\overline{B}\,\overline{C} + AB\overline{C} + \overline{A}B\overline{C}
Binary value of each term (the input that makes it 1): 101, 100, 110, 010, i.e. rows 5, 4, 6, 2.
X = \sum m(2, 4, 5, 6)
Truth table: 1 on those rows, 0 everywhere else.




























A\,B\,C000001010011100101110111X00101110
Example 8: Nonstandard POS to standard POS

Like Lecture 3, Examples 12–13 and 15

Convert X = (A + \overline{B})(B + C) to standard POS and find the rows where it’s 0.

Add C\overline{C} to the first term and A\overline{A} to the second, then split with Rule 12:
\begin{aligned}
A + \overline{B} &= (A + \overline{B} + C)(A + \overline{B} + \overline{C}) \\
B + C &= (A + B + C)(\overline{A} + B + C)
\end{aligned}

Binary value of each sum term (the input that makes it 0): 010, 011, 000, 100.
X = (A + B + C)(A + \overline{B} + C)(A + \overline{B} + \overline{C})(\overline{A} + B + C) = \prod M(0, 2, 3, 4)

So X = 0 on rows 0, 2, 3, 4 and X = 1 on rows 1, 5, 6, 7.
Example 9: Truth table to SOP and POS

Like Lecture 3, Example 16

Write the standard SOP and POS for this truth table.



























A\,B\,C000001010011100101110111X01010011
SOP from the 1s (rows 1, 3, 6, 7). A 0 in the row becomes a complemented variable:
X = \overline{A}\,\overline{B}C + \overline{A}BC + AB\overline{C} + ABC = \sum m(1, 3, 6, 7)
POS from the 0s (rows 0, 2, 4, 5). A 1 in the row becomes a complemented variable:
X = (A + B + C)(A + \overline{B} + C)(\overline{A} + B + C)(\overline{A} + B + \overline{C}) = \prod M(0, 2, 4, 5)


                  
                  Both describe the same function. The SOP simplifies to \overline{A}C + AB; Ch 4 shows how to see that at a glance.
                  
                

Example 10: NAND logic with dual symbols

Like Lecture 4, Examples 7–8

Implement X = A\overline{B} + CD using only NAND gates, drawn with dual symbols.

Start from AND-OR: two ANDs (A\overline{B} and CD) feeding an OR.
Swap every gate for a NAND. The output gate is drawn as a negative-OR so its input bubbles meet the bubbles of G2 and G3 and cancel.
\overline{B} needs its own inverter: a NAND with its inputs tied together (G4).


Figure 2.3: NAND-only implementation of X = A\overline{B} + CD.
Check:
X = \overline{\overline{A\overline{B}}\;\overline{CD}} = \overline{\overline{A\overline{B}}} + \overline{\overline{CD}} = A\overline{B} + CD \;✓
Example 11: NOR logic

Like Lecture 4, Examples 9–10

Implement X = (A + B)(\overline{C} + D) using only NOR gates.

Start from OR-AND: ORs for A + B and \overline{C} + D, then an AND.
Swap every gate for a NOR. G2 = NOR(A, B), G3 = NOR(\overline{C}, D), and the output G1 = NOR, drawn as a negative-AND so the bubbles cancel.
\overline{C} comes from a NOR with its inputs tied together.

Check:
X = \overline{\overline{A + B} + \overline{\overline{C} + D}} = \overline{\overline{A + B}}\;\overline{\overline{\overline{C} + D}} = (A + B)(\overline{C} + D) \;✓
Example 12: Output waveform of a circuit

Like Lecture 4, “Pulse Waveform Operation” and Examples 11–12

The circuit X = \overline{A(B + C)} is an OR gate (Y = B + C) feeding a NAND with A. The inputs over eight equal time intervals are below. Find Y and X.


















































































Interval12345678A01111011B00100110C10010010Y = B + C10110110AY00110010X = \overline{AY}11001101


                  
                  Find the intermediate waveforms first (here Y), one gate at a time. Trying to jump straight to X is where mistakes happen.
                  
                

Example 13: Design a majority circuit

Like the §2.8 design examples

Design a circuit for three judges (A, B, C) that outputs f = 1 when at least two judges vote yes (1). Simplify it.

Truth table: f = 1 on rows with two or three 1s: 011, 101, 110, 111.
Standard SOP:
f = \sum m(3, 5, 6, 7) = \overline{A}BC + A\overline{B}C + AB\overline{C} + ABC
Simplify. Use Rule 5 to copy ABC twice, so it can pair with each of the others:
\begin{aligned}
f &= (\overline{A}BC + ABC) + (A\overline{B}C + ABC) + (AB\overline{C} + ABC) \\
&= BC(\overline{A} + A) + AC(\overline{B} + B) + AB(\overline{C} + C) \\
&= AB + AC + BC
\end{aligned}

Circuit: three 2-input ANDs feeding a 3-input OR (or five NAND gates, by Example 10’s method).

Common mistakes

Treating Boolean 1 + 1 like binary: in Boolean algebra (OR), 1 + 1 = 1, not 10.
Splitting a bar without changing the operation: \overline{AB} \neq \overline{A}\,\overline{B}. It’s \overline{A} + \overline{B}.
Dropping the parentheses when applying DeMorgan: \overline{A + BC} = \overline{A}\,(\overline{B} + \overline{C}), not \overline{A}\,\overline{B} + \overline{C}.
Mixing up the two lists: SOP comes from the 1s (0 → complemented), POS comes from the 0s (1 → complemented).
Giving an XOR gate more than two inputs. A multi-input “XOR” is a chain of 2-input XORs (it’s 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1).
In NAND/NOR diagrams, connecting a bubble output to a plain input and forgetting that variable now has a bar.

courses/coe-328/ch03-implementation-tech.title: Ch 3: Implementation Technology
courses/coe-328/ch03-implementation-tech.content:
Overview


                  
                  Readings Brown & Vranesic §3.1–3.3, 3.5–3.6, 3.8.8, 3.9 · Lecture 5 · week 5
                  
                

How logic gates are actually built. Transistors act as voltage-controlled switches: NMOS pulls an output down to ground and PMOS pulls it up to V_{DD}. Arranging them in series and parallel gives NAND, NOR, and more complex gates, and CMOS pairs the two types so no current flows when the gate is idle. The second half covers how gates are packaged and sold: 7400-series chips, then programmable devices (PLAs, CPLDs, FPGAs), plus fan-out and transmission gates.
Notes
Logic values as voltages
Logic 0 and 1 are voltage ranges, with an undefined region in between that signals only pass through during a transition.





















Range (V_{DD} = 5\ \text{V})Meaning (positive logic)2\ \text{V} to V_{DD}Logic 1 (HIGH)0.8\ \text{V} to 2\ \text{V}UndefinedV_{SS} = 0\ \text{V} to 0.8\ \text{V}Logic 0 (LOW)

V_{SS} is ground (0 V). V_{DD} is the positive supply.
The exact thresholds depend on the technology.

Transistors as switches
For logic analysis, a MOSFET is treated as an ideal switch controlled by its gate voltage. There are two types, and they’re opposite:























TransistorGate HIGH (1)Gate LOW (0)Used to…NMOSON (closed)OFF (open)pull down: connect the output to GNDPMOS (bubble on its gate)OFF (open)ON (closed)pull up: connect the output to V_{DD}


                  
                  "Pull down" doesn't mean the NMOS makes 0 V. It means that when it's ON, it gives the output a low-resistance path to ground. Same for PMOS and V_{DD}.
                  
                

NMOS logic gates
An NMOS gate is a pull-down network of NMOS transistors plus a pull-up resistor (or pull-up device) to V_{DD}. When the pull-down network conducts, the output is LOW; otherwise the resistor holds it HIGH.









































GateNMOS arrangementOutput 0 when…ResultNOTOne NMOSx = 1f = \overline{x}NANDTwo NMOS in seriesA = 1 and B = 1f = \overline{AB}NORTwo NMOS in parallelA = 1 or B = 1f = \overline{A + B}ANDNAND followed by NOT—f = ABORNOR followed by NOT—f = A + B

Series = AND (current flows only if every switch is closed).
Parallel = OR (current flows if any switch is closed).
The output is always the complement of the pull-down condition, which is why NAND and NOR are the natural gates and AND/OR need an extra inverter.

The drawback: whenever the output is LOW, current flows from V_{DD} through the resistor and the NMOS network to ground, wasting power.
CMOS logic gates
CMOS (complementary MOS) replaces the resistor with a pull-up network (PUN) of PMOS transistors. The PUN and the pull-down network (PDN) of NMOS transistors are designed so that for every input, exactly one of them conducts:

PUN conducts → output connected to V_{DD} → f = 1
PDN conducts → output connected to GND → f = 0

The duality rule: the PUN and PDN are duals of each other. Wherever the PDN has NMOS in series, the PUN has PMOS in parallel, and vice versa.









































GatePUN (PMOS)PDN (NMOS)TransistorsNOT1 PMOS1 NMOS2NANDparallelseries4NORseriesparallel4ANDNAND + NOTNAND + NOT6ORNOR + NOTNOR + NOT6
Why the CMOS NAND looks like that. f = \overline{AB} is 1 when A = 0 or B = 0. PMOS turns on with a 0, and “or” means parallel, so the PUN is two PMOS in parallel. f is 0 when A = 1 and B = 1. NMOS turns on with a 1, and “and” means series, so the PDN is two NMOS in series.


















































ABPMOS APMOS BNMOS ANMOS Bf00ONONOFFOFF101ONOFFOFFON110OFFONONOFF111OFFOFFONON0
The big advantage: in any steady state one network is OFF, so there’s no direct path from V_{DD} to GND and essentially no static current. That’s the main reason CMOS became the dominant logic technology.
Try it: pick a gate and flip the inputs. ON transistors are drawn solid, OFF ones faded, and the network that’s connected to the output is highlighted.
Interactive CMOS gates (open this page on the site to use it).
Designing complex CMOS gates
You don’t have to build everything out of NAND/NOR/NOT. Any function of the form f = \overline{(\ldots)} can be built directly as one PUN + PDN:

Write the condition for f = 1 in terms of complemented inputs → build the PUN (PMOS turn on for 0s). AND → series, OR → parallel.
Write the condition for f = 0, i.e. \overline{f}, in terms of uncomplemented inputs → build the PDN (NMOS turn on for 1s). AND → series, OR → parallel.
Check that the PDN is the dual of the PUN (series ↔ parallel).
Connect the PUN to V_{DD}, the PDN to GND, and join them at the output.

Textbook Example 3.1: f = \overline{x_1} + \overline{x_2}\,\overline{x_3}

PUN: f = 1 when x_1 = 0 OR (x_2 = 0 AND x_3 = 0) → PMOS x_1 in parallel with a series pair x_2, x_3.
PDN: \overline{f} = x_1(x_2 + x_3) → NMOS x_1 in series with a parallel pair x_2, x_3.

Textbook Example 3.2: f = \overline{x_1} + (\overline{x_2} + \overline{x_3})\,\overline{x_4}

PUN: x_1 in parallel with [(x_2 ∥ x_3) in series with x_4].
PDN: \overline{f} = x_1(x_2 x_3 + x_4) → x_1 in series with [(x_2 series x_3) ∥ x_4].

This uses fewer transistors than building each AND and OR as a separate gate.
Speed of logic gates
The ideal-switch model explains what a gate does, not how fast. In a real circuit:

An ON transistor has some resistance.
The wires and the transistors’ own structure have capacitance.
Changing the output means charging or discharging that capacitance through that resistance, which takes time: the propagation delay.

Detailed timing analysis isn’t covered in this course, but keep the idea: more load (more capacitance) → slower gate.
Fan-in and fan-out (§3.8.8)

Fan-in: the number of inputs a gate has.
Fan-out: the number of other gate inputs that one gate output drives. Each one adds capacitance C, so driving n gates is like driving C_n = n \cdot C. The propagation delay increases in direct proportion to n.

Transmission gates (§3.9)
A transmission gate is an NMOS and a PMOS in parallel, driven by complementary control signals s and \overline{s}. It’s a switch that passes 0s and 1s equally well (NMOS passes 0s well, PMOS passes 1s well):

s = 1 (\overline{s} = 0): both transistors ON, so f = x.
s = 0: both OFF, so the output is disconnected.

Uses:

XOR gate: built from gates, x_1 \oplus x_2 = x_1\overline{x_2} + \overline{x_1}x_2 takes 22 transistors in CMOS (two ANDs and an OR at 6 each, two NOTs at 2 each). With two transmission gates and two inverters it takes 8: when x_1 = 0 one transmission gate passes x_2, and when x_1 = 1 the other passes \overline{x_2}.
2-to-1 multiplexer: two transmission gates controlled by s and \overline{s}. s = 0 passes x_1, s = 1 passes x_2.

Standard chips: the 7400 series (§3.5)
Before programmable logic, circuits were built by wiring together standard chips, each with a few fixed gates.

Packaged in a dual-inline package (DIP): two rows of pins (leads), with one pin for V_{DD}, one for GND, and the rest wired to the gates inside.
The part number says what’s inside:


























ChipContents7404Six NOT gates7408Four 2-input AND gates7432Four 2-input OR gates74244Eight tri-state buffers (20-pin package)

The suffix letters give the technology, not the function: 74LS00 is TTL (transistor-transistor logic), 74HC00 is CMOS. Both are quad 2-input NANDs.
Many manufacturers make the same parts, which keeps them cheap and available.
Packages shrank over time: the SOIC (small-outline IC) is the same idea as a DIP but much smaller.

Buffers. A buffer outputs the same logic value it’s given (Y = A). It doesn’t change the logic; it drives the signal more strongly (more current), which helps speed when there’s a big load. A tri-state buffer adds an enable input: when enabled, Y = A; when disabled, the output is disconnected (high impedance). Buffers are one of the main uses of standard chips today.
Integration scale






























ScaleSizeNotesSSI (small)A few gatesEarly chips, e.g. 7400 seriesMSI (medium)About 10–100 gatesMore circuitry per chipLSI (large)Beyond MSIVLSI (very large)Thousands to billions of transistorsModern chips
These labels are less useful now that chips are so large.
Programmable logic devices (§3.6)
Standard chips have fixed functions and few gates each, so a big circuit needs many chips, many wires, and a lot of board space. A programmable logic device (PLD) is one general-purpose chip whose internal connections the designer configures:
\text{PLD} = \text{logic elements} + \text{programmable switches}
PLA (programmable logic array): implements functions in SOP form.

Input buffers provide every input in true and complemented form (x_i and \overline{x_i}).
A programmable AND plane forms product terms P_1, P_2, \ldots from any of those literals.
A programmable OR plane sums any of the product terms to make each output f_1, f_2, \ldots

A product term can be shared by several outputs, which saves AND gates.
CPLD (complex PLD): several PAL/PLA-like blocks on one chip, with a programmable interconnect between them.

Programmed in-system (ISP) through a JTAG port (an IEEE standard using 4 wires), since big chips are too fragile for programming sockets.
Nonvolatile: keeps its configuration with the power off.

FPGA (field-programmable gate array): much larger (up to millions of equivalent gates).

Made of logic blocks, I/O blocks, and routing channels with programmable switches.
No AND/OR planes. Each logic block uses a lookup table (LUT) instead, usually with 4 or 5 inputs, and often a flip-flop for sequential logic.
Volatile: the configuration is lost at power-off and must be reloaded every power-up, usually from a PROM on the board.
This course’s labs use an FPGA board.

How a LUT works: a LUT is a tiny memory that stores a truth table. A 2-input LUT has 2^2 = 4 storage cells, one per row. The inputs x_1, x_2 drive the select lines of a tree of multiplexers that pick the cell for the current row. So any function of 2 variables fits in a 2-input LUT; you only change the stored bits.
Key formulas
CMOS duality
\text{PDN series} \;\leftrightarrow\; \text{PUN parallel}, \qquad \text{PDN parallel} \;\leftrightarrow\; \text{PUN series} \tag{3.1}
PDN condition
\text{PDN conducts} \iff \overline{f} = 1 \tag{3.2}

The PDN realizes \overline{f} with uncomplemented inputs (NMOS on for 1).
The PUN realizes f with complemented inputs (PMOS on for 0).

Fan-out load
C_n = n \cdot C \tag{3.3}

C_n: total load capacitance on the driving gate’s output
n: fan-out, the number of gate inputs being driven
C: input capacitance of one driven gate

LUT size
\text{storage cells} = 2^k \tag{3.4}

k: number of LUT inputs

Examples
These follow the lecture’s examples and check-your-understanding questions, with different functions.
Example 1: Reading an NMOS circuit

Like the lecture’s NMOS NAND/NOR slides

An NMOS gate has a pull-up resistor to V_{DD}. Its pull-down network is NMOS A in series with NMOS B, and that pair is in parallel with NMOS C. Find f.

When does the PDN conduct? Series = AND, parallel = OR, so it conducts when AB + C = 1.
The output is LOW whenever the PDN conducts, so it’s the complement:
f = \overline{AB + C}

Example 2: Designing a complex CMOS gate

Like textbook Examples 3.1–3.2

Design a CMOS circuit for f = \overline{AB + C} and count its transistors.

PDN realizes \overline{f} = AB + C: NMOS A and B in series, that pair in parallel with NMOS C.
PUN is the dual: PMOS A and B in parallel, that pair in series with PMOS C.
Check the PUN directly: by DeMorgan, f = \overline{AB}\,\overline{C} = (\overline{A} + \overline{B})\,\overline{C}. That’s (A = 0 or B = 0) and C = 0: PMOS A ∥ B, in series with C ✓


Figure 3.1: CMOS circuit for f = \overline{AB + C}.
6 transistors. Building it as an AND gate (6), a NOR gate (4) would take 10.
Example 3: CMOS gate from an expression with complemented inputs

Like the lecture’s “Derive a CMOS Network” worked example

Design the CMOS networks for f = \overline{A}\,\overline{B} + \overline{C}.

PUN from f = 1: (A = 0 AND B = 0) OR C = 0 → PMOS A series B, that pair parallel with PMOS C.
PDN from \overline{f}: by DeMorgan, \overline{f} = \overline{\overline{A}\,\overline{B}}\;\overline{\overline{C}} = (A + B)\,C → NMOS A parallel B, that pair in series with NMOS C.
Duality check: the PUN’s series pair (A, B) is a parallel pair in the PDN, and C swaps from parallel to series ✓

Example 4: Transistor states in a CMOS NOR

Like the CMOS NAND truth-table slide

For a 2-input CMOS NOR with A = 0, B = 1: which transistors are ON, and what is f?

PUN (two PMOS in series): PMOS A is ON (gate 0), PMOS B is OFF (gate 1). Series needs both, so the PUN is off.
PDN (two NMOS in parallel): NMOS A is OFF, NMOS B is ON. Parallel needs one, so the PDN conducts.
The output is connected to GND, so f = 0. Check: \overline{0 + 1} = 0 ✓

Example 5: Implementing a function with 7400-series chips

Like the lecture’s chip-level implementation of f = x_1 x_2 + \overline{x_2} x_3

Implement f = \overline{x_1}\,x_3 + x_2 x_3 with 7400-series chips. Which chips are needed, and how many gates are left over?

Operations needed: one NOT (\overline{x_1}), two 2-input ANDs (\overline{x_1}x_3 and x_2x_3), one 2-input OR.
Chips: a 7404 for the NOT, a 7408 for the ANDs, a 7432 for the OR, each with power and ground connected.
Spare gates: 5 NOTs, 2 ANDs, and 3 ORs are unused and available for other logic.



                  
                  Simplify first: f = x_3(\overline{x_1} + x_2) needs just one NOT, one OR, and one AND. Still three chips, but fewer wires.
                  
                

Example 6: XOR transistor count

Like the §3.9.1 discussion

How many transistors does a CMOS XOR take when built from AND, OR, and NOT gates, versus with transmission gates?

Gates: x_1\overline{x_2} + \overline{x_1}x_2 needs 2 NOTs (2 transistors each), 2 ANDs (6 each), and 1 OR (6):
2(2) + 2(6) + 6 = 22
Transmission gates: 2 inverters (2 each) + 2 transmission gates (2 each) = 8.

Example 7: PLA product terms

Like the lecture’s PLA slide

A PLA must implement f_1 = x_1x_2 + \overline{x_1}\,x_3 and f_2 = x_1x_2 + x_3. How many product terms does the AND plane need?

List the distinct products: P_1 = x_1x_2, P_2 = \overline{x_1}\,x_3, P_3 = x_3.
OR plane: f_1 = P_1 + P_2, f_2 = P_1 + P_3.

3 product terms, since P_1 is shared by both outputs.
Example 8: Programming a LUT

Like the LUT description (Figure 3.36)

What bits are stored in a 2-input LUT to make it an XNOR gate? What would change to make it a NAND?

One cell per truth-table row (x_1x_2 = 00, 01, 10, 11). XNOR is 1 when the inputs match: 1, 0, 0, 1.
NAND is 0 only for 11: 1, 1, 1, 0. Only the stored bits change; the multiplexer tree stays the same.

Common mistakes

Swapping NMOS and PMOS behavior: NMOS is ON with a 1, PMOS is ON with a 0 (the bubble).
Putting PMOS in the pull-down network or NMOS in the pull-up network.
Building the PDN for f instead of \overline{f}. The PDN conducts when the output should be 0.
Forgetting duality: if the PDN is series, the PUN must be parallel (and vice versa).
Thinking a CMOS AND is “simpler” than a NAND. It’s a NAND plus an inverter (6 transistors vs 4).
Confusing which PLDs are volatile: CPLDs keep their configuration without power, FPGAs lose it.

courses/coe-328/ch04-optimization-of-com.content:
Overview


                  
                  Readings Brown & Vranesic §4.2 · Lecture 3 (second half: Karnaugh Map) · week 4
                  
                

A Karnaugh map (K-map) is a truth table rearranged so that terms which can be combined sit next to each other. Grouping the 1s gives the minimum SOP expression; grouping the 0s gives the minimum POS. This chapter covers 3- and 4-variable maps, the grouping rules, “don’t care” conditions, and switching between SOP and POS on the map.
Notes
Why K-maps work
Simplifying with algebra (Ch 2) keeps using one move: two terms that differ in only one variable combine, and that variable drops out.
AB\overline{C} + ABC = AB(\overline{C} + C) = AB
A K-map lays out the cells so that any two neighboring cells differ in exactly one variable. Then every pair (or group of 4, 8, …) of neighboring 1s is a term you can combine by eye.
The map layout

The number of cells is 2^n, the same as the rows of the truth table: 8 for 3 variables, 16 for 4.
Rows are labeled with AB and columns with C (3 variables) or CD (4 variables).
The labels go in Gray code order: 00, 01, 11, 10, not 00, 01, 10, 11. That’s what makes neighbors differ by one bit.
Each cell’s value is the row label followed by the column label. In a 4-variable map, the top-right cell is 0010 and the bottom-right cell is 1010.

4-variable map, with each cell’s minterm number:








































AB \backslash CD00011110000132014576111213151410891110
3-variable map:






























AB \backslash C010001012311671045
Cell adjacency

Cells that share a side are adjacent. Cells that only touch at a corner (diagonal) are not.
The map wraps around: the top row is adjacent to the bottom row, and the left column to the right column (think of it rolled into a cylinder). So in a 4-variable map, the four corners are all adjacent to each other.

For example, in the 3-variable map, cell 010 is adjacent to 000, 011, and 110, but not to 001, 111, 100, or 101.
Mapping an expression
Standard SOP: put a 1 in the cell for each minterm (the input that makes the term 1).
Nonstandard SOP: each term with missing variables covers several cells. A term missing one variable covers 2 cells, missing two covers 4, and so on. Either expand it to standard form first, or fill in every cell that matches the variables that are there. For example, with domain A, B, C:
\overline{A} \to 000, 001, 010, 011 \qquad A\overline{B} \to 100, 101 \qquad ABC \to 111
Truth table: put each output value straight into its cell. Remember the Gray-code order when copying rows 2–3 and 6–7.
Grouping the 1s (SOP)
The goal is the biggest groups possible, and as few groups as possible.

A group must contain 1, 2, 4, 8, or 16 cells (a power of 2).
A group must be a rectangle of adjacent cells (wrap-around counts).
Make every group as large as possible.
Every 1 must be in at least one group.
Groups may overlap, but only if each group includes at least one 1 that no other group covers. Don’t add a group that’s already fully covered.

Reading the product term from a group
In each group, keep the variables that don’t change, and drop the ones that appear both complemented and uncomplemented.



































Group size3-variable map4-variable map1 cell3 literals4 literals2 cells2 literals3 literals4 cells1 literal2 literals8 cellswhole map: X = 11 literal16 cells—whole map: X = 1
Each doubling of the group size removes one variable. The minimum SOP is the OR of all the group terms.
Try it: click cells to cycle 0 → 1 → X (don’t care) → 0. The map finds the minimum expression and draws its groups. Switch to POS to group the 0s instead.
Interactive Karnaugh map (open this page on the site to use it).
Textbook terms
Brown & Vranesic name the pieces of this process:

Implicant: any valid group (a product term that’s 1 only where f is 1 or don’t care).
Prime implicant: a group that can’t be made any bigger.
Essential prime implicant: a prime implicant that covers some 1 no other prime implicant covers. It must be in the answer.

So the method is: find the essential prime implicants first, then add as few other prime implicants as needed to cover the remaining 1s.
Don’t care conditions
Sometimes certain input combinations can never happen, so the output for them doesn’t matter. The classic case is BCD: codes 1010 to 1111 are never used, so a circuit reading BCD digits doesn’t care what it outputs for them.

Mark these cells with an X.
When grouping, treat an X as a 1 if it makes a group bigger, and as a 0 otherwise.
You never need to cover an X. Never make a group of only Xs.

POS minimization (grouping the 0s)
The same map, used the other way round:

Put 0s in the cells where the output is 0 (for a standard POS expression, the cell for each sum term is the input that makes it 0).
Group the 0s with exactly the same rules.
Each group gives a sum term: keep the variables that don’t change, writing a variable uncomplemented if it’s 0 in the group and complemented if it’s 1.
The minimum POS is the AND of the sum terms.

Converting between SOP and POS on the map
Every cell that isn’t a 1 is a 0, and vice versa. So once a function is on the map:

Group the 1s for the minimum SOP.
Group the 0s for the minimum POS.

Compare the two and build whichever needs fewer gates.
Key formulas
Number of cells
\text{cells} = 2^n \tag{4.1}

n: number of variables (3 → 8 cells, 4 → 16 cells)

Literals in a group’s term
\text{literals} = n - \log_2(\text{group size}) \tag{4.2}

Group sizes are always 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.

Combining adjacent terms
PX + P\overline{X} = P, \qquad (S + X)(S + \overline{X}) = S \tag{4.3}

P: the rest of a product term (SOP)
S: the rest of a sum term (POS)
X: the one variable that differs between the two cells

Cell numbering (4 variables, A = MSB)
\text{minterm number} = 8A + 4B + 2C + D \tag{4.4}
Examples
These follow the lecture’s K-map examples, with different functions. Each map is live: click cells to experiment.
Example 1: Minimize a standard SOP

Like Lecture 3, Example 21

Minimize X = \overline{A}\,\overline{B}\,\overline{C} + \overline{A}\,\overline{B}C + A\overline{B}\,\overline{C} + A\overline{B}C + AB\overline{C}.

Binary values: 000, 001, 100, 101, 110 → cells 0, 1, 4, 5, 6.
Group of 4: cells 0, 1, 4, 5 are rows 00 and 10, which are adjacent by wrap-around. B = 0 throughout, and A, C both change → \overline{B}.
Group of 2 for cell 6: pair it with cell 4 (row 10, column 0) → A = 1, C = 0 → A\overline{C}.

X = \overline{B} + A\overline{C}
Karnaugh map for Example 1 (open this page on the site to use it).
Example 2: Map a nonstandard SOP

Like Lecture 3, “Mapping a Nonstandard SOP Expression” and Example 17

Map and minimize X = \overline{B}\,\overline{C} + AB + A\overline{B}C (domain A, B, C).

Expand each term:

\overline{B}\,\overline{C} is missing A: cells 000 and 100 (0, 4)
AB is missing C: cells 110 and 111 (6, 7)
A\overline{B}C is standard: cell 101 (5)


Group of 4: cells 4, 5, 6, 7 (the whole A = 1 half) → A.
Cell 0 pairs with cell 4 → \overline{B}\,\overline{C}.

X = A + \overline{B}\,\overline{C}
Example 3: Wrap-around and corners

Like Lecture 3, Example 22

Minimize X = \sum m(0, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 15).

The four corners (0, 2, 8, 10) are all adjacent by wrap-around. B = 0, D = 0 in all of them → \overline{B}\,\overline{D}.
The middle square (5, 7, 13, 15): B = 1, D = 1 → BD.

X = BD + \overline{B}\,\overline{D}
This is the map loaded in the interactive above. It’s also \overline{B \oplus D}: the output only depends on whether B and D match.
Example 4: Overlapping groups

Like Lecture 3, Examples 19–20

Minimize X = \sum m(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11).

Group of 8: rows 00 and 10 (cells 0–3 and 8–11) are adjacent by wrap-around. Only B = 0 stays fixed → \overline{B}.
Cells 4 and 6 are left. Group them with 0 and 2 (they’re the left and right columns of the top two rows, adjacent by wrap-around): A = 0, D = 0 → \overline{A}\,\overline{D}.

X = \overline{B} + \overline{A}\,\overline{D}


                  
                  Reusing cells 0 and 2 is allowed because the new group also covers cells (4 and 6) that nothing else covers. A group of 4 beats two separate pairs. 
                  
                

Karnaugh map for Example 4 (open this page on the site to use it).
Example 5: Don’t cares with BCD inputs

Like Lecture 3, Example 23 (7-segment display)

A circuit reads a BCD digit ABCD and outputs X = 1 when the digit is 5 or more. Minimize it, using don’t cares for the invalid codes.

1s: digits 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. Don’t cares: 10–15 (invalid BCD).
Treat the Xs as 1s where they help:

Cells 8–15 (bottom two rows) are 8, 9 plus six Xs → group of 8 → A
Cells 5, 7, 13, 15 → BD
Cells 6, 7, 14, 15 → BC



X = A + BD + BC
Without the don’t cares, the best you could do is A\overline{B}\,\overline{C} + \overline{A}BD + \overline{A}BC: three 3-literal terms instead of one literal and two 2-literal terms.
Karnaugh map for Example 5 (open this page on the site to use it).
Example 6: POS minimization

Like Lecture 3, Example 25

Minimize X = \prod M(0, 2, 4, 5) as a POS expression.

0s go in cells 0, 2, 4, 5.
Group cells 0 and 2 (rows 00 and 01, column 0): A = 0, C = 0. Both are 0, so both stay uncomplemented → (A + C).
Group cells 4 and 5 (row 10): A = 1, B = 0 → (\overline{A} + B).

X = (A + C)(\overline{A} + B)
This is the same function as Example 9 in Ch 2. Its minimum SOP, from the 1s, is \overline{A}C + AB.
Karnaugh map for Example 6 (open this page on the site to use it).
Example 7: 4-variable POS

Like Lecture 3, Examples 24 and 26

Minimize X = \prod M(0, 2, 3, 8, 10, 11).

The four corners (0, 2, 8, 10): B = 0, D = 0 → (B + D).
Cells 2, 3, 10, 11 (columns 11 and 10 of rows 00 and 10; the rows are adjacent by wrap-around): B = 0, C = 1 → (B + \overline{C}).

X = (B + D)(B + \overline{C})
Example 8: SOP and POS from the same map

Like Lecture 3, Example 27

For the function in Example 7, find the standard SOP and the minimum SOP. Which form is cheaper?

Standard SOP: every cell that isn’t a 0 is a 1:
X = \sum m(1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 12, 13, 14, 15)
Group the 1s:

Rows 01 and 11 (cells 4–7 and 12–15) → B
Column 01 (cells 1, 5, 9, 13) → \overline{C}D


Minimum SOP:
X = B + \overline{C}D

The SOP needs one AND and one OR (plus an inverter for \overline{C}). The POS from Example 7 needs two ORs and an AND. They’re equal: by Rule 12, (B + D)(B + \overline{C}) = B + \overline{C}D.
Common mistakes

Labeling rows or columns 00, 01, 10, 11. It must be 00, 01, 11, 10 (Gray code).
Grouping diagonal cells, or a group of 3 or 6. Groups must be rectangles of 1, 2, 4, 8, or 16 cells.
Forgetting wrap-around: the edges (and the four corners) are adjacent.
Stopping at small groups when a bigger one is possible.
Adding a group whose cells are all already covered. Every group needs at least one 1 of its own.
Covering a don’t care for no reason, or making a group of only don’t cares.
In POS, writing the sum-term literals the SOP way. In POS a 0 → uncomplemented, a 1 → complemented.
