courses/coe-328/ch05-number-representati.content:
Overview


                  
                  Readings Brown & Vranesic §5.1–5.3 · Lecture 6 · week 5–6
                  
                

The same bit pattern can mean different numbers depending on the representation. This chapter covers unsigned numbers (and octal/hex as shorthand), the circuits that add them (half adder → full adder → ripple-carry adder), the three ways to write signed numbers (sign-magnitude, 1’s complement, 2’s complement), and why 2’s complement wins: one adder circuit does both addition and subtraction. It ends with overflow, when a result doesn’t fit.
Notes
Unsigned numbers
An n-bit unsigned number B = b_{n-1} \ldots b_1 b_0 uses positional notation (see Ch 1):
V(B) = b_{n-1} 2^{n-1} + \cdots + b_1 2^1 + b_0 2^0
With n bits the range is 0 to 2^n - 1 (8 bits: 0 to 255).


                  
                  Always state the representation before reading a bit pattern. 1111\,1011 is 251 unsigned, -5 in 2's complement, -4 in 1's complement, and -123 in sign-magnitude.
                  
                

Octal and hexadecimal
Both are shorthand for long binary numbers:

Octal (base 8): each digit is 3 bits. Group from the LSB in 3s. 101\ 011\ 010\ 111_2 = 5327_8
Hex (base 16): each digit is 4 bits. Group from the LSB in 4s. 11\ 0110\ 1000_2 = 0011\ 0110\ 1000_2 = 368_{16}
Pad with 0s on the left if the bit count isn’t a multiple of 3 or 4: 10\ 111\ 011_2 = 273_8
































































































BinaryOctalHexDecimalBinaryOctalHexDecimal0000000100010880001111100111990010222101012A100011333101113B110100444110014C120101555110115D130110666111016E140111777111117F15
Hex is the usual way to display values from FPGAs and memory.
The half adder
Adding two bits x and y gives a sum bit s and a carry bit c:



































xycs0000010110011110
s = x \oplus y \qquad c = xy

XOR gives the sum: it’s 1 when exactly one input is 1.
AND gives the carry: it’s 1 only when both inputs are 1.
A half adder has no carry-in, so it can only be used for the least significant bit.

The full adder
Every other bit position also has to add the carry coming in from the position to its right. A full adder adds three bits, x_i, y_i, and carry-in c_i:




































































x_iy_ic_ic_{i+1}s_i0000000101010010111010001101101101011111
s_i = x_i \oplus y_i \oplus c_i \qquad c_{i+1} = x_i y_i + x_i c_i + y_i c_i

The sum is 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1.
The carry-out is 1 when at least two inputs are 1 (the majority function from Ch 2).

A full adder can be built from two half adders and an OR gate (Figure 5.1): the first adds x and y, the second adds that sum to c_{in}, and either one producing a carry gives a carry-out.

Figure 5.1: A full adder built from two half adders and an OR gate.
The ripple-carry adder
To add two n-bit numbers, chain n full adders:

Full adder i adds bits x_i and y_i.
The carry-out of stage i is the carry-in of stage i + 1.
For plain unsigned addition, the first carry-in is c_0 = 0.
The last carry-out, c_n, is the extra bit of the sum.

The problem is speed. A carry made in the lowest bit can change the next stage, which can change the next, all the way up the chain. The result isn’t settled until the carry has rippled through every stage, so the worst-case delay grows with n. Faster adders (carry-lookahead, §5.4) compute carries in parallel at the cost of more logic; they’re not covered in this course.
Signed numbers
The MSB is the sign bit: 0 for positive, 1 for negative. Positive numbers look the same in all three systems. They differ in how negatives are written.





























RepresentationHow to negate8-bit rangeZerosSign-magnitudeflip the sign bit only-127 to +127two (+0 and -0)1’s complementflip every bit: K_1 = (2^n - 1) - P-127 to +127two (0000\,0000 and 1111\,1111)2’s complementflip every bit, then add 1: K_2 = 2^n - P-128 to +127one

In 4 bits, +5 = 0101. Then -5 is 1101 (sign-magnitude), 1010 (1’s complement), or 1011 (2’s complement).
Since K_2 = K_1 + 1, the easy way to get a 2’s complement in hardware is: invert, then add 1.
2’s complement gets one extra negative number: it has only one zero, so the pattern 1000\,0000 that would have been -0 is -128 instead.

Reading a 2’s complement number: if the MSB is 0, read it normally. If it’s 1, take the 2’s complement to find the magnitude and put a minus sign in front. (1111\,0111 → 0000\,1001 = 9 → -9.) Or: give the MSB a weight of -2^{n-1} instead of +2^{n-1}.
Try it: click bits to see the same pattern read four ways. Use the buttons to take complements.
Interactive number representations (open this page on the site to use it).
Adding signed numbers
1’s complement addition sometimes needs a fix: if there’s a carry-out of the sign bit, add it back into the LSB (the end-around carry). That second addition can double the time, which is why 1’s complement isn’t used for arithmetic.
\begin{aligned}
(+5) + (-2): \quad 0101 + 1101 &= 1\,0010 \\
\text{add the carry back:}\quad 0010 + 1 &= 0011 = +3 \;✓
\end{aligned}
2’s complement addition always works directly. Add the bit patterns with an ordinary adder and ignore any carry out of the sign bit. The signs of the operands don’t matter.






























SumBitsResult(+5) + (+2)0101 + 00100111 = +7(-5) + (+2)1011 + 00101101 = -3(+5) + (-2)0101 + 1110\cancel{1}\,0011 = +3(-5) + (-2)1011 + 1110\cancel{1}\,1001 = -7
2’s complement subtraction: negate the subtrahend (take its 2’s complement) and add:
A - B = A + \overline{B} + 1
A helpful picture is the number circle: in 4 bits the patterns 0000 to 1111 go around a circle, with 0111 (+7) next to 1000 (−8). Adding moves clockwise, subtracting moves counterclockwise, and crossing the +7/−8 boundary means the answer is wrong (overflow).
The adder/subtractor unit
One n-bit adder can do both operations, controlled by a signal \overline{\text{Add}}/\text{Sub} (0 = add, 1 = subtract; the bar over Add means “add when this is 0”):

Each bit y_i goes through an XOR gate with the control signal. XOR with 0 passes y_i through; XOR with 1 inverts it. So the adder sees Y when adding and \overline{Y} when subtracting.
The control signal is also the carry-in c_0. When subtracting, c_0 = 1 supplies the “+1” that turns \overline{Y} into the 2’s complement.

\text{Add } (\text{control} = 0): \; X + Y + 0 \qquad \text{Sub } (\text{control} = 1): \; X + \overline{Y} + 1 = X - Y
Try it: set X and Y, switch between add and subtract, and follow the carries through the four full adders.
Interactive 4-bit adder/subtractor (open this page on the site to use it).
Arithmetic overflow
With n bits, a 2’s complement result must be between -2^{n-1} and 2^{n-1} - 1 (4 bits: −8 to +7). If the true answer is outside that range, the result is wrong: arithmetic overflow.

Only possible when adding two numbers with the same sign. A positive plus a negative always fits.
Sign check: overflow happened if two positives give a negative, or two negatives give a positive.
Carry check (what the hardware uses): overflow = c_n \oplus c_{n-1}, the carry out of the sign bit XOR the carry into it.









































Sum (4-bit)Bitsc_4c_3Overflow?(+7) + (+2)0111 + 0010 = 100101Yes (got −7, not +9)(-7) + (+2)1001 + 0010 = 101100No (−5)(+7) + (-2)0111 + 1110 = 1\,010111No (+5)(-7) + (-2)1001 + 1110 = 1\,011110Yes (got +7, not −9)


                  
                  For unsigned numbers the rule is different: the result is wrong when c_n = 1 (the sum needs one more bit).
                  
                

Key formulas
Unsigned value
V(B) = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} b_i\,2^i, \qquad 0 \le V \le 2^n - 1 \tag{5.1}

b_i: bit i (b_0 is the LSB)
n: number of bits

Half adder
s = x \oplus y, \qquad c = xy \tag{5.2}
Full adder
s_i = x_i \oplus y_i \oplus c_i, \qquad c_{i+1} = x_i y_i + x_i c_i + y_i c_i \tag{5.3}

x_i, y_i: the two operand bits at position i
c_i: carry into position i
s_i: sum bit at position i
c_{i+1}: carry out of position i (into position i + 1)

Complements
K_1 = (2^n - 1) - P, \qquad K_2 = 2^n - P = K_1 + 1 \tag{5.4}

P: the positive number being negated
K_1, K_2: its 1’s and 2’s complement (the bit patterns for -P)

2’s complement subtraction
X - Y = X + \overline{Y} + 1 \tag{5.5}

\overline{Y}: Y with every bit inverted

Signed range (n-bit 2’s complement)
-2^{n-1} \le V \le 2^{n-1} - 1 \tag{5.6}
Overflow (2’s complement)
\text{Overflow} = c_n \oplus c_{n-1} \tag{5.7}

c_n: carry out of the sign bit
c_{n-1}: carry into the sign bit

Examples
These follow the lecture’s worked examples and practice questions, with different numbers.
Example 1: Hex, octal, and decimal

Like Practice 1

Convert 1011\,0110_2 to hex, octal, and decimal.

Hex (groups of 4): 1011\ 0110 = B6_{16}
Octal (groups of 3 from the right, pad to 010\ 110\ 110): 266_8
Decimal: B6_{16} = 11 \times 16 + 6 = 182. Check in binary: 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 182 ✓

Example 2: Full adder outputs

Like Practice 2–3

Find s and c_{out} for a full adder with x = 1, y = 0, c_{in} = 1, and explain why a half adder couldn’t do this.

Sum: 1 \oplus 0 \oplus 1 = 0 (an even number of 1s).
Carry: xy + xc_{in} + yc_{in} = 0 + 1 + 0 = 1 (two of the three inputs are 1).

So 1 + 0 + 1 = 10_2: s = 0, c_{out} = 1. A half adder only has two inputs, so it has nowhere to take the carry-in.
Example 3: Ripple-carry addition

Like the lecture’s ripple-carry adder slide

Add X = 0110 and Y = 0111 with a 4-bit ripple-carry adder (c_0 = 0). Give every carry.













































Stage ix_iy_ic_is_ic_{i+1}001010111001211111300110
S = 1101 = 13 and c_4 = 0. Check: 6 + 7 = 13 ✓


                  
                  Stage 3 can't settle until c_3 arrives, which waits on c_2, which waits on c_1. That chain is the ripple delay.
                  
                

Example 4: Subtraction with 2’s complement

Like the lecture’s “13 − 5” worked example

Compute 22 - 9 using 8-bit 2’s complement.

Operands: 22 = 0001\,0110, 9 = 0000\,1001
Negate 9: invert → 1111\,0110, add 1 → 1111\,0111
Add:
0001\,0110 + 1111\,0111 = \cancel{1}\,0000\,1101
Drop the carry out of the 8-bit word: 0000\,1101 = 13 ✓

Example 5: A negative result

Like Practice 4

Compute 14 - 25 using 8-bit 2’s complement.

Operands: 14 = 0000\,1110, 25 = 0001\,1001
Negate 25: invert → 1110\,0110, add 1 → 1110\,0111
Add: 0000\,1110 + 1110\,0111 = 1111\,0101 (no carry out)
Read it: the MSB is 1, so it’s negative. Its 2’s complement is 0000\,1011 = 11, so the result is -11 ✓

Example 6: Three signed representations

Like the lecture’s signed-number table

Write -37 in 8-bit sign-magnitude, 1’s complement, and 2’s complement.

Start from +37: 0010\,0101
Sign-magnitude: set the sign bit → 1010\,0101
1’s complement: flip every bit → 1101\,1010
2’s complement: add 1 → 1101\,1011

Example 7: 1’s complement addition

Like Figure 5.9

Add (-4) + (-2) in 4-bit 1’s complement.

Operands: +4 = 0100 \to -4 = 1011; +2 = 0010 \to -2 = 1101
Add: 1011 + 1101 = 1\,1000
End-around carry: there’s a carry out, so add it to the LSB: 1000 + 1 = 1001
Check: +6 = 0110, so -6 = 1001 ✓

Example 8: Detecting overflow

Like Figure 5.14 and Practice 5

In 4-bit 2’s complement, does (a) (+5) + (+4) or (b) (-6) + (-3) overflow?
(a) 0101 + 0100:

Bits 0–1 produce no carries; bit 2 is 1 + 1 = 10, so c_3 = 1; bit 3 is 0 + 0 + 1 = 1, so c_4 = 0.
Result 1001. c_4 \oplus c_3 = 0 \oplus 1 = 1: overflow. Two positives gave a negative (-7); the true answer +9 needs more than 4 bits.

(b) 1010 + 1101:

Bits 0–2 produce no carries (c_3 = 0); bit 3 is 1 + 1 = 10, so c_4 = 1.
Result 0111. c_4 \oplus c_3 = 1 \oplus 0 = 1: overflow. Two negatives gave a positive (+7); the true answer -9 is below -8.

Example 9: Adder/subtractor unit

Like Figure 5.13

A 4-bit adder/subtractor has X = 0110, Y = 0011, and the control set to Sub (1). What does the adder see, and what’s the output?

XOR gates invert each y_i: the adder’s second input is \overline{Y} = 1100.
Carry-in c_0 = 1.
Add:
0110 + 1100 + 1 = \cancel{1}\,0011
Result 0011 = 3, and 6 - 3 = 3 ✓. c_4 = 1, c_3 = 1, so no overflow.

Common mistakes

Reading a bit pattern without fixing the representation first.
Using a half adder where there’s a carry-in. Only bit 0 can use a half adder.
Forgetting the +1 when subtracting with 2’s complement (it’s the carry-in in hardware).
Keeping the carry out of the sign bit in 2’s complement. It’s ignored (in 1’s complement it’s added back).
Calling it overflow whenever there’s a carry-out. For signed numbers, check c_n \oplus c_{n-1} (or the signs), not c_n alone.
Thinking the 8-bit 2’s complement range is symmetric. It’s −128 to +127.

courses/coe-328/ch06-combinational-build.title: Ch 6: Combinational Circuit Building Blocks
courses/coe-328/ch06-combinational-build.content:
Overview


                  
                  Readings Brown & Vranesic §6.1–6.5 · Lecture 7 · week 6
                  
                

Some combinational circuits come up so often that they’re sold as ready-made chips (or used as blocks in CAD tools) instead of being built from gates every time. This chapter covers comparators, decoders (including the BCD-to-7-segment decoder), encoders, multiplexers, demultiplexers, and parity generators/checkers.
Notes
Comparators
A comparator tells you how two binary numbers relate.
Equality. An XNOR gate is a 1-bit comparator: its output is 1 when the two bits are equal. To compare two multi-bit numbers, XNOR each pair of matching bits and AND the results. The numbers are equal only if every bit pair matches.

Figure 6.1: A 2-bit equality comparator.
Magnitude (inequality). A magnitude comparator also has A > B and A < B outputs. To decide, start at the most significant bit:

A_3 = 1 and B_3 = 0 → A > B.
A_3 = 0 and B_3 = 1 → A < B.
A_3 = B_3 → no decision yet; move to the next bit down and repeat.

The first bit position where the numbers differ decides the answer. If no position differs, A = B.
Decoders
A decoder detects a specific bit combination (code) on its inputs and signals it with an output level. In general it has n inputs and up to 2^n outputs.
Decoding one code. An AND gate is the basic decoding element because it’s 1 only when every input is 1. Invert the inputs that should be 0. For example, to detect 1001:
X = A_3\,\overline{A_2}\,\overline{A_1}\,A_0
For an active-LOW output, use a NAND gate instead.
Decoding every code. A decoder that has one output per input combination is called an n-line-to-2^n-line decoder, or a 1-of-2^n decoder because exactly one output is active at a time.

4-line-to-16-line (1-of-16): 4 inputs, 16 outputs, one AND (or NAND) gate per output.
BCD-to-decimal (4-line-to-10-line, 1-of-10): only the 10 valid BCD codes get an output.
2-line-to-4-line: with inputs S_1 S_0, the outputs are Y_0 = \overline{S_1}\,\overline{S_0}, Y_1 = \overline{S_1}S_0, Y_2 = S_1\overline{S_0}, Y_3 = S_1 S_0. Each output is one minterm.

BCD-to-7-segment decoder. Takes a BCD digit and lights the right segments (a–g) of a 7-segment display to show it. Each segment is its own output function of the 4 BCD inputs, simplified with a K-map using the six invalid codes as don’t cares (Ch 4). For segment a, lit for digits 0, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9:
a = A + C + BD + \overline{B}\,\overline{D}
Try it: set a BCD code and see which segments light. Each segment’s expression is listed underneath.
Interactive BCD-to-7-segment decoder (open this page on the site to use it).
Encoders
An encoder does the reverse of a decoder: it takes an active level on one of its inputs (a digit or symbol) and outputs the matching code.
Decimal-to-BCD encoder (10-line-to-4-line): ten inputs, one per decimal digit, and four BCD outputs. Each output bit is the OR of the digits whose BCD code has a 1 in that position:



































Output bitWeight1 for digits…ExpressionA_388, 9A_3 = 8 + 9A_244, 5, 6, 7A_2 = 4 + 5 + 6 + 7A_122, 3, 6, 7A_1 = 2 + 3 + 6 + 7A_011, 3, 5, 7, 9A_0 = 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9
(Here “8 + 9” means the OR of input lines 8 and 9.) Input 0 needs no gate: all outputs are 0 when nothing else is active.
Multiplexers (data selectors)
A multiplexer (MUX) routes one of several data inputs onto a single output line. The data-select inputs choose which one. With n select lines it can choose among 2^n data inputs.
4-to-1 MUX: data inputs D_0–D_3, select inputs S_1 S_0:






























S_1S_0Y00D_001D_110D_211D_3
Y = D_0\,\overline{S_1}\,\overline{S_0} + D_1\,\overline{S_1}\,S_0 + D_2\,S_1\overline{S_0} + D_3\,S_1 S_0
That’s four 3-input ANDs, a 4-input OR, and two inverters for \overline{S_1} and \overline{S_0}. Each AND gate is enabled by exactly one select combination (a decoder built into the MUX). The 2-to-1 MUX from Ch 2, f = \overline{s}\,x_1 + s\,x_2, is the smallest case.
Try it: set the data inputs and the select lines. The selected path lights up through the MUX.
Interactive 4-to-1 multiplexer (open this page on the site to use it).
A MUX as a logic function generator. A 2^n-to-1 MUX can implement any function of n variables: connect the variables to the select lines, and tie each data input to the function’s output for that row (HIGH for 1, LOW for 0). The MUX then just looks up the truth table, like an FPGA LUT (Ch 3). This usually replaces several gate chips with one MUX chip.
A smaller trick: a 2^{n-1}-to-1 MUX can do an n-variable function. Put n - 1 variables on the select lines, and feed each data input with 0, 1, the last variable, or its complement (see Example 5).
Demultiplexers
A demultiplexer (DEMUX) does the reverse of a MUX: it takes data from one line and sends it to one of several output lines, chosen by the select inputs. It’s also called a data distributor.
1-to-4 DEMUX: the data input goes to all four AND gates, and the select lines enable only one of them:
D_0 = \text{Data}\cdot\overline{S_1}\,\overline{S_0}, \quad D_1 = \text{Data}\cdot\overline{S_1}S_0, \quad D_2 = \text{Data}\cdot S_1\overline{S_0}, \quad D_3 = \text{Data}\cdot S_1S_0
The unselected outputs stay at 0.
A decoder is a DEMUX. A decoder with an enable input already has this structure: use the decoder inputs as the select lines and the enable as the data input. For example, a 4-line-to-16-line decoder with two active-LOW chip-select inputs works as a 1-to-16 DEMUX: one chip select carries the data, and the other is held LOW to enable the chip.
Parity generators and checkers
Parity is a simple way to detect a single-bit error. An extra parity bit is sent with the data so that the total number of 1s is:

Even parity: even
Odd parity: odd

The key fact: the XOR (sum without carries) of an even number of 1s is 0, and of an odd number of 1s is 1. So XORing all the bits together counts the 1s mod 2:
X = b_{n-1} \oplus \cdots \oplus b_1 \oplus b_0

Generator: XOR the data bits. For even parity the parity bit is X; for odd parity it’s \overline{X}.
Checker: XOR all received bits including the parity bit. For even parity, X = 0 means OK and X = 1 means an error. (Odd parity: the other way round.)

A single flipped bit always changes the count of 1s by one, so it’s always caught. Two flipped bits cancel out and aren’t.
Key formulas
2-bit equality comparator
(A = B) = \overline{A_1 \oplus B_1}\;\cdot\;\overline{A_0 \oplus B_0} \tag{6.1}

A_1 A_0, B_1 B_0: the two 2-bit numbers being compared

Decoder outputs
\text{outputs} \le 2^n \tag{6.2}

n: number of input lines. Each output is one minterm of the inputs.

4-to-1 multiplexer
Y = D_0\,\overline{S_1}\,\overline{S_0} + D_1\,\overline{S_1}\,S_0 + D_2\,S_1\overline{S_0} + D_3\,S_1 S_0 \tag{6.3}

D_0–D_3: data inputs
S_1 S_0: select inputs; the binary number S_1S_0 is the index of the data input passed to Y

1-to-4 demultiplexer
D_i = \text{Data} \cdot m_i(S_1, S_0) \tag{6.4}

m_i: the minterm of the select lines for output i (e.g. m_2 = S_1\overline{S_0})

Parity
X = b_{n-1} \oplus \cdots \oplus b_1 \oplus b_0 \tag{6.5}

X = 1 when the bits contain an odd number of 1s

Examples
These follow the lecture examples, with different numbers.
Example 1: Comparing two numbers

Like Lecture 7, Example 2 and the magnitude-comparator slides

(a) Is A = 10 equal to B = 10 using a 2-bit equality comparator? (b) Compare A = 1011 and B = 1001 with a magnitude comparator.
(a) Bit 1: \overline{1 \oplus 1} = 1. Bit 0: \overline{0 \oplus 0} = 1. AND: 1 \cdot 1 = 1, so A = B.
(b) Start at the MSB:

A_3 = B_3 = 1: no decision
A_2 = B_2 = 0: no decision
A_1 = 1, B_1 = 0: A > B (bit 0 doesn’t matter)

Check: 11 > 9 ✓
Example 2: Decoding one code

Like the lecture’s “decode 1001” slide

Write the decoding expression for the code 1011 (A_3 is the MSB), with an active-HIGH output and with an active-LOW output.

Invert the inputs that should be 0 (only A_2 here):
X = A_3\,\overline{A_2}\,A_1\,A_0 \quad (\text{AND gate, active-HIGH})
Active-LOW: use a NAND gate instead:
\overline{X} = \overline{A_3\,\overline{A_2}\,A_1\,A_0}

The output is 1 (or 0 for active-LOW) only for 1011.
Example 3: Decimal-to-BCD encoder

Like the decimal-to-BCD encoder slide

Input line 6 of a decimal-to-BCD encoder is HIGH (all others LOW). What are the outputs?

Check which output expressions include input 6: A_2 = 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 and A_1 = 2 + 3 + 6 + 7 do; A_3 and A_0 don’t.
Outputs: A_3A_2A_1A_0 = 0110, which is 6 in BCD ✓

Example 4: Multiplexer output waveform

Like Lecture 7, Example 1

A 4-to-1 MUX has D_0 = 1, D_1 = 0, D_2 = 1, D_3 = 0 held constant. The select lines step through S_1S_0 = 00, 01, 10, 11, 10, 00. What is Y in each interval?
































S_1S_0000110111000SelectedD_0D_1D_2D_3D_2D_0Y101011
Example 5: A MUX as a function generator

Like Lecture 7, Example 2

Implement Y = \sum m(0, 3, 5, 6) (variables A, B, C; A is the MSB) using (a) an 8-to-1 MUX and (b) a 4-to-1 MUX.
(a) Connect A, B, C to the three select lines. Tie D_0, D_3, D_5, D_6 HIGH and D_1, D_2, D_4, D_7 LOW.
(b) Connect A, B to S_1, S_0. For each pair of rows with the same AB, see how Y depends on C:



































ABY when C = 0Y when C = 1Data input0010D_0 = \overline{C}0101D_1 = C1001D_2 = C1110D_3 = \overline{C}
One 4-to-1 MUX and one inverter. (This function is \overline{A \oplus B \oplus C}, which needs two XOR-type gates otherwise.)
Example 6: Demultiplexer

Like Lecture 7, Example 3

Serial data 1, 0, 1, 1 arrives on the data input of a 1-to-4 DEMUX, one bit per interval, while the select lines go S_1S_0 = 00, 01, 10, 11. Where does each bit end up?






















































Interval1234S_1S_000011011Data in1011D_01000D_10000D_20010D_30001
Each bit appears only on the selected output during its interval; the other outputs stay 0.
Example 7: Parity

Like the parity-checker slide

(a) Find the even and odd parity bits for the data 1011001. (b) The byte 1101\,0110 (7 data bits + even parity bit) is received. Is there an error?
(a) The data has four 1s (even), so X = 1 \oplus 0 \oplus 1 \oplus 1 \oplus 0 \oplus 0 \oplus 1 = 0.

Even parity bit: 0 (the total stays at four 1s)
Odd parity bit: 1 (makes five 1s)

(b) The received byte has five 1s, so the checker outputs X = 1. With even parity that means an error (at least one bit flipped).
Example 8: A 7-segment segment equation

Like Lecture 3, Example 23

Check that a = A + C + BD + \overline{B}\,\overline{D} lights segment a for digit 5 but not for digit 4.

Digit 5 = 0101: A = 0, C = 0, BD = 1 \cdot 1 = 1 → a = 1, lit ✓
Digit 4 = 0100: A = 0, C = 0, BD = 1 \cdot 0 = 0, \overline{B}\,\overline{D} = 0 \cdot 1 = 0 → a = 0, off ✓ (a “4” has no top bar)

Common mistakes

Comparing magnitudes from the LSB. Always start at the MSB; the first difference decides.
Mixing up decoders and encoders: a decoder turns a code into one active line; an encoder turns one active line into a code.
Reading the select lines in the wrong order. S_1 is the MSB: S_1S_0 = 10 selects D_2, not D_1.
Thinking unselected DEMUX outputs “hold” their old value. They’re 0.
For a MUX function generator, tying data inputs to the wrong rows (check that the select variables are wired MSB-first, the same as the truth table).
Thinking parity can correct errors or catch two-bit errors. It only detects an odd number of flipped bits.

courses/coe-328/ch07-intro-to-sequential.title: Ch 7: Introduction to Sequential Circuits
courses/coe-328/ch07-intro-to-sequential.content:
Overview


                  
                  Readings Brown & Vranesic §7.1–7.8 · Lecture 8 · weeks 7–8
                  
                

Everything so far has been combinational: the output depends only on the inputs right now. A sequential circuit also depends on what happened before, because it stores a bit. This chapter covers the two basic storage elements: latches (level-sensitive) and flip-flops (edge-triggered), in the S-R, D, and J-K varieties, plus the asynchronous preset and clear inputs.
Notes
Latches vs flip-flops
Both are bistable: they have two stable states (storing a 0 or a 1) and stay in one until told to change. Both get this from feedback: each gate’s output is wired back to the input of the other gate.
The difference is when they’re allowed to change:




















DeviceChanges state…Sensitive toLatchany time its inputs (and enable) say sothe level of the enableFlip-floponly at a clock edgethe edge (transition) of the clock
The outputs are always Q and \overline{Q}, which are normally complements of each other. SET means Q = 1; RESET (clear) means Q = 0.
The S-R latch
Active-HIGH S-R latch: two cross-coupled NOR gates.

Figure 7.1: An active-HIGH S-R latch made of cross-coupled NOR gates.








































SRQ\overline{Q}Mode00Q\overline{Q}No change (holds the stored bit)1010Set0101Reset1100Invalid (Q = \overline{Q})
Why it holds: with S = R = 0, each NOR acts as an inverter of the other gate’s output, so Q keeps feeding back \overline{Q} and vice versa. Whichever state it’s in reinforces itself.
Why S = R = 1 is invalid: both NOR outputs are forced to 0, so Q and \overline{Q} are no longer complements. Worse, if both inputs then return to 0 at the same time, the latch ends up in an unpredictable state.
Active-LOW \overline{S}-\overline{R} latch: two cross-coupled NAND gates. Same idea, but the inputs are active-LOW: a 0 sets or resets it, \overline{S} = \overline{R} = 1 holds, and \overline{S} = \overline{R} = 0 is invalid (both outputs go to 1).



































\overline{S}\overline{R}QMode11QNo change011Set100Reset001 (and \overline{Q} = 1)Invalid
Try it: click time slots of S and R to change them. The latch starts RESET. Red marks the invalid state.
Interactive S-R latch (open this page on the site to use it).
Gated latches
A gated latch adds an enable input (EN, sometimes G). The latch only responds to its other inputs while EN is HIGH. It’s level-sensitive: for the whole time EN = 1, the output follows the inputs.
Gated S-R latch. Two AND (or NAND) gates pass S and R through only when EN = 1:

EN = 0: no change, whatever S and R do.
EN = 1: behaves like a normal S-R latch (S = R = 1 is still invalid).

Gated D latch. Removes the invalid state by having just one data input D, with S = D and R = \overline{D} inside:





























ENDQMode0XQNo change100Reset111Set
In short: while EN = 1, Q follows D. When EN goes to 0, Q holds the last value of D.
Try it: switch between the gated S-R and D latch, and edit the inputs. The shaded columns are where EN is HIGH: those are the only places Q can change.
Interactive gated latches (open this page on the site to use it).
Edge-triggered flip-flops
A flip-flop changes state only at one instant: the triggering edge of the clock (CLK, or control input C). Everywhere else, its inputs are ignored.

Positive edge-triggered: changes on the rising edge (0 → 1). Symbol: no bubble on C.
Negative edge-triggered: changes on the falling edge (1 → 0). Symbol: a bubble on C.
The small triangle at the C input (the dynamic input indicator) is how to tell a flip-flop from a latch on a schematic.

The data inputs (D, or J and K) are called synchronous inputs because their effect is synchronized with the clock.
D flip-flop
On the triggering edge, Q takes the value of D. Between edges, D can change freely without affecting Q, except for a very short window right around the edge (where it must be stable).























DCLKQMode1↑1Set (stores 1)0↑0Reset (stores 0)
So Q follows D at the clock edge, and holds that value until the next edge.
J-K flip-flop
Like an S-R flip-flop (J = set, K = reset), but J = K = 1 is useful instead of invalid: it toggles the output.








































JKCLKQ after the edgeMode00↑QNo change01↑0Reset10↑1Set11↑\overline{Q}Toggle
Try it: switch between the D and J-K flip-flops. The clock is fixed; the dashed lines mark its rising edges, the only instants Q can change.
Interactive flip-flops (open this page on the site to use it).
Asynchronous preset and clear
Most flip-flop chips also have asynchronous inputs that act immediately, regardless of the clock:

Preset (PRE, or direct set S_D): forces Q = 1.
Clear (CLR, or direct reset R_D): forces Q = 0.

They’re usually active-LOW (bubbles on the symbol):






























\overline{PRE}\overline{CLR}Effect11Normal clocked operation01Q = 1 right away10Q = 0 right away00Not used (invalid)
For normal synchronous operation, keep both HIGH. They’re typically used to put the flip-flop in a known state at power-up.
Try it: pull \overline{PRE} or \overline{CLR} LOW and watch Q change immediately, not at the next edge.
Interactive D flip-flop with preset and clear (open this page on the site to use it).
Key formulas
S-R latch (active-HIGH)
S = 1, R = 0 \Rightarrow Q = 1; \quad S = 0, R = 1 \Rightarrow Q = 0; \quad S = R = 0 \Rightarrow \text{hold}; \quad S = R = 1 \text{ invalid} \tag{7.1}
Gated D latch
Q = \begin{cases} D & EN = 1 \\ Q_{\text{previous}} & EN = 0 \end{cases} \tag{7.2}
D flip-flop
Q_{\text{next}} = D \quad (\text{at the triggering edge}) \tag{7.3}

Q_{\text{next}}: the output right after the clock edge
D: the data input just before the edge

J-K flip-flop
Q_{\text{next}} = J\,\overline{Q} + \overline{K}\,Q \quad (\text{at the triggering edge}) \tag{7.4}

Q: the output before the edge
J: set input; K: reset input. J = K = 1 toggles.

Check: J = K = 0 gives Q (hold), J = K = 1 gives \overline{Q} (toggle).
Examples
These follow the Lecture 8 examples, with different input sequences written as tables (each column is one time interval).
Example 1: S-R latch

Like the S-R latch slides

An active-HIGH S-R latch starts RESET (Q = 0). Find Q for this input sequence.









































Interval123456S100010R001000Q110011

Interval 1: set. Interval 2: hold (stays 1). Interval 3: reset. Interval 4: hold (stays 0). Interval 5: set. Interval 6: hold.

Example 2: Active-LOW latch

Like the NAND latch slide

A NAND \overline{S}-\overline{R} latch starts SET (Q = 1). Find Q for \overline{S}\,\overline{R} = 11, 10, 11, 01, 11.





























\overline{S}11101\overline{R}10111Q10011

11: hold. 10: \overline{R} is LOW, so reset. 11: hold. 01: \overline{S} is LOW, so set. 11: hold.

Example 3: Gated S-R latch

Like Lecture 8, Example 1

A gated S-R latch starts RESET. Find Q.























































Interval1234567EN0101101S1100010R0001000Q0110000

Interval 1: S = 1 but EN = 0, so nothing happens.
Interval 2: EN = 1, S = 1 → set.
Interval 4: EN = 1, R = 1 → reset.
Interval 6: S = 1 again, but EN = 0, so it stays 0. Interval 7: EN = 1 but S = R = 0 → hold.

Example 4: Gated D latch

Like Lecture 8, Example 2

A gated D latch starts RESET. Find Q.

















































Interval12345678EN11001100D10101101Q10001111
While EN = 1, Q copies D (intervals 1–2 and 5–6). While EN = 0, Q keeps whatever D was when EN fell, no matter what D does.
Example 5: D flip-flop

Like Lecture 8, “D Flip-Flop” example

A positive edge-triggered D flip-flop starts RESET. The value of D at each of five rising clock edges is 1, 1, 0, 1, 0. Find Q after each edge.





























Rising edge12345D at the edge11010Q after11010
\overline{Q} is always the opposite: 0, 0, 1, 0, 1. Any changes in D between edges have no effect.
Example 6: J-K flip-flop

Like Lecture 8, Example 4

A positive edge-triggered J-K flip-flop starts RESET. Find Q after each edge.


















































Rising edge123456J101101K001111ModesetholdtoggletoggleresettoggleQ after110101
Example 7: Latch vs flip-flop on the same inputs

Ties together Examples 4 and 5

D and a control signal are fed to both a gated D latch (control = EN) and a positive edge-triggered D flip-flop (control = CLK). Both start RESET. The control goes HIGH during interval 2 and stays HIGH through interval 4, and D goes 0, 1, 0, 1, 0 across intervals 1–5. Compare Q.













































Interval12345Control01110D01010Q (D latch)01011Q (D flip-flop)01111

The latch is transparent the whole time the control is HIGH, so it copies every change of D in intervals 2–4, then holds the last value (1).
The flip-flop only looks at D at the single rising edge (start of interval 2), where D = 1, and ignores the rest.

Example 8: Asynchronous preset and clear

Like Lecture 8, Example 5

A positive edge-triggered D flip-flop with active-LOW \overline{PRE} and \overline{CLR} starts with Q = 0, and D = 1 the whole time. Find Q.


















































Interval123456Rising edge at start?noyesnoyesnoyes\overline{PRE}111101\overline{CLR}001110Q000110

Intervals 1–2: \overline{CLR} is LOW, so Q is held at 0 even though there’s an edge with D = 1 in interval 2.
Interval 4: both inputs HIGH, so the edge clocks in D = 1.
Interval 5: \overline{PRE} LOW forces Q = 1 (it already is).
Interval 6: \overline{CLR} LOW forces Q = 0 immediately, overriding the clock edge.

Common mistakes

Treating a gated latch like a flip-flop. A latch follows its inputs for the whole time EN is HIGH, not just at the edge.
Forgetting that the NAND latch is active-LOW: \overline{S} = 0 sets it, and 11 is the hold state.
Using S = R = 1 on an S-R latch. It’s invalid; the J-K flip-flop is the version where 1, 1 is allowed (toggle).
Letting Q change between clock edges on a flip-flop. Only the edge (and the asynchronous inputs) can change it.
Reading D after the edge instead of just before it.
Waiting for a clock edge to apply \overline{PRE} or \overline{CLR}. They’re asynchronous: they act immediately.

courses/ele-302/ch05-operational-amplifi.title: Ch 5: Operational Amplifiers
courses/ele-302/ch05-operational-amplifi.content:
Overview


                  
                  Readings Alexander & Sadiku, Ch 5
                  
                

An operational amplifier (op amp) takes the voltage difference between its two inputs, multiplies it by a very large gain, and outputs the result. With external resistors providing negative feedback, it becomes a precise building block for amplifiers, summers, buffers, and more.
Components



































TerminalNameWhat it doesV_-Inverting inputSignal here is subtracted: raising V_- pushes V_{out} down. Usually where feedback connects.V_+Non-inverting inputSignal here is added: raising V_+ pushes V_{out} up.V_{CC+}Positive supplyPowers the op amp; sets the upper limit of V_{out}.V_{CC-}Negative supplyPowers the op amp; sets the lower limit of V_{out}.V_{out}OutputAmplified difference A(V_+ - V_-), clipped between the supply rails.
Try it: pick a terminal to see what it does, then move the sliders. Turn A up to a real op amp’s 10^5 and watch the output hit a rail unless the inputs are almost equal.
Interactive op amp diagram (open this page on the site to use it).


                  
                  Supply pins are usually left off circuit diagrams, but they're always there and they're why the output saturates. 
                  
                

Notes
Open Loop
Open loop means the op amp is used on its own, with nothing connecting the output back to either input (Figure 5.1). The output is just:
v_o = A\,(v_+ - v_-) \tag{5.1}

Figure 5.1: An open-loop op amp (left) and its output vs. the input difference (right).
This isn’t very useful as an amplifier, for two reasons:

It saturates almost instantly. A is huge (around 10^5), so with \pm 15\ \text{V} supplies the output hits a rail once the inputs differ by more than 15 / 10^5 = 0.15\ \text{mV}. Any real signal is bigger than that, so the output just sits at +15 or -15\ \text{V}.
The gain is unreliable. A changes a lot between chips, with temperature, and with frequency, so even a tiny signal wouldn’t get a predictable gain.



                  
                  Open loop is still useful as a comparator: the output tells you which input is bigger (high rail if v_+ > v_-, low rail if v_+ < v_-).
                  
                

Negative Feedback
Negative feedback fixes the open-loop problem by connecting the output back to the inverting input (v_-), either through a resistor or a plain wire, as in the buffer in Figure 5.2.

Figure 5.2: A buffer, the simplest negative feedback circuit. The output is wired straight back to v_-.
Why it works: the op amp corrects itself

Say v_o is a bit too high which happens where there’s a larger difference between v_+ - v_- .
Some of v_o is fed back to v_-, so v_- rises too.
That makes v_+ - v_- smaller, so A(v_+ - v_-) pulls v_o back down.
The same thing happens in reverse if v_o is too low.

The output settles at whatever voltage makes v_- almost exactly equal to v_+. That’s where the virtual short (v_+ = v_-) comes from.


                  
                  Buffer with A = 10^5 and v_i = 2\ \text{V}
                  
                

The output is wired straight to v_-, so v_- = v_o:
v_o = A(v_i - v_o) \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_o = \frac{A}{1 + A}\,v_i = \frac{10^5}{100\,001}(2) \approx 1.99998\ \text{V}
The inputs differ by only 2 - 1.99998 = 20\ \mu\text{V}. In practice that’s v_+ = v_-.


The gain is set by the resistors, not by A
If a fraction \beta of the output gets fed back to v_-, the gain of the whole circuit is:
A_{CL} = \frac{A}{1 + A\beta} \approx \frac{1}{\beta} \quad (\text{when } A\beta \gg 1) \tag{5.2}

A_{CL}: closed-loop gain, v_o / v_i for the whole circuit with feedback connected
A: open-loop gain of the op amp itself
\beta: feedback factor, the fraction of v_o that reaches v_-. For a non-inverting amp, \beta = \frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_f}

For the non-inverting amp, \frac{1}{\beta} = \frac{R_1 + R_f}{R_1} = 1 + \frac{R_f}{R_1}, which is exactly its gain formula, Eq. (5.5). A cancels out, which is the whole point: A varies a lot from chip to chip and with temperature, but resistor values are precise and stable.
Positive Feedback
Positive feedback connects the output back to the non-inverting input (v_+) instead. Now the feedback pushes the output the same way it’s already going, so instead of correcting itself, the op amp runs away:

Say v_o goes up a little.
Some of v_o is fed back to v_+, so v_+ rises too.
That makes v_+ - v_- bigger, so A(v_+ - v_-) pushes v_o up even more.
This repeats until v_o hits the supply rail, and it stays there.

So the output is never in between: it’s always at +V_{sat} or -V_{sat}, and the virtual short (v_+ = v_-) does not apply. That makes positive feedback useless for amplifying, but useful for switching circuits.
Where it’s used: the Schmitt trigger
A Schmitt trigger is a comparator with positive feedback added. The input goes to v_-, and R_1 and R_2 feed a fraction of the output back to v_+ (Figure 5.3):

Figure 5.3: An inverting Schmitt trigger (left) and its hysteresis loop (right).
Because no current flows into v_+, R_1 and R_2 form a voltage divider from the output:
v_+ = \beta\,v_o, \qquad \beta = \frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2} \tag{5.3}

v_+: voltage at the non-inverting input, which acts as the switching threshold
v_o: output voltage, either +V_{sat} or -V_{sat}
\beta: fraction of the output fed back to v_+
R_1: resistor from v_+ to ground
R_2: feedback resistor, from the output to v_+

Since v_o can only be \pm V_{sat}, there are two thresholds, +\beta V_{sat} and -\beta V_{sat}. With R_1 = 10\ \text{k}\Omega, R_2 = 40\ \text{k}\Omega and \pm 12\ \text{V} supplies, \beta = \frac{10}{50} = 0.2, so the thresholds are \pm 2.4\ \text{V}:

While v_o = +12\ \text{V}, v_+ = +2.4\ \text{V}. The output only flips to -12\ \text{V} once v_i rises above +2.4\ \text{V}.
While v_o = -12\ \text{V}, v_+ = -2.4\ \text{V}. The output only flips back once v_i drops below -2.4\ \text{V}.

This gap between the two thresholds is called hysteresis (the loop in Figure 5.3). It’s the reason to use one: a noisy signal wobbling around a single threshold would make a plain comparator flip back and forth rapidly, but a Schmitt trigger ignores any wobble smaller than the gap.
Spotting the Feedback Type

Figure 5.4: The three possibilities. The feedback path, if there is one, is highlighted.





























Output connects back to…FeedbackWhat happensCan you use v_+ = v_-?v_- (inverting input)NegativeOutput settles at a stable valueYesv_+ (non-inverting input)PositiveOutput runs away to a supply railNoNothing (open loop)NoneOutput saturates (comparator)No


                  
                  Every amplifier circuit in this chapter uses negative feedback. If you can't find a path from the output back to v_-, don't assume the virtual short.
                  
                

Ideal Op Amp Model
In the ideal world, op amps are a lot easier to work with. This is because you can assume A \to \infty, R_i \to \infty, R_o \to 0. This gives two rules:

No current into the inputs: i_+ = i_- = 0
Inputs are at the same voltage (virtual short): v_+ = v_- (only valid with negative feedback)



                  
                  Solving method Apply the two ideal rules, then do KCL at the inverting node. Never write KCL at the output node (the op amp sources unknown current there).
                  
                

Real Op Amp Model

Modeled as input resistance R_i between the inputs, and a dependent source A v_d in series with output resistance R_o.
Typical values: A \approx 10^5–10^8, R_i \approx 10^6–10^{13}\ \Omega, R_o \approx 10–100\ \Omega.
Saturation: output can’t exceed the supplies, so V_{CC-} \le v_o \le V_{CC+}.

Try it: pick each part of the model, then switch to the ideal op amp to see where the two ideal rules come from.
Interactive op amp model (open this page on the site to use it).
Key formulas
General
v_o = A\,v_d = A\,(v_+ - v_-) \tag{5.1}

v_o: output voltage
A: open-loop gain (the op amp’s built-in gain, with no feedback)
v_d: differential input voltage, v_+ - v_-
v_+: voltage at the non-inverting input
v_-: voltage at the inverting input

Inverting amplifier
v_o = -\frac{R_f}{R_1}\,v_i \tag{5.4}

v_o: output voltage
v_i: input voltage, fed through R_1 into the inverting input
R_1: input resistor, from v_i to the inverting input
R_f: feedback resistor, from the output back to the inverting input

Non-inverting amplifier
v_o = \left(1 + \frac{R_f}{R_1}\right) v_i \tag{5.5}

v_o: output voltage
v_i: input voltage, applied directly to the non-inverting input
R_1: resistor from the inverting input to ground
R_f: feedback resistor, from the output back to the inverting input

Voltage follower (buffer)
v_o = v_i \tag{5.6}

v_o: output voltage (the output is wired straight to the inverting input)
v_i: input voltage, applied to the non-inverting input

Summing amplifier (inverting)
v_o = -\left(\frac{R_f}{R_1}v_1 + \frac{R_f}{R_2}v_2 + \frac{R_f}{R_3}v_3\right) \tag{5.7}

v_o: output voltage
v_1, v_2, v_3: input voltages being summed
R_1, R_2, R_3: input resistors, one per input, each going to the inverting input
R_f: feedback resistor, from the output back to the inverting input

Difference amplifier (general)
v_o = -\frac{R_2}{R_1}\,v_1 + \frac{R_4}{R_3 + R_4}\left(1 + \frac{R_2}{R_1}\right) v_2 \tag{5.8}
Difference amplifier (when R_1/R_2 = R_3/R_4)
v_o = \frac{R_2}{R_1}\,(v_2 - v_1) \tag{5.9}

v_o: output voltage
v_1: input voltage on the inverting side
v_2: input voltage on the non-inverting side
R_1: input resistor, from v_1 to the inverting input
R_2: feedback resistor, from the output back to the inverting input
R_3: input resistor, from v_2 to the non-inverting input
R_4: resistor from the non-inverting input to ground

Eq. (5.8) is just superposition: the v_1 term is an inverting amp, and the v_2 term is a voltage divider (R_3, R_4) followed by a non-inverting amp. Eq. (5.9) is the special case where the ratios match.
Cascaded stages
A_{total} = A_1 \cdot A_2 \cdot A_3 \cdots \tag{5.10}

A_{total}: overall gain of the chain (final output ÷ first input)
A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots: closed-loop gain of each individual stage

Examples
These follow the assigned textbook problems for Chapter 5, with different numbers. Tutorial problems are marked (T); the quiz problems will be similar to those.
Example 1: Op amp equivalent model

Like Prob. 5.1

The equivalent model of an op amp is shown in Figure 5.5. Determine (a) the input resistance, (b) the output resistance, and (c) the voltage gain in dB.

Figure 5.5: Equivalent model for Example 1.
Read the model straight off the diagram:

(a) The resistance between the input terminals: R_i = 2\ \text{M}\Omega
(b) The resistance in series with the output: R_o = 50\ \Omega
(c) The open-loop gain is the number in front of v_d, so A = 2 \times 10^5. In decibels:
A_{dB} = 20\log_{10}A = 20\log_{10}(2 \times 10^5) = 106.02\ \text{dB}

Example 2: Non-ideal voltage follower

Like Prob. 5.5

The op amp in Figure 5.6 has an open-loop gain of 50,000, an input resistance of 20 kΩ, and an output resistance of 50 Ω. Find the voltage gain v_o/v_i using the non-ideal model.

Figure 5.6: Voltage follower for Example 2.

Replace the op amp with its model. R_i sits between v_+ = v_i and v_- = v_o, and the output is A v_d in series with R_o, where
v_d = v_+ - v_- = v_i - v_o
KCL at the output node. The current through R_i (from v_i to v_o) plus the current through R_o (from the source to v_o) must add to zero, since nothing else is connected:
\frac{v_i - v_o}{R_i} + \frac{A(v_i - v_o) - v_o}{R_o} = 0
Multiply through by R_i R_o and solve:
\frac{v_o}{v_i} = \frac{R_o + A R_i}{R_o + (A + 1)R_i} = \frac{50 + (5 \times 10^4)(20\text{k})}{50 + (50\,001)(20\text{k})} = 0.99998



                  
                  The ideal answer is exactly 1. The non-ideal model is only worth the algebra when the question asks for it, as this one does. 
                  
                

Example 3: Non-ideal inverting amplifier (T)

Like Prob. 5.7 (T)

The op amp in Figure 5.7 has R_i = 200\ \text{k}\Omega, R_o = 50\ \Omega, and A = 200{,}000. Find the differential voltage v_d and the output voltage v_o.

Figure 5.7: Inverting amplifier for Example 3.
Call the inverting-input node v_1. Since v_+ = 0, v_d = v_+ - v_- = -v_1, and the op amp’s output source is A v_d = -A v_1.

KCL at v_1 (in through 20 kΩ = out through R_i to ground + out through 100 kΩ):
\frac{2\text{m} - v_1}{20\text{k}} = \frac{v_1}{200\text{k}} + \frac{v_1 - v_o}{100\text{k}}
Multiplying by 200k: \quad 20\text{m} = 13\,v_1 - 2\,v_o
KCL at v_o (in through 100 kΩ = out through R_o into the source):
\frac{v_1 - v_o}{100\text{k}} = \frac{v_o - (-A v_1)}{50}
Multiplying by 100k: \quad v_1 - v_o = 2000\,v_o + (4 \times 10^8)\,v_1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_1 \approx -5.0025 \times 10^{-6}\,v_o
Substitute into step 1:
20\text{m} = 13(-5.0025 \times 10^{-6})\,v_o - 2\,v_o \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_o \approx -9.9997\ \text{mV}
Then v_1 = (-5.0025 \times 10^{-6})(-9.9997\text{m}) \approx 50.02\ \text{nV}, so
v_d = -v_1 \approx -50.02\ \text{nV}



                  
                  Check: the ideal answer is -\frac{100}{20}(2\ \text{mV}) = -10\ \text{mV}, and v_d is tiny, so the virtual short is a very good approximation.
                  
                

Example 4: Sources connected directly to the inputs

Like Prob. 5.9

Determine v_o in the op amp circuit of Figure 5.8.

Figure 5.8: Circuit for Example 4.

v_+ is fixed by the voltage source: v_+ = 3\ \text{V}, so v_- = 3\ \text{V} too.
No current enters the op amp, so all 2 mA from the current source has to leave the v_- node through the 5 kΩ resistor:
\frac{v_- - v_o}{5\text{k}} = 2\text{m} \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3 - v_o = 10 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_o = -7\ \text{V}

Example 5: Find v_o and i_o

Like Probs. 5.13 and 5.29

Find v_o and i_o in the circuit of Figure 5.9.

Figure 5.9: Circuit for Example 5.

v_+ from the divider (no current into v_+, so the divider is unloaded):
v_+ = 2 \cdot \frac{30}{20 + 30} = 1.2\ \text{V}
Non-inverting gain, Eq. (5.5):
v_o = \left(1 + \frac{40}{10}\right)(1.2) = 6\ \text{V}
i_o is the op amp’s output current. It splits between the 12 kΩ load and the feedback path (40 kΩ then 10 kΩ to ground):
i_o = \frac{6}{12\text{k}} + \frac{6}{40\text{k} + 10\text{k}} = 0.5\ \text{mA} + 0.12\ \text{mA} = 0.62\ \text{mA}



                  
                  The feedback path counts as a load too. Forgetting it is the most common mistake on i_o questions.
                  
                

Example 6: T-network in the feedback (T)

Like Prob. 5.15 (T)

(a) Determine the ratio v_o/i_s for the circuit in Figure 5.10. (b) Evaluate it for R_1 = 10\ \text{k}\Omega, R_2 = 5\ \text{k}\Omega, R_3 = 20\ \text{k}\Omega.

Figure 5.10: Circuit for Example 6. Call the middle node of the T v_m.
(a)

v_- = v_+ = 0. All of i_s flows from the v_- node through R_1 to v_m:
\frac{0 - v_m}{R_1} = i_s \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_m = -i_s R_1
KCL at v_m (in through R_1 = out through R_2 + out through R_3):
i_s = \frac{v_m}{R_2} + \frac{v_m - v_o}{R_3}
Solve for v_o and substitute v_m:
v_o = v_m\left(1 + \frac{R_3}{R_2}\right) - R_3\,i_s \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{v_o}{i_s} = -\left(R_1 + R_3 + \frac{R_1 R_3}{R_2}\right)

(b)
\frac{v_o}{i_s} = -\left(10\text{k} + 20\text{k} + \frac{(10\text{k})(20\text{k})}{5\text{k}}\right) = -70\ \text{k}\Omega


                  
                  The ratio has units of ohms because it's volts out per amp in. The T-network gives a large gain (70 kΩ) without needing any single large resistor. 
                  
                

Example 7: Find i_o with a resistor network on the input

Like Prob. 5.19

Determine i_o in the circuit of Figure 5.11.

Figure 5.11: Circuit for Example 7.

Replace everything left of the 2 kΩ with its Thévenin equivalent (1.5 V source, 3 kΩ, 6 kΩ):
V_{th} = 1.5 \cdot \frac{6}{3 + 6} = 1\ \text{V}, \qquad R_{th} = 3\text{k} \parallel 6\text{k} = 2\ \text{k}\Omega
Now it’s a plain inverting amp with an input resistance of R_{th} + 2\text{k} = 4\ \text{k}\Omega. By Eq. (5.4):
v_o = -\frac{8}{4}(1) = -2\ \text{V}
i_o flows down through the 4 kΩ load:
i_o = \frac{v_o}{4\text{k}} = \frac{-2}{4\text{k}} = -0.5\ \text{mA}

So 0.5 mA actually flows up through the load, into the op amp’s output.


                  
                  Thévenin works here because the 2 kΩ connects to the virtual ground, so the circuit to its left sees a fixed load. Without Thévenin, you'd do KCL at the 6 kΩ node instead and get the same answer. 
                  
                

Example 8: Current source on the input, and power

Like Prob. 5.33

Refer to the op amp circuit in Figure 5.12. Calculate i_x and the power absorbed by the 6 kΩ load.

Figure 5.12: Circuit for Example 8.

v_+: no current enters the op amp, so all 1.5 mA flows through the 6 kΩ and 3 kΩ in parallel:
v_+ = (1.5\text{m})(6\text{k} \parallel 3\text{k}) = (1.5\text{m})(2\text{k}) = 3\ \text{V}
Non-inverting gain, Eq. (5.5):
v_o = \left(1 + \frac{4}{2}\right)(3) = 9\ \text{V}
Current and power in the load:
i_x = \frac{9}{6\text{k}} = 1.5\ \text{mA}, \qquad P = v_o\,i_x = (9)(1.5\text{m}) = 13.5\ \text{mW}

Example 9: Summing amplifier, find an unknown input

Like Prob. 5.39

For the circuit in Figure 5.13, determine the value of v_2 that makes v_o = -9\ \text{V}.

Figure 5.13: Summing amplifier for Example 9.

Write Eq. (5.7) with R_f = 60\ \text{k}\Omega:
v_o = -\left(\frac{60}{20}(2) + \frac{60}{30}\,v_2 + \frac{60}{40}(-4)\right) = -(6 + 2v_2 - 6) = -2\,v_2
Set it equal to the target:
-2\,v_2 = -9 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_2 = 4.5\ \text{V}

Example 10: Design problem

Like Prob. 5.45

Design an op amp circuit to perform v_o = 2v_1 - 3v_2. All resistances must be ≤ 100 kΩ.

Pick the circuit. One input is subtracted and one is added, so use a difference amplifier. The subtracted input (v_2) goes to the inverting side and v_1 to the non-inverting side, so v_1 and v_2 swap places compared with Eq. (5.8).
Match the inverting term using Eq. (5.8): we need \frac{R_2}{R_1} = 3. Choose R_1 = 20\ \text{k}\Omega, R_2 = 60\ \text{k}\Omega.
Match the non-inverting term. The non-inverting gain is 1 + \frac{R_2}{R_1} = 4, but we only want 2, so the divider has to halve v_1 first:
\frac{R_4}{R_3 + R_4} \cdot 4 = 2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{R_4}{R_3 + R_4} = \frac{1}{2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad R_3 = R_4
Choose R_3 = R_4 = 50\ \text{k}\Omega.
Check: v_o = -\frac{60}{20}v_2 + \frac{50}{100}(4)\,v_1 = 2v_1 - 3v_2 ✓, and every resistor is ≤ 100 kΩ ✓.


Figure 5.14: One possible design for Example 10. Many other resistor values work too.


                  
                  Design questions have many right answers. Pick one resistor freely (here R_1), then solve for the rest from the gains.
                  
                

Example 11: Difference amplifier with mismatched resistors

Like Prob. 5.47

The circuit in Figure 5.15 is a difference amplifier. Find v_o given v_1 = 2\ \text{V} and v_2 = 3\ \text{V}.

Figure 5.15: Difference amplifier for Example 11.

Check the ratios first: R_1/R_2 = 5/20 = 0.25 but R_3/R_4 = 10/30 = 0.33. They don’t match, so the shortcut Eq. (5.9) does not apply.
v_+ from the divider:
v_+ = 3 \cdot \frac{30}{10 + 30} = 2.25\ \text{V} = v_-
KCL at v_-:
\frac{2 - 2.25}{5\text{k}} = \frac{2.25 - v_o}{20\text{k}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2.25 - v_o = -1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_o = 3.25\ \text{V}
Check with Eq. (5.8): -\frac{20}{5}(2) + \frac{30}{40}\left(1 + \frac{20}{5}\right)(3) = -8 + 11.25 = 3.25\ \text{V} ✓



                  
                  Using the shortcut here would give \frac{20}{5}(3 - 2) = 4\ \text{V}, which is wrong. Always check the ratios.
                  
                

Example 12: Cascaded stages (T)

Like Prob. 5.59 (T)

In the circuit of Figure 5.16, determine the voltage gain v_o/v_s. Take R = 10\ \text{k}\Omega.

Figure 5.16: Two cascaded stages for Example 12.

Stage 1 is non-inverting (v_s on v_+, R to ground, 3R feedback). By Eq. (5.5):
A_1 = \frac{v_1}{v_s} = 1 + \frac{3R}{R} = 4
Stage 2 is inverting (R in, 2R feedback). By Eq. (5.4):
A_2 = \frac{v_o}{v_1} = -\frac{2R}{R} = -2
Multiply, Eq. (5.10):
\frac{v_o}{v_s} = A_1 A_2 = (4)(-2) = -8



                  
                   R cancels out of every ratio, so its value (10\ \text{k}\Omega) doesn't affect the answer. Stage 1's output can feed stage 2 directly because an op amp output acts like an ideal voltage source.
                  
                

Common mistakes

Writing KCL at the output node instead of the inverting input
Assuming v_+ = v_- when there’s no negative feedback (e.g. comparators)
Forgetting the minus sign on inverting and summing amps
Ignoring saturation: a “gain of 100” on 1 V with ±15 V rails gives 15 V, not 100 V
Mixing up R_1 and R_f in the non-inverting gain (1 + R_f/R_1, not R_1/R_f)

courses/ele-302/ch08-second-order-circui.title: Ch 8: Second-Order Circuits
