Overview


                  
                  Readings Alexander & Sadiku, Ch 8 (§8.1–8.7)
                  
                

A second-order circuit has two energy-storage elements, usually an inductor and a capacitor, that can’t be combined into one. They can’t be merged because they relate voltage and current in opposite ways: an inductor’s voltage depends on the derivative of its current, while a capacitor’s voltage depends on the integral of its current. Having both in one circuit makes it obey a second-order differential equation, so its response needs two initial conditions instead of one. Depending on how much resistance there is, the response either dies away smoothly or rings (oscillates) as energy sloshes back and forth between the L and the C.
Every problem in this chapter is solved with basically the same four steps:

Write the differential equation for the circuit after the switch moves, using KVL and/or KCL.
Find the natural solution from the homogeneous equation and its characteristic equation.
Find the initial conditions from the circuit before and just after switching.
Write the total solution (natural + forced) and use the initial conditions to find the constants.



                  
                  Background pages 
                  
                

This chapter sticks to the method for solving second-order circuits. These pages explain the ideas behind it in more detail:

Capacitors and Inductors: the element laws, stored energy, and why v_C and i_L can’t jump
LC Oscillation: why energy swings back and forth between L and C
Damping in Series and Parallel RLC: why R does opposite things in series and parallel
Second-Order Differential Equations: why the method works, the three cases, and finding the constants
Source Transformation: simplifying a circuit before solving it



Notes
Key Concept: Energy Can’t Change Instantly
Everything in this chapter rests on one physical fact: the energy stored in an inductor or a capacitor can’t change instantaneously. Here’s why, and what it means.


                  
                  Need a refresher on the elements themselves? Capacitors and Inductors covers how each one is built, where its element law comes from, series and parallel combinations, and worked examples.
                  
                

Inductor. The voltage across an inductor depends on how fast its current changes. Capacitor. The current into a capacitor depends on how fast its voltage changes:
v_L = L\frac{di_L}{dt}, \qquad i_C = C\frac{dv_C}{dt} \tag{8.1}
Suppose the inductor current jumped from one value to another in zero time. Then \frac{di_L}{dt} = \frac{\Delta i}{\Delta t} with \Delta t \to 0 would be infinite, so v_L would be infinite. No real circuit can supply an infinite voltage, so inductor current can’t jump. The same argument with i_C = C\frac{dv_C}{dt} shows that capacitor voltage can’t jump (it would need infinite current).
The same idea in terms of energy: integrating power p = vi over time gives the stored energy
w_L = \tfrac{1}{2} L\,i_L^2, \qquad w_C = \tfrac{1}{2} C\,v_C^2 \tag{8.2}
Changing that energy in zero time would need infinite power. Since w_L depends only on i_L and w_C only on v_C, those are the two quantities that must be continuous at a switching instant:
i_L(0^+) = i_L(0^-), \qquad v_C(0^+) = v_C(0^-) \tag{8.3}
Here 0^- means “just before the switch moves” and 0^+ means “just after”. Nothing else is protected: resistor voltages, the capacitor’s current and the inductor’s voltage are all allowed to jump.


                  
                  Integral forms 
                  
                

Rearranging Eq. (8.1) and integrating from 0 to t gives each element’s value at any time, starting from its initial value (more on the integral form). You’ll use these in Step 1 to write KVL/KCL with only one unknown:
i_L(t) = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^t v_L\,dt + i_L(0), \qquad v_C(t) = \frac{1}{C}\int_0^t i_C\,dt + v_C(0)


At DC steady state (a circuit that has been switched on for a long time, or t \to \infty), nothing is changing anymore, so every derivative is zero:

v_L = L \cdot 0 = 0: the inductor has no voltage across it, so it acts like a short circuit.
i_C = C \cdot 0 = 0: the capacitor passes no current, so it acts like an open circuit.

You can also see this from impedance. DC means \omega = 0, so Z_L = j\omega L = 0 (a short) and Z_C = \frac{1}{j\omega C} \to \infty (an open). See DC steady state for the matching rules at the instant a source switches on.

Figure 8.1: At DC steady state, an inductor acts like a short and a capacitor acts like an open.
Why Energy Swings Between L and C
A capacitor stores energy in its voltage (\frac{1}{2}Cv^2) and an inductor in its current (\frac{1}{2}Li^2). Connected together, they keep handing that energy to each other: the capacitor discharges into the inductor, and the inductor’s current (which can’t stop instantly) carries on and charges the capacitor the other way. So the voltage and current oscillate, like a mass bouncing on a spring. A resistor acts like friction, turning a little energy into heat on every swing, so the oscillation dies out. That’s the damping that decides which of the three cases in Step 2 you get.


                  
                  The full story, with a graph of one cycle, the mass-on-a-spring analogy and a worked example, is in LC Oscillation.
                  
                

Step 1: Write the Differential Equation
Use the circuit after the switch moves (t > 0). Pick the variable you’re solving for, write KVL and/or KCL, then turn everything into that one variable:

Write KVL (around a loop) or KCL (at a node).
Replace each element’s voltage or current using Eq. (8.1), or the integral forms above, so the only unknown is your chosen variable.
If there’s an integral, differentiate the whole equation once to get rid of it. Any constant (like a DC source, or v_C(0)) differentiates to 0.
Divide by the coefficient of the highest derivative, so the equation is in standard form.

Example: series RLC. In Figure 8.2, the same current i flows through every element. KVL around the loop, with a source V_s if there is one:

Figure 8.2: A series RLC circuit driven by a source V_s. All four elements carry the same current i. For a source-free circuit, V_s = 0.
Ri + L\frac{di}{dt} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{C}\int_0^t i\,dt + v_C(0)}_{v_C} = V_s
Differentiate once (the integral becomes i; the constants v_C(0) and DC V_s become 0), then divide by L:
\frac{d^2 i}{dt^2} + \frac{R}{L}\frac{di}{dt} + \frac{1}{LC}\,i = 0 \tag{8.4}
Example: parallel RLC. In Figure 8.3, every element has the same voltage v. KCL at the top node, with a source current I_s if there is one:

Figure 8.3: A parallel RLC circuit driven by a source I_s. All four elements share the same voltage v. For a source-free circuit, I_s = 0.
\frac{v}{R} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{L}\int_0^t v\,dt + i_L(0)}_{i_L} + C\frac{dv}{dt} = I_s
Differentiate once, then divide by C:
\frac{d^2 v}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{RC}\frac{dv}{dt} + \frac{1}{LC}\,v = 0 \tag{8.5}
Standard form. Every second-order circuit ends up looking like this, where x is whichever voltage or current you chose and f is whatever’s left on the right (often 0 or a constant):
\frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} + 2\alpha\frac{dx}{dt} + \omega_0^2\,x = f \tag{8.6}
Matching Eqs. (8.4) and (8.5) against Eq. (8.6) gives two numbers that describe the circuit:
\alpha = \frac{R}{2L} \quad \text{(series)} \tag{8.7}
\alpha = \frac{1}{2RC} \quad \text{(parallel)} \tag{8.8}
\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} \quad \text{(both)} \tag{8.9}
\alpha (the neper frequency, in Np/s) measures how fast resistance drains energy out of the circuit. \omega_0 (the resonant frequency, in rad/s) measures how fast energy wants to swing between L and C.
R does opposite things in series and parallel. In a series circuit the oscillating current flows through the resistor, so a bigger R burns more energy and means more damping. In a parallel circuit the resistor sits beside L and C and only the current leaking through it is lost, so a bigger R means less damping. That’s why Eq. (8.7) grows with R and Eq. (8.8) shrinks. The power argument, a comparison table and the critical resistance are in Damping in Series and Parallel RLC.


                  
                  Eqs. (8.7) and (8.8) only apply to a pure series or pure parallel RLC, and many circuits are neither (Example 11 is one). When in doubt, derive the circuit's own differential equation with KVL/KCL, put it in standard form, and read \alpha off the middle coefficient, which is 2\alpha. That always works.
                  
                



                  
                  A source transformation often turns a messier circuit into a plain series or parallel RLC: a current source with a resistor in parallel can be swapped for a voltage source with the same resistor in series ( V = IR), and the other way round. See Source Transformation.
                  
                

Step 2: Find the Natural Solution
The natural solution x_N is how the circuit behaves on its own, with no source pushing it. Get it from the homogeneous equation: set the right-hand side of Eq. (8.6) to 0.
\frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} + 2\alpha\frac{dx}{dt} + \omega_0^2\,x = 0
How to solve it. Try x = Ae^{st}. Every derivative of e^{st} is just s times itself (\frac{d}{dt}Ae^{st} = sAe^{st}, \frac{d^2}{dt^2}Ae^{st} = s^2Ae^{st}), so substituting gives
(s^2 + 2\alpha s + \omega_0^2)\,Ae^{st} = 0
Ae^{st} is never zero (unless the whole response is zero), so the bracket must be. That’s the characteristic equation:
s^2 + 2\alpha s + \omega_0^2 = 0 \tag{8.10}
It’s a quadratic, so the quadratic formula gives its two roots:
s_{1,2} = -\alpha \pm \sqrt{\alpha^2 - \omega_0^2} \tag{8.11}
What’s under the square root decides which of three cases you’re in:





























CaseConditionRootsNatural solutionOverdamped\alpha > \omega_0Two different real numbersEq. (8.12): decays, no oscillationCritically damped\alpha = \omega_0One repeated real number, s = -\alphaEq. (8.13): fastest decay without oscillatingUnderdamped\alpha < \omega_0Complex pair, s = -\alpha \pm j\omega_dEq. (8.14): oscillates inside a decaying envelope

Figure 8.4: The three cases, all starting from the same value with zero initial slope.
x_N = A_1 e^{s_1 t} + A_2 e^{s_2 t} \tag{8.12}
x_N = A_1 e^{-\alpha t} + A_2\,t\,e^{-\alpha t} \tag{8.13}
x_N = A\,e^{-\alpha t}\cos(\omega_d t + \theta) \tag{8.14}
\omega_d = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \alpha^2} \tag{8.15}

In the underdamped case, e^{-\alpha t} is the shrinking envelope, \omega_d is how fast it oscillates, and \theta is a phase shift.
The constants (A_1, A_2, or A and \theta) are unknown until Step 4.
The textbook writes the underdamped case as e^{-\alpha t}(B_1\cos\omega_d t + B_2\sin\omega_d t). It’s the same function, and either form gets full marks.



                  
                  Why the repeated root needs the extra t, how complex roots turn into a decaying cosine (Euler's formula), and how to convert between the two underdamped forms are covered in Second-Order Differential Equations.
                  
                

Step 3: Find the Initial Conditions
A second-order equation needs two initial conditions: the starting value x(0) and the starting slope \frac{dx}{dt}(0), for the variable you chose in Step 1.
Before switching (t = 0^-). If the circuit has been in this state for a long time, it’s at DC steady state. Redraw it with every inductor as a short and every capacitor as an open (Figure 8.1), then use ordinary DC analysis to find i_L(0^-) and v_C(0^-).
After switching (t = 0^+). Redraw the circuit with the switch in its new position. By Eq. (8.3), the inductor still carries i_L(0^-) and the capacitor still holds v_C(0^-), so treat them as a current source and a voltage source with those values. Then use KVL/KCL on this circuit to find whatever else you need, especially the inductor voltage or capacitor current, which give the slopes (measure them with the passive sign convention, or the slope’s sign flips):
\frac{di_L}{dt}(0^+) = \frac{v_L(0^+)}{L}, \qquad \frac{dv_C}{dt}(0^+) = \frac{i_C(0^+)}{C} \tag{8.16}


                  
                  If your Step 1 variable isn't i_L or v_C (say, a resistor current), find its value and slope from the 0^+ circuit too. Only i_L and v_C are guaranteed to carry over from 0^-.
                  
                

Step 4: Write the Total Solution
The forced solution x_F is where the circuit ends up as t \to \infty, once all the transients have died out. With DC sources, that’s another DC steady state: redraw the final circuit with L shorted and C open and solve it. (You can also get it from Eq. (8.6) by setting the derivatives to 0: \omega_0^2\,x_F = f.)
The total solution is the two added together:
x_T = x_N + x_F \tag{8.17}
Now use the two initial conditions from Step 3 on the total solution x_T (not on x_N alone) to get two equations for the two unknown constants.
For the underdamped form, the derivative at t = 0 is the part that trips people up. Differentiating with the product rule:
\frac{d}{dt}\left[A e^{-\alpha t}\cos(\omega_d t + \theta)\right] = A e^{-\alpha t}\left[-\alpha\cos(\omega_d t + \theta) - \omega_d\sin(\omega_d t + \theta)\right]
At t = 0, e^0 = 1, so the two conditions become:
A\cos\theta = x(0) - x_F, \qquad -\alpha A\cos\theta - \omega_d A\sin\theta = \frac{dx}{dt}(0) \tag{8.18}
Solve the first for A\cos\theta, then the second for A\sin\theta. Then:

A = \sqrt{(A\cos\theta)^2 + (A\sin\theta)^2}
\theta is the angle whose cosine and sine have those signs. Picture the point (A\cos\theta,\ A\sin\theta) on a graph and take its angle from the positive horizontal axis, in radians.



                  
                  A calculator's \tan^{-1} only returns angles between -\frac{\pi}{2} and \frac{\pi}{2}. If A\cos\theta is negative, the real angle is in the second or third quadrant, so add \pi to the calculator's answer. Always check that \cos\theta and \sin\theta come out with the right signs. Second-Order Differential Equations has a table for all four quadrants and a third-quadrant example.
                  
                

Key formulas
Element laws and stored energy
v_L = L\frac{di_L}{dt}, \qquad i_C = C\frac{dv_C}{dt} \tag{8.1}
w_L = \tfrac{1}{2} L\,i_L^2, \qquad w_C = \tfrac{1}{2} C\,v_C^2 \tag{8.2}

v_L, i_L: inductor voltage and current
v_C, i_C: capacitor voltage and current
L: inductance (H); C: capacitance (F)
w_L, w_C: energy stored (J)

Continuity at a switching instant
i_L(0^+) = i_L(0^-), \qquad v_C(0^+) = v_C(0^-) \tag{8.3}

0^-, 0^+: just before and just after the switch moves

Standard form of the differential equation
\frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} + 2\alpha\frac{dx}{dt} + \omega_0^2\,x = f \tag{8.6}

x: the voltage or current being solved for
f: whatever is left on the right-hand side (0 if there’s no source after switching)

Neper frequency and resonant frequency
\alpha = \frac{R}{2L} \quad \text{(series)} \tag{8.7}
\alpha = \frac{1}{2RC} \quad \text{(parallel)} \tag{8.8}
\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} \tag{8.9}

\alpha: how fast the response decays (Np/s)
\omega_0: undamped natural frequency (rad/s)
R: the resistance in the series or parallel RLC, with the sources turned off

Characteristic equation and roots
s^2 + 2\alpha s + \omega_0^2 = 0 \tag{8.10}
s_{1,2} = -\alpha \pm \sqrt{\alpha^2 - \omega_0^2} \tag{8.11}

s_1, s_2: natural frequencies of the circuit (s⁻¹)

Natural solution
x_N = A_1 e^{s_1 t} + A_2 e^{s_2 t} \quad (\alpha > \omega_0) \tag{8.12}
x_N = A_1 e^{-\alpha t} + A_2\,t\,e^{-\alpha t} \quad (\alpha = \omega_0) \tag{8.13}
x_N = A\,e^{-\alpha t}\cos(\omega_d t + \theta) \quad (\alpha < \omega_0) \tag{8.14}
\omega_d = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \alpha^2} \tag{8.15}

A_1, A_2, A: constants found in Step 4
\theta: phase angle, in radians
\omega_d: damped natural frequency, the actual frequency of the oscillation (rad/s)

Initial slopes
\frac{di_L}{dt}(0^+) = \frac{v_L(0^+)}{L}, \qquad \frac{dv_C}{dt}(0^+) = \frac{i_C(0^+)}{C} \tag{8.16}
Total solution
x_T = x_N + x_F \tag{8.17}
A\cos\theta = x(0) - x_F, \qquad -\alpha A\cos\theta - \omega_d A\sin\theta = \frac{dx}{dt}(0) \tag{8.18}

x_T: total solution, the final answer
x_F: forced solution, the value as t \to \infty (DC analysis with L shorted and C open)
Eq. (8.18) is for the underdamped case only

Examples
These follow the assigned textbook problems for Chapter 8, with different numbers. Tutorial problems are marked (T); the quiz problems will be similar to those.
Example 1: Initial and final values

Like Prob. 8.1

The switch in Figure 8.5 has been closed for a long time and opens at t = 0. Find (a) i(0^+) and v(0^+), (b) \frac{di}{dt}(0^+) and \frac{dv}{dt}(0^+), (c) i(\infty) and v(\infty).

Figure 8.5: Circuit for Example 1.
(a) Before switching. The switch has been closed for a long time, so the circuit is at DC steady state: replace the inductor with a short and the capacitor with an open (Figure 8.6).

Figure 8.6: Example 1 at t = 0^-. The inductor is a short and the capacitor is an open.

Inductor branch: with the inductor shorted, the 10 V source sees only the 4 Ω, so i(0^-) = \frac{10}{4} = 2.5\ \text{A}.
Capacitor branch: the open capacitor blocks current, so nothing flows through the 6 Ω and it drops 0 V. The capacitor therefore sees the full source voltage: v(0^-) = 10\ \text{V}.

By Eq. (8.3), inductor current and capacitor voltage don’t jump:
i(0^+) = 2.5\ \text{A}, \qquad v(0^+) = 10\ \text{V}
(b) After switching. The switch is now open, so the source is disconnected. Redraw the circuit with the inductor carrying 2.5 A and the capacitor holding 10 V (Figure 8.7).

Figure 8.7: Example 1 at t = 0^+. The source is cut off and the two branches form one loop.

Capacitor slope. The two branches now form a single loop. The 2.5 A flowing down the inductor branch has nowhere to go except back up the capacitor branch, so the capacitor current (measured downward, into its + terminal) is i_C = -2.5\ \text{A}. By Eq. (8.16):
\frac{dv}{dt}(0^+) = \frac{i_C}{C} = \frac{-2.5}{0.5} = -5\ \text{V/s}
Inductor slope. We need v_L. Both branches connect the same top node to the same bottom rail, so they have the same voltage across them. Going down the capacitor branch: 6\,i_C + v = 6(-2.5) + 10 = -5\ \text{V}. Going down the inductor branch: 4i + v_L. Setting them equal:
4(2.5) + v_L = -5 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_L = -15\ \text{V} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{di}{dt}(0^+) = \frac{v_L}{L} = \frac{-15}{1} = -15\ \text{A/s}

(c) Final values. There’s no source left after t = 0, so the resistors eventually turn all the stored energy into heat:
i(\infty) = 0, \qquad v(\infty) = 0
Example 2: Initial values with a step source

Like Prob. 8.3

For the circuit in Figure 8.8, find (a) i_L(0^+), v_C(0^+) and v_R(0^+), (b) \frac{di_L}{dt}(0^+), \frac{dv_C}{dt}(0^+) and \frac{dv_R}{dt}(0^+), (c) i_L(\infty), v_C(\infty) and v_R(\infty).

Figure 8.8: Circuit for Example 2.
(a) Before switching. u(t) is the unit step: 0 for t < 0 and 1 for t > 0. So before t = 0 the source is 0 A, there’s no other source, and nothing in the circuit has ever been charged:
i_L(0^-) = 0, \qquad v_C(0^-) = 0
By Eq. (8.3) these carry over: i_L(0^+) = 0 and v_C(0^+) = 0. The 4 Ω is connected directly across the capacitor, so it has the same voltage: v_R(0^+) = 0.
(b) After switching. At t = 0^+ the source switches on to 2 A, but the capacitor still holds 0 V and the inductor still carries 0 A (Figure 8.9).

Figure 8.9: Example 2 at t = 0^+.

The 4 Ω has 0 V across it, so it takes \frac{0}{4} = 0 A.
The inductor branch carries 0 A.
KCL at the top node: the 2 A from the source has to go somewhere, and the only place left is the capacitor, so i_C = 2\ \text{A}.

By Eq. (8.16):
\frac{dv_C}{dt}(0^+) = \frac{i_C}{C} = \frac{2}{1/4} = 8\ \text{V/s}, \qquad \frac{dv_R}{dt}(0^+) = 8\ \text{V/s} \quad (\text{same voltage as the capacitor})
For the inductor, KVL around the right-hand loop gives v_L = v_C - 2\,i_L = 0 - 0 = 0, so \frac{di_L}{dt}(0^+) = \frac{0}{1/2} = 0.
(c) Final values. As t \to \infty the circuit reaches DC steady state again with the source at 2 A. Short the inductor and open the capacitor (Figure 8.10).

Figure 8.10: Example 2 as t \to \infty.
The 2 A now splits between the 4 Ω and the 2 Ω (whose bottom is shorted to the rail by the inductor). They’re in parallel, 4 \parallel 2 = \frac{4 \cdot 2}{4 + 2} = \frac{4}{3}\ \Omega:
v_C(\infty) = v_R(\infty) = (2)\left(\tfrac{4}{3}\right) = 2.67\ \text{V}, \qquad i_L(\infty) = \frac{2.67}{2} = 1.33\ \text{A}


                  
                  With a step source and nothing stored beforehand, every initial value is 0, but the initial slopes usually aren't. The source's current has to go somewhere the instant it turns on.
                  
                

Example 3: Type of damping

Like Prob. 8.7

A series RLC circuit has R = 50\ \Omega, L = 10\ \text{mH} and C = 1\ \mu\text{F}. What type of damping does it have? What value of R would make it critically damped?
The type of damping depends only on how \alpha compares with \omega_0 (Step 2), so find both.

Neper frequency, series circuit, Eq. (8.7):
\alpha = \frac{R}{2L} = \frac{50}{2(0.01)} = 2500\ \text{Np/s}
Resonant frequency, Eq. (8.9):
\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(0.01)(10^{-6})}} = \frac{1}{10^{-4}} = 10\,000\ \text{rad/s}
Compare. \alpha = 2500 < \omega_0 = 10\,000, so the circuit is underdamped: it will oscillate as it decays, at \omega_d = \sqrt{10\,000^2 - 2500^2} = 9682\ \text{rad/s} (Eq. 8.15).
Critical damping needs \alpha = \omega_0:
\frac{R}{2L} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad R = 2\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = 2\sqrt{\frac{0.01}{10^{-6}}} = 2(100) = 200\ \Omega
Any R above 200 Ω makes it overdamped.

Example 4: Source-free series RLC (T)

Like Prob. 8.16 (T)

The switch in Figure 8.11 has been closed for a long time and opens at t = 0. Find i(t) for t > 0.

Figure 8.11: Circuit for Example 4.
Step 1: Differential equation. Once the switch opens, the 18 V source and the 3 Ω are cut off. What’s left is one loop: the 6 Ω shunt, the 6 Ω, the capacitor and the inductor, all carrying the same current i. Take i flowing down the right-hand branch (into the capacitor’s + terminal) and back up through the 6 Ω shunt. KVL around that loop, with no source:
6i + v_C + L\frac{di}{dt} + 6i = 0, \qquad \text{where } v_C = \frac{1}{C}\int_0^t i\,dt + v_C(0)
Combine the two resistors and substitute v_C:
12i + L\frac{di}{dt} + \frac{1}{C}\int_0^t i\,dt + v_C(0) = 0
Differentiate once (v_C(0) is a constant, so it becomes 0) and divide by L = 1, with \frac{1}{C} = \frac{1}{0.01} = 100:
\frac{d^2 i}{dt^2} + 12\frac{di}{dt} + 100\,i = 0
Step 2: Natural solution. The characteristic equation (Eq. 8.10) is
s^2 + 12s + 100 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad s = \frac{-12 \pm \sqrt{12^2 - 4(100)}}{2} = -6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 100} = -6 \pm j8
The roots are complex, so it’s underdamped with \alpha = 6 and \omega_d = 8:
i_N = A\,e^{-6t}\cos(8t + \theta)
Step 3: Initial conditions.
Before switching: the switch has been closed for a long time, so short the inductor and open the capacitor (Figure 8.12).

Figure 8.12: Example 4 at t = 0^-.

The open capacitor blocks the right-hand branch, so i(0^-) = 0.
With no current in that branch, the 6 Ω in it drops nothing and the inductor (a short) drops nothing, so the capacitor has the same voltage as the 6 Ω shunt. That’s a voltage divider of the 18 V source:
v_C(0^-) = 18 \cdot \frac{6}{3 + 6} = 12\ \text{V} \quad (+\text{ at the top})

By Eq. (8.3): i(0^+) = 0 and v_C(0^+) = 12\ \text{V}.
After switching: the switch is open, the capacitor holds 12 V and the loop current starts at 0 (Figure 8.13).

Figure 8.13: Example 4 at t = 0^+.
Use the Step 1 KVL at t = 0^+. With i = 0 the resistors drop nothing, so v_C + v_L = 0:
12 + v_L(0^+) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_L(0^+) = -12\ \text{V} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{di}{dt}(0^+) = \frac{v_L}{L} = -12\ \text{A/s}
Step 4: Total solution. With no source in the loop, all the energy is eventually lost in the resistors, so i_F = 0 and
i_T = A\,e^{-6t}\cos(8t + \theta)
Apply the initial conditions with Eq. (8.18), using \alpha = 6, \omega_d = 8:

A\cos\theta = i(0) - i_F = 0
-6(0) - 8A\sin\theta = -12, so A\sin\theta = 1.5

The point (0,\ 1.5) is straight up the vertical axis, so \theta = \frac{\pi}{2} and A = \sqrt{0^2 + 1.5^2} = 1.5:
i(t) = 1.5\,e^{-6t}\cos\!\left(8t + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\ \text{A}
Since \cos(x + \frac{\pi}{2}) = -\sin x, this is the same as -1.5\,e^{-6t}\sin 8t A. The minus sign means the current first flows up the branch, as the capacitor discharges out of its + terminal.
Example 5: Switch from A to B, overdamped

Like Prob. 8.17

In Figure 8.14, the switch has been at A for a long time and moves to B at t = 0 (a make-before-break switch, so the inductor current is never interrupted). Find v(t) for t \geq 0.

Figure 8.14: Circuit for Example 5.
Step 1: Differential equation. At B, the current source and 6 Ω are disconnected. The 5 Ω, the 1 H and the ¼ F form one series loop with no source. We want v, the capacitor voltage. Take the loop current i flowing through the inductor toward the capacitor’s + terminal; then i = C\frac{dv}{dt}. KVL around the loop:
5i + L\frac{di}{dt} + v = 0
Substitute i = C\frac{dv}{dt}, so \frac{di}{dt} = C\frac{d^2 v}{dt^2}:
5C\frac{dv}{dt} + LC\frac{d^2 v}{dt^2} + v = 0
Divide by LC = (1)(\frac{1}{4}) = \frac{1}{4}:
\frac{d^2 v}{dt^2} + 5\frac{dv}{dt} + 4v = 0
Step 2: Natural solution.
s^2 + 5s + 4 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad s = \frac{-5 \pm \sqrt{25 - 16}}{2} = \frac{-5 \pm 3}{2} = -1,\ -4
Two different real roots, so it’s overdamped (Eq. 8.12):
v_N = A_1 e^{-t} + A_2 e^{-4t}
Step 3: Initial conditions.
Before switching: at A for a long time, so short the inductor and open the capacitor (Figure 8.15).

Figure 8.15: Example 5 at t = 0^-, with the switch at A.

The open capacitor blocks the inductor–capacitor branch, so i_L(0^-) = 0.
All 3 A therefore flows through the 6 Ω, giving a node voltage of (3)(6) = 18 V. The inductor (a short) drops nothing, so the capacitor has that voltage: v(0^-) = 18\ \text{V}.

After switching: at B, the capacitor holds 18 V and the inductor carries 0 A (Figure 8.16).

Figure 8.16: Example 5 at t = 0^+, with the switch at B.
The capacitor is in series with the inductor, so its current is the inductor current, i_C(0^+) = 0. By Eq. (8.16), \frac{dv}{dt}(0^+) = \frac{0}{C} = 0.
Step 4: Total solution. No source is left in the loop, so v_F = 0 and v_T = A_1 e^{-t} + A_2 e^{-4t}. Apply the two initial conditions:

v(0) = 18: \quad A_1 + A_2 = 18
\frac{dv}{dt}(0) = 0: differentiating gives -A_1 e^{-t} - 4A_2 e^{-4t}, so at t = 0, \quad -A_1 - 4A_2 = 0

The second equation gives A_1 = -4A_2. Substituting into the first: -4A_2 + A_2 = 18, so A_2 = -6 and A_1 = 24:
v(t) = \begin{cases} 18\ \text{V}, & t < 0 \\ 24e^{-t} - 6e^{-4t}\ \text{V}, & t \geq 0 \end{cases}
Example 6: Source-free parallel RLC (T)

Like Prob. 8.18 (T)

The switch in Figure 8.17 has been closed for a long time and opens at t = 0. Find v(t) for t > 0.

Figure 8.17: Circuit for Example 6.
Step 1: Differential equation. After the switch opens, the source side is cut off and the 1 Ω, 0.32 H and ⅛ F are left in parallel, all with the same voltage v. KCL at the top node, with every current measured downward:
\frac{v}{R} + i_L + C\frac{dv}{dt} = 0, \qquad \text{where } i_L = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^t v\,dt + i_L(0)
Substitute i_L, differentiate once (i_L(0) becomes 0), and divide by C:
\frac{d^2 v}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{RC}\frac{dv}{dt} + \frac{1}{LC}\,v = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{d^2 v}{dt^2} + 8\frac{dv}{dt} + 25v = 0
using \frac{1}{RC} = \frac{1}{(1)(1/8)} = 8 and \frac{1}{LC} = \frac{1}{(0.32)(1/8)} = 25.
Step 2: Natural solution.
s^2 + 8s + 25 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad s = -4 \pm \sqrt{16 - 25} = -4 \pm j3
Underdamped, with \alpha = 4 and \omega_d = 3:
v_N = A\,e^{-4t}\cos(3t + \theta)
Step 3: Initial conditions.
Before switching: short the inductor and open the capacitor (Figure 8.18).

Figure 8.18: Example 6 at t = 0^-.

The shorted inductor sits directly across the 1 Ω and the capacitor, so they all have 0 V: v(0^-) = 0.
The source sees only the 4 Ω before the short, so all of its current goes through the inductor: i_L(0^-) = \frac{20}{4} = 5\ \text{A}.

After switching: the capacitor still has 0 V and the inductor still carries 5 A downward (Figure 8.19).

Figure 8.19: Example 6 at t = 0^+.
KCL from Step 1 at t = 0^+:
\frac{0}{1} + 5 + \frac{1}{8}\frac{dv}{dt}(0^+) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{dv}{dt}(0^+) = -40\ \text{V/s}
The inductor’s 5 A has to keep flowing, and the only place it can come from is the capacitor, which drives the voltage negative.
Step 4: Total solution. No source, so v_F = 0. Eq. (8.18) with \alpha = 4, \omega_d = 3:

A\cos\theta = 0 - 0 = 0
-4(0) - 3A\sin\theta = -40, so A\sin\theta = 13.33

The point (0,\ 13.33) gives \theta = \frac{\pi}{2} and A = 13.33:
v(t) = 13.33\,e^{-4t}\cos\!\left(3t + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\ \text{V} \quad \left(= -13.33\,e^{-4t}\sin 3t\right)
Example 7: Choose C for a given \alpha

Like Prob. 8.23

For the network in Figure 8.20, what value of C makes the response underdamped with \alpha = 2\ \text{Np/s}?

Figure 8.20: Parallel network for Example 7.

Simplify. Every element is connected between the same two rails, so this is a parallel RLC. Capacitors in parallel add, so the two capacitors act as one: C_{eq} = C + 0.02.
Use the parallel \alpha, Eq. (8.8), and solve for C_{eq}:
\alpha = \frac{1}{2RC_{eq}} = 2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad C_{eq} = \frac{1}{2(5)(2)} = 0.05\ \text{F}
C = C_{eq} - 0.02 = 0.05 - 0.02 = 30\ \text{mF}
Check it’s underdamped. That needs \alpha < \omega_0. By Eq. (8.9), \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(0.1)(0.05)}} = 14.14\ \text{rad/s}, which is bigger than \alpha = 2 ✓. It oscillates at \omega_d = \sqrt{200 - 4} = 14\ \text{rad/s}.

Example 8: Solving a step-response equation

Like Prob. 8.27

A branch voltage in an RLC circuit is described by
\frac{d^2 v}{dt^2} + 6\frac{dv}{dt} + 25v = 50
If v(0) = 0 and \frac{dv}{dt}(0) = 0, find v(t).
Step 1: Differential equation. It’s given, already in standard form. Comparing with Eq. (8.6): 2\alpha = 6, so \alpha = 3, and \omega_0^2 = 25, so \omega_0 = 5.
Step 2: Natural solution. Set the right-hand side to 0. The characteristic equation is
s^2 + 6s + 25 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad s = -3 \pm \sqrt{9 - 25} = -3 \pm j4
Underdamped, with \alpha = 3 and \omega_d = 4:
v_N = A\,e^{-3t}\cos(4t + \theta)
Step 3: Initial conditions. Given: v(0) = 0 and \frac{dv}{dt}(0) = 0.
Step 4: Total solution. The forced solution is where v settles. Once it settles, it stops changing, so both derivatives are 0 and the equation becomes 25\,v_F = 50, giving v_F = 2\ \text{V}:
v_T = 2 + A\,e^{-3t}\cos(4t + \theta)
Eq. (8.18) with \alpha = 3, \omega_d = 4:

A\cos\theta = v(0) - v_F = 0 - 2 = -2
-3(-2) - 4A\sin\theta = 0, so A\sin\theta = 1.5

So A = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + 1.5^2} = \sqrt{6.25} = 2.5. For \theta: the cosine is negative and the sine is positive, so the angle is in the second quadrant. A calculator gives \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1.5}{-2}\right) = -0.6435, which is in the fourth quadrant (wrong signs), so add \pi:
\theta = -0.6435 + \pi = 2.498\ \text{rad}
Check: 2.5\cos(2.498) = -2 ✓ and 2.5\sin(2.498) = 1.5 ✓.
v(t) = 2 + 2.5\,e^{-3t}\cos(4t + 2.498)\ \text{V}
Example 9: General circuit with two sources

Like Prob. 8.41

For the circuit in Figure 8.21, find i(t) and v(t) for t > 0.

Figure 8.21: Circuit for Example 9. The capacitor voltage v is + on the right.
Step 1: Differential equation. First, simplify with a source transformation: the 12u(t) A source with 2 Ω in parallel becomes a (12u(t))(2) = 24u(t) V source with 2 Ω in series. Now everything is in one series loop: R = 2 + 4 = 6\ \Omega, L = 1\ \text{H}, C = 0.04\ \text{F}, plus two sources.
Go around the loop clockwise, in the direction of i: a rise of 24u(t) through the transformed source, then drops across the 6 Ω, the inductor, the 10 V source (entering its + side) and the capacitor (entering its + side, on the right):
24u(t) - 6i - L\frac{di}{dt} - 10 - v = 0
For t > 0, u(t) = 1. Substitute v = \frac{1}{C}\int_0^t i\,dt + v(0) and rearrange:
6i + L\frac{di}{dt} + \frac{1}{C}\int_0^t i\,dt + v(0) = 14
Differentiate once (14 and v(0) are constants, so they become 0), with L = 1 and \frac{1}{C} = 25:
\frac{d^2 i}{dt^2} + 6\frac{di}{dt} + 25\,i = 0
For v instead, substitute i = C\frac{dv}{dt} into the KVL and divide by LC = 0.04:
\frac{d^2 v}{dt^2} + 6\frac{dv}{dt} + 25\,v = 350
Same left-hand side, so the same natural solution. Only the right-hand side, and so the forced solution, is different.
Step 2: Natural solution.
s^2 + 6s + 25 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad s = -3 \pm j4
Underdamped with \alpha = 3, \omega_d = 4. Both i and v have the form A\,e^{-3t}\cos(4t + \theta), each with its own A and \theta.
Step 3: Initial conditions.
Before switching: u(t) = 0, so the current source is off (0 A), but the 10 V source is still there. Short the inductor and open the capacitor (Figure 8.22).

Figure 8.22: Example 9 at t = 0^-. The step source is off.

The open capacitor breaks the loop, so i(0^-) = 0.
With no current, every resistor and inductor drop is 0, so KVL around the loop reduces to 0 - 10 - v = 0, giving v(0^-) = -10\ \text{V}. (The capacitor is charged “backwards” by the 10 V source.)

After switching: the step source turns on (12 A, or 24 V after the transformation), and i and v keep their values (Figure 8.23).

Figure 8.23: Example 9 at t = 0^+. The step source is on.
From the KVL in Step 1 at t = 0^+, with i = 0 and v = -10:
24 - 0 - v_L - 10 - (-10) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_L(0^+) = 24\ \text{V} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{di}{dt}(0^+) = \frac{24}{1} = 24\ \text{A/s}
\frac{dv}{dt}(0^+) = \frac{i(0^+)}{C} = 0
Step 4: Total solution. As t \to \infty the capacitor is open again, so i_F = 0, and KVL with no current gives 24 - 10 - v_F = 0, so v_F = 14\ \text{V}. (Check with the v equation: 25\,v_F = 350 gives 14 ✓.)
For i: Eq. (8.18) with \alpha = 3, \omega_d = 4:

A\cos\theta = 0 - 0 = 0
-3(0) - 4A\sin\theta = 24, so A\sin\theta = -6

The point (0, -6) is straight down, so \theta = -\frac{\pi}{2} and A = 6:
i(t) = 6\,e^{-3t}\cos\!\left(4t - \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\ \text{A} \quad \left(= 6\,e^{-3t}\sin 4t\right)
For v:

A\cos\theta = -10 - 14 = -24
-3(-24) - 4A\sin\theta = 0, so A\sin\theta = 18

A = \sqrt{24^2 + 18^2} = 30. Cosine negative, sine positive, so second quadrant: \theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{18}{-24}\right) + \pi = -0.6435 + \pi = 2.498\ \text{rad}:
v(t) = 14 + 30\,e^{-3t}\cos(4t + 2.498)\ \text{V}


                  
                  Check: i = C\frac{dv}{dt} should hold. Differentiating v(t) and multiplying by 0.04 gives exactly 6e^{-3t}\sin 4t ✓.
                  
                

Example 10: Choose R and C for a given \alpha and \omega_d

Like Prob. 8.43

The switch in Figure 8.24 is opened at t = 0 after the circuit has reached steady state. (a) Choose R and C so that \alpha = 10\ \text{Np/s} and \omega_d = 20\ \text{rad/s}. (b) With those values, find i(t) for t > 0.

Figure 8.24: Circuit for Example 10.
(a) After the switch opens, the source and 4 Ω are cut off, and L, R and C form one series loop. So use the series formulas.

From Eq. (8.7), \alpha = \frac{R}{2L}, so R = 2\alpha L = 2(10)(0.25) = 5\ \Omega.
From Eq. (8.15), \omega_d^2 = \omega_0^2 - \alpha^2, so \omega_0^2 = \omega_d^2 + \alpha^2 = 400 + 100 = 500.
From Eq. (8.9), \omega_0^2 = \frac{1}{LC}, so C = \frac{1}{\omega_0^2 L} = \frac{1}{(500)(0.25)} = 8\ \text{mF}.

(b)
Step 1: Differential equation. Take i flowing down through the inductor. In the loop it comes back up through the R–C branch. The inductor and the R–C branch are connected across the same two nodes, so they have the same voltage. Measuring top-to-bottom, the R–C branch carries -i downward:
L\frac{di}{dt} = R(-i) + v_C, \qquad \text{where } v_C = \frac{1}{C}\int_0^t (-i)\,dt + v_C(0)
Move everything to one side, differentiate once and divide by L:
\frac{d^2 i}{dt^2} + \frac{R}{L}\frac{di}{dt} + \frac{1}{LC}\,i = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{d^2 i}{dt^2} + 20\frac{di}{dt} + 500\,i = 0
Step 2: Natural solution.
s^2 + 20s + 500 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad s = -10 \pm \sqrt{100 - 500} = -10 \pm j20
Exactly the \alpha and \omega_d we designed for:
i_N = A\,e^{-10t}\cos(20t + \theta)
Step 3: Initial conditions.
Before switching: short the inductor and open the capacitor (Figure 8.25).

Figure 8.25: Example 10 at t = 0^-.

The source sees only the 4 Ω before the short, so i(0^-) = \frac{12}{4} = 3\ \text{A}.
The R–C branch is connected across the shorted inductor, so it has 0 V across it, and with no current through R, v_C(0^-) = 0.

After switching: the inductor carries 3 A and the capacitor holds 0 V (Figure 8.26).

Figure 8.26: Example 10 at t = 0^+.
From the Step 1 relation at t = 0^+:
v_L(0^+) = R(-3) + 0 = -15\ \text{V} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{di}{dt}(0^+) = \frac{-15}{0.25} = -60\ \text{A/s}
Step 4: Total solution. No source, so i_F = 0. Eq. (8.18) with \alpha = 10, \omega_d = 20:

A\cos\theta = 3 - 0 = 3
-10(3) - 20A\sin\theta = -60, so A\sin\theta = 1.5

A = \sqrt{3^2 + 1.5^2} = 3.354. Both are positive, so \theta is in the first quadrant and the calculator answer is right: \theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1.5}{3}\right) = 0.4636\ \text{rad}.
i(t) = 3.354\,e^{-10t}\cos(20t + 0.4636)\ \text{A}
Example 11: Step response with L in parallel with C (T)

Like Prob. 8.46 (T)

In Figure 8.27, no energy is stored at t = 0^-. Find i(t) for t > 0.

Figure 8.27: Circuit for Example 11.
i isn’t an inductor current or a capacitor voltage, so it’s easier to solve for one that is (i_L) and convert at the end.
Step 1: Differential equation. Let v_x be the voltage across the L‖C pair, which is also the capacitor voltage. Three relations describe the circuit for t > 0:

KVL around the outer loop: \quad 12 = v_x + 2i
KCL at the L‖C pair: \quad i = i_L + C\frac{dv_x}{dt}
Inductor law, Eq. (8.1): \quad v_x = L\frac{di_L}{dt}

Substitute the last into the middle to get i = i_L + LC\frac{d^2 i_L}{dt^2}, then put both into the KVL:
12 = L\frac{di_L}{dt} + 2\left(i_L + LC\frac{d^2 i_L}{dt^2}\right)
Divide by 2LC = 2(2.5)(0.1) = 0.5:
\frac{d^2 i_L}{dt^2} + 5\frac{di_L}{dt} + 4\,i_L = 24
Step 2: Natural solution.
s^2 + 5s + 4 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad s = \frac{-5 \pm \sqrt{25 - 16}}{2} = -1,\ -4
Overdamped: \quad i_{L,N} = A_1 e^{-t} + A_2 e^{-4t}
Step 3: Initial conditions. No energy is stored, so i_L(0) = 0 and v_x(0) = 0. From the inductor law, \frac{di_L}{dt}(0) = \frac{v_x(0)}{L} = 0.
Step 4: Total solution. Forced solution: as t \to \infty the inductor is a short, so the source sees just the 2 Ω and i_{L,F} = \frac{12}{2} = 6\ \text{A}. (Check with the equation: 4\,i_{L,F} = 24 ✓.)
i_L = 6 + A_1 e^{-t} + A_2 e^{-4t}

i_L(0) = 0: \quad 6 + A_1 + A_2 = 0, so A_1 + A_2 = -6
\frac{di_L}{dt}(0) = 0: \quad -A_1 - 4A_2 = 0, so A_1 = -4A_2

Then -4A_2 + A_2 = -6, so A_2 = 2 and A_1 = -8:
i_L(t) = 6 - 8e^{-t} + 2e^{-4t}\ \text{A}
Convert back to i. First v_x = L\frac{di_L}{dt} = 2.5(8e^{-t} - 8e^{-4t}) = 20(e^{-t} - e^{-4t}). Then from the KVL, i = \frac{12 - v_x}{2}:
i(t) = 6 - 10e^{-t} + 10e^{-4t}\ \text{A}


                  
                   i(0^+) = 6\ \text{A} even though i(0^-) = 0. That's allowed, because i isn't an inductor current. At the first instant the uncharged capacitor acts like a short across the inductor, so the source sees just the 2 Ω.
                  
                

Example 12: Step response of a parallel RLC

Like Prob. 8.47

The switch in Figure 8.28 has been closed for a long time and opens at t = 0. Find v_o(t) for t > 0.

Figure 8.28: Circuit for Example 12. The switch shorts out the series 1 Ω until t = 0.
Step 1: Differential equation. For t > 0 the switch is open, so the series 1 Ω is back in the circuit. Simplify the source side with source transformations:

6 A with 1 Ω in parallel becomes 6 \times 1 = 6 V with 1 Ω in series.
Add the series 1 Ω: 6 V with 2 Ω in series.
Convert back: \frac{6}{2} = 3 A with 2 Ω in parallel.

So the circuit is a parallel RLC (2 Ω, 1.25 H, 50 mF) driven by 3 A. KCL at the top node, every current measured downward:
3 = \frac{v_o}{2} + i_L + 0.05\frac{dv_o}{dt}, \qquad \text{where } i_L = \frac{1}{1.25}\int_0^t v_o\,dt + i_L(0)
Substitute i_L, differentiate once (3 and i_L(0) become 0), and divide by C = 0.05:
\frac{d^2 v_o}{dt^2} + 10\frac{dv_o}{dt} + 16\,v_o = 0
Step 2: Natural solution.
s^2 + 10s + 16 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad s = \frac{-10 \pm \sqrt{100 - 64}}{2} = \frac{-10 \pm 6}{2} = -2,\ -8
Overdamped: \quad v_N = A_1 e^{-2t} + A_2 e^{-8t}
Step 3: Initial conditions.
Before switching: the switch is closed (shorting the series 1 Ω), and the inductor is a short (Figure 8.29).

Figure 8.29: Example 12 at t = 0^-.

The shorted inductor is directly across the output, so v_o(0^-) = 0.
With the switch and the inductor both shorts, the source’s top node is shorted straight to the bottom rail. The 1 Ω across the source has 0 V and takes no current, so all 6 A goes through the inductor: i_L(0^-) = 6\ \text{A}.

After switching: the inductor still carries 6 A and the capacitor still has 0 V (Figure 8.30).

Figure 8.30: Example 12 at t = 0^+.
KCL from Step 1 at t = 0^+:
3 = \frac{0}{2} + 6 + 0.05\frac{dv_o}{dt}(0^+) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{dv_o}{dt}(0^+) = -60\ \text{V/s}
Step 4: Total solution. As t \to \infty the inductor is a short across the output, so v_F = 0 (and the inductor current settles at 3 A).

v_o(0) = 0: \quad A_1 + A_2 = 0
\frac{dv_o}{dt}(0) = -60: \quad -2A_1 - 8A_2 = -60

From the first, A_1 = -A_2. Substituting: 2A_2 - 8A_2 = -60, so A_2 = 10 and A_1 = -10:
v_o(t) = -10e^{-2t} + 10e^{-8t}\ \text{V}
Common mistakes

Using the series \alpha = R/2L on a parallel circuit, or the other way round. If unsure, derive the equation with KVL/KCL
Forgetting to differentiate away the integral (and constants like v_C(0)) when writing the differential equation
Applying the initial conditions to x_N only and forgetting x_F in Eq. (8.17)
Assuming i_C or v_L can’t jump at t = 0. Only v_C and i_L are continuous
Getting the sign of \frac{dx}{dt}(0^+) wrong. Mark the reference directions on the circuit before writing KCL/KVL
Using \omega_0 instead of \omega_d inside the cosine of an underdamped answer
Trusting the calculator’s \tan^{-1} when A\cos\theta is negative (add \pi), or leaving \theta in degrees instead of radians
Finding \alpha and \omega_0 with the sources still on. The natural solution is for the circuit with the sources turned off

courses/ele-302/concepts/capacitors-and-.title: Capacitors and Inductors
courses/ele-302/concepts/capacitors-and-.content:
Capacitors and inductors are the two energy-storage elements: a capacitor stores energy in an electric field set up by its voltage, and an inductor stores energy in a magnetic field set up by its current.
Resistors only turn energy into heat. Capacitors and inductors store it and give it back later, which is why circuits with them have a history: what they do now depends on what happened before. Everything in Ch 8 comes from the two element laws on this page.
Intuition
The capacitor
A capacitor is two conductors (plates) separated by an insulator called the dielectric (Figure 1, left). Push current into one terminal and charge +q builds up on that plate, while the same amount leaves the other plate, leaving it at -q. No charge actually crosses the gap. The separated charge sets up an electric field E between the plates, and that field is where the energy is stored.
The more charge on the plates, the bigger the voltage between them. The ratio is the capacitance:
q = C\,v, \qquad C = \frac{\varepsilon A}{d}

q: charge on the plates (C)
C: capacitance, in farads (F)
\varepsilon: permittivity of the dielectric
A: plate area; d: gap between the plates

Bigger plates or a smaller gap hold more charge per volt. Real values range from picofarads (pF) to millifarads (mF); 1 F is huge.
Where i = C\frac{dv}{dt} comes from. Current is the rate charge arrives, i = \frac{dq}{dt}. Differentiate q = Cv:
i_C = C\frac{dv_C}{dt}
So a capacitor’s current depends on how fast its voltage changes, not on the voltage itself. A capacitor sitting at a steady 100 V carries no current at all. To change its voltage quickly you need a large current, and to change it instantly you’d need an infinite one.


                  
                  Water analogy: a capacitor is like a tank with a stretchy rubber membrane across the middle. Water (charge) pushed in one side bulges the membrane and pushes the same amount out the other side, so it looks like water flows "through", even though none crosses. The bulge (voltage) builds up gradually and pushes back. 
                  
                

The inductor
An inductor is a coil of wire (Figure 1, right). Current through the coil sets up a magnetic field B through its middle, and that field is where the energy is stored. The total magnetic flux linking the coil, \lambda, is proportional to the current. The ratio is the inductance:
\lambda = L\,i, \qquad L = \frac{N^2 \mu A}{\ell}

\lambda: flux linkage (Wb·turns)
L: inductance, in henries (H)
N: number of turns; \mu: permeability of the core
A: cross-sectional area of the coil; \ell: its length

More turns, a bigger coil or an iron core all give more inductance. Real values range from microhenries (µH) to a few henries.
Where v = L\frac{di}{dt} comes from. Faraday’s law says a changing flux induces a voltage, v = \frac{d\lambda}{dt}. Differentiate \lambda = Li:
v_L = L\frac{di_L}{dt}
So an inductor’s voltage depends on how fast its current changes. A steady current, however large, produces no voltage. By Lenz’s law the induced voltage always opposes the change that caused it: try to speed the current up and the inductor pushes back, try to stop it and the inductor pushes forward to keep it going. This is the inductor’s “inertia”, the reason an LC circuit overshoots and rings.

Figure 1: A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its plates (left). An inductor stores energy in the magnetic field through its coil (right).
Passive sign convention
Both laws assume the passive sign convention: the current arrow points into the + terminal of the voltage. If your current arrow points into the - terminal instead, put a minus sign in front: i_C = -C\frac{dv_C}{dt}, v_L = -L\frac{di_L}{dt}.


                  
                  Most sign errors in Ch 8 slopes come from this. Before writing \frac{dv_C}{dt} = \frac{i_C}{C}, check that i_C is the current flowing into the capacitor's + terminal.
                  
                

The two elements are mirror images
Swap v \leftrightarrow i and C \leftrightarrow L and every capacitor result turns into an inductor result. This is called duality, and it means you only really have to learn one of them:











































































CapacitorInductorPhysical formTwo plates and an insulatorA coil of wireStores energy inElectric fieldMagnetic fieldDefining relationq = Cv\lambda = LiElement lawi = C\frac{dv}{dt}v = L\frac{di}{dt}Integral formv(t) = \frac{1}{C}\int_{t_0}^{t} i\,dt + v(t_0)i(t) = \frac{1}{L}\int_{t_0}^{t} v\,dt + i(t_0)Stored energyw = \frac{1}{2}Cv^2w = \frac{1}{2}Li^2Can’t jumpVoltage v_CCurrent i_LCan jumpCurrent i_CVoltage v_LAt DC steady stateOpen circuit (i = 0)Short circuit (v = 0)In series\frac{1}{C_{eq}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \cdotsL_{eq} = L_1 + L_2 + \cdotsIn parallelC_{eq} = C_1 + C_2 + \cdots\frac{1}{L_{eq}} = \frac{1}{L_1} + \frac{1}{L_2} + \cdotsImpedanceZ_C = \frac{1}{j\omega C}Z_L = j\omega LMechanical analogySpringMass
The rest of this page goes through each row.
Integral form
Integrating the element law from a starting time t_0 gives the value at any later time:
v_C(t) = \frac{1}{C}\int_{t_0}^{t} i_C\,dt + v_C(t_0), \qquad i_L(t) = \frac{1}{L}\int_{t_0}^{t} v_L\,dt + i_L(t_0)
The integral adds up everything that has happened since t_0, and the last term is where it started. That’s the “memory”: a capacitor’s voltage now depends on all the current that has ever flowed into it, not just the current right now. This is also why you need initial conditions to solve any circuit with C or L in it.
Stored energy
The power into any element is p = vi. For a capacitor, substitute i = C\frac{dv}{dt} and integrate from an uncharged state (v = 0):
w_C = \int p\,dt = \int C v \frac{dv}{dt}\,dt = \int_0^{v} C v\,dv = \tfrac{1}{2}C v^2
The inductor works the same way with v = L\frac{di}{dt}:
w_L = \int L i \frac{di}{dt}\,dt = \int_0^{i} L i\,di = \tfrac{1}{2}L i^2
Three things follow from these:

The energy is never negative (it’s a square), so an ideal C or L can only give back energy it took in earlier. It can’t generate any.
Ideal capacitors and inductors don’t dissipate. If p is positive the element is absorbing and storing energy; if negative, it’s releasing what it stored. Over a full cycle of a steady AC signal, they absorb and release the same amount.
The energy depends only on v_C (or i_L). That’s the link to continuity, next.

Why v_C and i_L can’t jump
Suppose a capacitor’s voltage jumped from v_1 to v_2 in zero time. Then:

\frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{0} is infinite, so i_C = C\frac{dv}{dt} would be infinite.
Equivalently, the stored energy would change from \frac{1}{2}Cv_1^2 to \frac{1}{2}Cv_2^2 in zero time, which needs infinite power.

Neither is possible in a real circuit, so capacitor voltage is continuous. The same argument with v_L = L\frac{di}{dt} shows inductor current is continuous. At a switching instant t = 0:
v_C(0^+) = v_C(0^-), \qquad i_L(0^+) = i_L(0^-)
The other variable has no such protection. A capacitor’s current can jump instantly (it only sets the slope of the voltage), and so can an inductor’s voltage. In a graph, a jump in i_C shows up as a sudden change of slope (a corner) in v_C, never a step (see Example 1 below).


                  
                  At t = 0^+ you can replace a capacitor with a voltage source of value v_C(0^-), and an inductor with a current source of value i_L(0^-). Ch 8 Step 3 uses exactly this.
                  
                

DC steady state
When a DC circuit has been on for a long time, every voltage and current has stopped changing, so every derivative is 0:

Capacitor: i_C = C \cdot 0 = 0. No current flows, so it acts like an open circuit. It still holds whatever voltage it charged to.
Inductor: v_L = L \cdot 0 = 0. No voltage across it, so it acts like a short circuit. It still carries whatever current is flowing.

These are the two rules for finding initial values (the circuit before switching) and final values (as t \to \infty) in Ch 8.
There’s a matching pair of rules for the instant a source is first switched on, if nothing was stored beforehand: an uncharged capacitor (v_C = 0) acts like a short at that instant, and an inductor with no current (i_L = 0) acts like an open. They then gradually change toward their DC steady-state behaviour.
Series and parallel
Capacitors combine like resistors the other way round; inductors combine exactly like resistors.
Capacitors in parallel add. Every capacitor has the same voltage v, and the currents add:
i = C_1\frac{dv}{dt} + C_2\frac{dv}{dt} + \cdots = (C_1 + C_2 + \cdots)\frac{dv}{dt} \quad\Rightarrow\quad C_{eq} = C_1 + C_2 + \cdots
Physically, parallel capacitors are like one capacitor with a bigger plate area.
Capacitors in series combine like parallel resistors. They all carry the same current, so they all gain the same charge, and the voltages add: v = \frac{q}{C_1} + \frac{q}{C_2} + \cdots, which gives \frac{1}{C_{eq}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \cdots. For two, C_{eq} = \frac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2}. Physically, it’s like one capacitor with a wider gap.
Inductors in series add, because they carry the same current and their voltages add: v = (L_1 + L_2 + \cdots)\frac{di}{dt}. Inductors in parallel combine like parallel resistors.


                  
                  Memory aid: L behaves like R. C behaves like \frac{1}{R} (a conductance), so it flips.
                  
                

Impedance: how they behave at different frequencies
For a sinusoid at angular frequency \omega, \frac{d}{dt} becomes multiplication by j\omega, so each element acts like a frequency-dependent resistance called impedance:
Z_C = \frac{1}{j\omega C}, \qquad Z_L = j\omega L




















FrequencyCapacitorInductorDC (\omega = 0)Z_C \to \infty: openZ_L = 0: shortVery high (\omega \to \infty)Z_C \to 0: shortZ_L \to \infty: open
This matches the DC steady-state rules above, and it’s also why a sudden change (which contains very high frequencies) gets through a capacitor but is blocked by an inductor. It’s the basis of filters in Ch 14.
Mechanical analogy

























ElectricalMechanicalWhyCapacitorSpringStores energy in how far it’s “stretched” (its voltage)InductorMassStores energy in how fast it’s “moving” (its current), and resists changes in it (inertia)ResistorFrictionTurns energy into heat
A charged capacitor connected to an inductor behaves like a stretched spring with a mass on it: it oscillates, at \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}. Adding resistance (friction) makes the oscillation die out. That’s the whole story of Ch 8.
Real components
Real parts are close to ideal, but not quite:

Capacitors leak a little: a very large resistance in parallel lets the charge slowly drain away. They also have a small series resistance (ESR) and a maximum voltage rating. Exceeding it breaks down the dielectric. Electrolytic capacitors are polarized and must be connected the right way round.
Inductors are made of wire, so they have a winding resistance in series. At DC a real inductor is a small resistor, not a perfect short. Inductors with iron cores also saturate at high current, where L drops.

In ELE 302 problems, assume ideal elements unless the question says otherwise.
Key formulas
Capacitor
q = Cv, \qquad i_C = C\frac{dv_C}{dt}, \qquad v_C(t) = \frac{1}{C}\int_{t_0}^{t} i_C\,dt + v_C(t_0), \qquad w_C = \tfrac{1}{2}Cv_C^2
Inductor
\lambda = Li, \qquad v_L = L\frac{di_L}{dt}, \qquad i_L(t) = \frac{1}{L}\int_{t_0}^{t} v_L\,dt + i_L(t_0), \qquad w_L = \tfrac{1}{2}Li_L^2
Continuity
v_C(0^+) = v_C(0^-), \qquad i_L(0^+) = i_L(0^-)
Combinations
C_{\parallel} = C_1 + C_2, \qquad C_{\text{series}} = \frac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2}, \qquad L_{\text{series}} = L_1 + L_2, \qquad L_{\parallel} = \frac{L_1 L_2}{L_1 + L_2}
Impedance
Z_C = \frac{1}{j\omega C}, \qquad Z_L = j\omega L

v_C, i_C: capacitor voltage and current; v_L, i_L: inductor voltage and current (passive sign convention)
C: capacitance (F); L: inductance (H)
w_C, w_L: stored energy (J)
t_0: the time you start integrating from, usually 0

Worked example
Example 1: Capacitor voltage from its current
A 0.5\ \text{F} capacitor starts at v(0) = 2\ \text{V}. Its current is 1\ \text{A} for 0 < t < 2\ \text{s}, then -0.5\ \text{A} for 2 < t < 4\ \text{s}, then 0. Find v(t) and the stored energy at t = 0, 2 and 4 s.

0 < t < 2: integral form, with \frac{1}{C} = 2:
v(t) = 2\int_0^t 1\,dt + 2 = 2 + 2t \quad\Rightarrow\quad v(2) = 6\ \text{V}
2 < t < 4: start from v(2) = 6 (the voltage can’t jump, even though the current does):
v(t) = 2\int_2^t (-0.5)\,dt + 6 = 6 - (t - 2) \quad\Rightarrow\quad v(4) = 4\ \text{V}
t > 4: no current, so the voltage just holds: v = 4\ \text{V}.
Energy, w = \frac{1}{2}Cv^2 = \frac{1}{4}v^2:
w(0) = 1\ \text{J}, \qquad w(2) = 9\ \text{J}, \qquad w(4) = 4\ \text{J}


Figure 2: Example 1. The current jumps at t = 2 and t = 4, but the voltage only changes slope.
From 0 to 2 s the capacitor absorbs 9 - 1 = 8\ \text{J}. From 2 to 4 s the current reverses and it gives 9 - 4 = 5\ \text{J} back to the circuit. After 4 s it keeps the remaining 4 J indefinitely (an ideal capacitor doesn’t leak).
Example 2: Inductor voltage from its current
The current in a 0.2\ \text{H} inductor is 0 for t < 0 and i(t) = 5(1 - e^{-10t})\ \text{A} for t \geq 0. Find v(t), and the energy stored as t \to \infty.

Check continuity: i(0^+) = 5(1 - 1) = 0 = i(0^-) ✓
Element law:
v(t) = L\frac{di}{dt} = 0.2 \cdot 5 \cdot 10\,e^{-10t} = 10\,e^{-10t}\ \text{V} \quad (t > 0)
The voltage jumps from 0 to 10 V at t = 0. That’s allowed: only the inductor’s current has to be continuous.
As t \to \infty: v \to 0 (the inductor becomes a short, as at DC steady state) and i \to 5\ \text{A}, so
w_L = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.2)(5)^2 = 2.5\ \text{J}

Example 3: Combining elements
(a) A 6\ \mu\text{F} and a 3\ \mu\text{F} capacitor in series, with that pair in parallel with a 4\ \mu\text{F}. (b) A 4\ \text{H} and a 12\ \text{H} inductor in parallel, with that pair in series with a 2\ \text{H}.
(a) Series first: \frac{6 \cdot 3}{6 + 3} = 2\ \mu\text{F}. Then parallel adds: C_{eq} = 2 + 4 = 6\ \mu\text{F}.
(b) Parallel first: \frac{4 \cdot 12}{4 + 12} = 3\ \text{H}. Then series adds: L_{eq} = 3 + 2 = 5\ \text{H}.
Common mistakes

Thinking capacitor current or inductor voltage must be continuous. Only v_C and i_L are
Mixing up the combination rules: capacitors in parallel add, inductors in series add
Forgetting the initial value (v_C(t_0) or i_L(t_0)) when using the integral form
Ignoring the passive sign convention, which flips the sign of i = C\frac{dv}{dt} or v = L\frac{di}{dt}
Treating a capacitor at DC steady state as having zero voltage. It has zero current; it can still hold a voltage
Thinking a large voltage on a capacitor means a large current. The current depends on how fast the voltage changes

Related

courses/ele-302/concepts/damping-series-.title: Damping in Series and Parallel RLC
courses/ele-302/concepts/damping-series-.content:
Damping is how quickly a resistor drains away the energy swinging between L and C. In a series RLC, a bigger R means more damping; in a parallel RLC, a bigger R means less.
In Ch 8 this shows up as two different formulas for the neper frequency \alpha, \frac{R}{2L} for series and \frac{1}{2RC} for parallel, which go in opposite directions as R changes. This page explains why, so the formulas aren’t just something to memorize.
Intuition
What damping measures
Without resistance, an L and a C pass energy back and forth forever (see LC Oscillation). A resistor turns some of that energy into heat on every swing. The neper frequency \alpha (in Np/s) measures how fast that happens, and comparing it with the resonant frequency \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} decides the shape of the response:

























ComparisonCaseWhat it looks like\alpha < \omega_0UnderdampedOscillates inside a decaying envelope\alpha = \omega_0Critically dampedFastest return to zero without overshooting\alpha > \omega_0OverdampedCreeps back to zero, no oscillation
So “more damping” means a bigger \alpha, which pushes the circuit toward overdamped. The question is how R affects \alpha, and that depends on how much power the resistor burns, which depends on how it’s connected.
Series: the resistor is in the path of the current

Figure 1: Series RLC. The current swinging between L and C has to pass through R.
In a series circuit, the current sloshing between L and C has to flow through the resistor. The power it burns is
P = i^2 R
For the same current, a bigger R burns more power, so the energy drains away faster and the oscillation dies sooner. Look at the two extremes:

R = 0: the resistor is just a wire. Nothing is burned, and the circuit rings forever (pure LC).
R very large: the resistor chokes the current so much that the capacitor can barely discharge, let alone swing past zero. Heavily overdamped.

That’s why the series formula grows with R:
\alpha = \frac{R}{2L}
The L underneath makes sense too: a bigger inductor carries more “inertia” (stores more energy for the same current), so the same resistor takes longer to drain it.
Parallel: the resistor sits beside the oscillation

Figure 2: Parallel RLC. R has the same voltage as L and C, and only the current that leaks through it is lost.
In a parallel circuit, the energy swings between L and C directly, and the resistor sits beside them with the same voltage v. Only the current that leaks through it, i_R = \frac{v}{R}, is lost. The power it burns is
P = \frac{v^2}{R}
Now a bigger R lets less current leak away, so less energy is burned and the oscillation lasts longer. The extremes are flipped:

R \to \infty: the resistor is an open circuit, as if it weren’t there. Nothing leaks, and the circuit rings forever.
R very small: the resistor is nearly a short across the LC, which kills the voltage almost immediately. Heavily overdamped.

That’s why the parallel formula shrinks as R grows:
\alpha = \frac{1}{2RC}
Same parts, connected both ways
Take L = 1\ \text{H} and C = \frac{1}{4}\ \text{F}, so \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1/4}} = 2 rad/s, and try two resistors:




















R = 1\ \OmegaR = 10\ \OmegaSeries, \alpha = \frac{R}{2L}\alpha = 0.5: underdamped\alpha = 5: overdampedParallel, \alpha = \frac{1}{2RC}\alpha = 2: critically damped\alpha = 0.2: underdamped
Going from 1 Ω to 10 Ω pushes the series circuit toward overdamped and the parallel circuit away from it.
The critical resistance
Setting \alpha = \omega_0 gives the resistance that makes each circuit exactly critically damped:
\text{Series: } \frac{R}{2L} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} \;\Rightarrow\; R_c = 2\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}, \qquad \text{Parallel: } \frac{1}{2RC} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} \;\Rightarrow\; R_c = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}
With the parts above, \sqrt{L/C} = 2, so R_c = 4\ \Omega in series and 1\ \Omega in parallel (which is why the parallel 1 Ω entry in the table is critically damped). Then:























CircuitUnderdampedCritically dampedOverdampedSeriesR < R_cR = R_cR > R_cParallelR > R_cR = R_cR < R_c
Circuits that are neither
The two formulas only apply to a pure series or pure parallel RLC: one R, one L and one C, all in series or all in parallel (after turning off the sources). Many circuits are neither. For example, in Ch 8 Example 11, L is in parallel with C, and the resistor is in series with that pair. Neither formula obviously fits.
When that happens, don’t guess. Derive the circuit’s own differential equation with KVL/KCL, put it in standard form, and read \alpha off it:
\frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} + \underbrace{2\alpha}_{\text{read }\alpha\text{ here}}\frac{dx}{dt} + \omega_0^2\,x = f
In Example 11 that gives \alpha = \frac{1}{2RC}: the parallel formula, even though the resistor is in series. Only the derivation tells you that. (It makes sense physically: the L and C swap energy directly with each other, and the resistor only sees the current going in and out of the pair.)


                  
                  Source transformations can often turn an awkward circuit into a pure series or parallel one first; see Source Transformation.
                  
                

Key formulas
Neper frequency
\alpha = \frac{R}{2L} \quad \text{(series)}, \qquad \alpha = \frac{1}{2RC} \quad \text{(parallel)}
Resonant frequency (same for both)
\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}
Critical resistance
R_c = 2\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} \quad \text{(series)}, \qquad R_c = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} \quad \text{(parallel)}
Power burned in the resistor
P = i^2 R \quad \text{(series: same current as L and C)}, \qquad P = \frac{v^2}{R} \quad \text{(parallel: same voltage as L and C)}

\alpha: neper frequency, how fast the response decays (Np/s)
\omega_0: resonant frequency (rad/s)
R_c: the resistance that makes the circuit critically damped
R, L, C: the resistance, inductance and capacitance with the sources turned off

Worked example
Example 1: Same parts, two connections
An inductor L = 0.5\ \text{H} and a capacitor C = 2\ \text{mF} are connected with a resistor R. (a) Find the critical resistance for a series connection and for a parallel connection. (b) Classify the response for R = 20\ \Omega and R = 5\ \Omega, both ways.
(a) First \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(0.5)(0.002)}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{0.001}} = 31.62\ \text{rad/s}, and \sqrt{L/C} = \sqrt{250} = 15.81.

Series: R_c = 2(15.81) = 31.62\ \Omega
Parallel: R_c = \frac{1}{2}(15.81) = 7.91\ \Omega

(b)


























RSeries \alpha = \frac{R}{2L}ResultParallel \alpha = \frac{1}{2RC}Result20 Ω\frac{20}{1} = 2020 < 31.62: underdamped\frac{1}{2(20)(0.002)} = 12.512.5 < 31.62: underdamped5 Ω\frac{5}{1} = 55 < 31.62: underdamped\frac{1}{2(5)(0.002)} = 5050 > 31.62: overdamped
Shrinking R from 20 Ω to 5 Ω made the series circuit less damped (\alpha fell from 20 to 5) but the parallel circuit more damped (\alpha rose from 12.5 to 50), enough to tip it into overdamped. You can read the same thing off part (a): 5 Ω is below the parallel R_c of 7.91 Ω, and in parallel a resistance below R_c means overdamped.
Common mistakes

Using \alpha = \frac{R}{2L} on a parallel circuit, or \frac{1}{2RC} on a series one
Assuming “more resistance always means more damping”. That’s only true in series
Forcing one of the two formulas onto a circuit that’s neither pure series nor pure parallel, instead of deriving its equation
Finding R with the sources still connected. \alpha comes from the circuit with independent sources turned off

Related

LC Oscillation: the undamped oscillation that resistance damps
Second-Order Differential Equations: reading \alpha and \omega_0 off any equation
Source Transformation: simplifying a circuit into series or parallel form

courses/ele-302/concepts/lc-oscillation.title: LC Oscillation
courses/ele-302/concepts/lc-oscillation.content:
When an inductor and a capacitor are connected together, energy passes back and forth between them, so the voltage and current oscillate as sine waves at \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}.
This is the reason second-order circuits can ring instead of just decaying. In Ch 8 the oscillation is always mixed with some resistance, which makes it die out; this page looks at the pure LC case first, so you can see what the resistance is fighting against. It builds on the element laws in Capacitors and Inductors.
Intuition
Two kinds of stored energy
The two elements store energy in different forms:

A capacitor stores energy in its electric field, w_C = \frac{1}{2}Cv^2. That energy depends on its voltage.
An inductor stores energy in its magnetic field, w_L = \frac{1}{2}Li^2. That energy depends on its current.

Neither can hold onto its energy when the other is connected across it. A charged capacitor wants to push current, and an inductor carrying current wants to keep pushing it. Put them together and each one keeps handing its energy to the other.

Figure 1: An LC circuit. The current i flows out of the capacitor’s + terminal and through the inductor.
Following one cycle
Start with the capacitor charged to +V_m and no current flowing, then let the circuit go. The numbers below match the circled numbers in Figure 2.

Start. The capacitor is fully charged and the current is 0. All the energy is in the capacitor.
The capacitor discharges. Its voltage pushes current through the inductor. The inductor resists sudden changes in current (v = L\frac{di}{dt}), so the current builds up gradually rather than all at once. As charge leaves the capacitor, its voltage falls while the current rises: energy moves from the electric field into the magnetic field. A quarter of the way through, the capacitor voltage reaches 0 and the current is at its maximum. All the energy is now in the inductor.
The inductor keeps the current going. An inductor can’t stop its current instantly (its current is continuous), so the current keeps flowing in the same direction even though nothing is pushing it anymore. That current piles charge onto the capacitor the other way round, so the capacitor voltage goes negative. Halfway through, the current has dropped to 0 and the capacitor is charged to -V_m. All the energy is back in the capacitor, just with the opposite polarity.
The whole thing runs in reverse. The capacitor now discharges the other way, the current flows backwards and reaches its most negative value when v_C passes through 0 again.
Back to the start. After one full period the capacitor is at +V_m again with no current, exactly as in step 1, and the cycle repeats forever.


Figure 2: Capacitor voltage (gold) and current (gray) over one period. The circled numbers are the stages in the list above.
Notice that the voltage and current are a quarter cycle (90°) apart: the current is at its peak exactly when the voltage passes through zero, and the current is zero exactly when the voltage is at a peak. That’s the energy changing hands: when one element holds all of it, the other holds none.
Energy is conserved
With no resistor, nothing turns the energy into heat, so the total never changes:
\tfrac{1}{2}Cv^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}Li^2 = \text{constant}
That gives a useful link between the peak voltage and the peak current. At stage 1 all the energy is in the capacitor (\frac{1}{2}CV_m^2), and at the quarter-cycle point all of it is in the inductor (\frac{1}{2}LI_m^2). Setting them equal:
\tfrac{1}{2}CV_m^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}LI_m^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad I_m = V_m\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}}
The mass-on-a-spring analogy
A mass on a spring does exactly the same thing. Stretch the spring and let go: the mass speeds up as the spring relaxes, shoots past the middle because of its inertia, stretches the spring the other way, stops, and comes back. The two systems match term by term:









































LC circuitMass on a springCharge on the capacitor, qPosition of the mass, xCurrent, i = \frac{dq}{dt}Velocity, \frac{dx}{dt}Capacitor, energy \frac{1}{2}Cv^2Spring, energy \frac{1}{2}kx^2Inductor, energy \frac{1}{2}Li^2, resists changes in currentMass, energy \frac{1}{2}mv^2, resists changes in velocity (inertia)LMass m\frac{1}{C}Spring stiffness k\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}ResistorFriction
The inductor’s “inertia” is what makes the circuit overshoot past 0 V instead of just settling there. Without an inductor (an RC circuit) the voltage simply decays to zero and never goes negative, just like a spring in thick honey with no mass to carry it past the middle.
The frequency formula makes sense through the analogy too: a heavier mass (bigger L) or a softer spring (bigger C, since k \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{C}) swings more slowly.
Where the sine wave comes from
You can get the oscillation straight from the element laws. In Figure 1, the current flows out of the capacitor’s + terminal, so by the passive sign convention i = -C\frac{dv}{dt}. The inductor is connected directly across the capacitor, so it has the same voltage: v = L\frac{di}{dt}. Substituting the first into the second:
v = L\frac{d}{dt}\left(-C\frac{dv}{dt}\right) = -LC\frac{d^2 v}{dt^2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{d^2 v}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{LC}\,v = 0
This is the Ch 8 standard form with \alpha = 0 (no resistance) and \omega_0^2 = \frac{1}{LC}. Its characteristic equation s^2 + \omega_0^2 = 0 has roots s = \pm j\omega_0: purely imaginary, so the response is a sine wave that never decays (see Second-Order Differential Equations). With v(0) = V_m and i(0) = 0:
v(t) = V_m\cos\omega_0 t, \qquad i(t) = -C\frac{dv}{dt} = V_m\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}}\,\sin\omega_0 t
Adding resistance
Real circuits always have some resistance, and a resistor acts like friction: on every swing it turns some of the energy into heat, so each swing is smaller than the last. How fast that happens is the damping, \alpha:

A little resistance (\alpha < \omega_0): it still oscillates, but inside a shrinking envelope. That’s the underdamped case.
A lot of resistance (\alpha > \omega_0): the energy is drained before it can swing even once, so it just creeps to zero. That’s the overdamped case, like a spring in honey.
Exactly enough (\alpha = \omega_0): the fastest return to zero without overshooting. That’s critically damped.


Figure 3: Adding resistance to an LC circuit. The pure LC case would keep oscillating at full size forever.
Whether more resistance means more or less damping depends on where it’s connected; see Damping in Series and Parallel RLC.
Key formulas
Resonant frequency, period and frequency in hertz
\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \qquad T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}, \qquad f_0 = \frac{\omega_0}{2\pi}
Energy conservation and peak values (no resistance)
\tfrac{1}{2}Cv^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}Li^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}CV_m^2, \qquad I_m = V_m\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}}
Pure LC response, starting from v(0) = V_m, i(0) = 0 (current direction as in Figure 1)
v(t) = V_m\cos\omega_0 t, \qquad i(t) = I_m\sin\omega_0 t

\omega_0: resonant (natural) frequency, rad/s
T: period, s; f_0: frequency, Hz
V_m: peak capacitor voltage; I_m: peak current
L: inductance (H); C: capacitance (F)

Worked example
Example 1: A capacitor discharging into an inductor
A 10\ \mu\text{F} capacitor charged to 5\ \text{V} is connected to a 25\ \text{mH} inductor at t = 0. There’s no resistance. Find (a) the frequency and period of the oscillation, (b) the stored energy and the peak current, (c) v(t) and i(t), and (d) the current at the moment the capacitor voltage is 3 V.
(a)
\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(25 \times 10^{-3})(10 \times 10^{-6})}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-7}}} = 2000\ \text{rad/s}
f_0 = \frac{2000}{2\pi} = 318.3\ \text{Hz}, \qquad T = \frac{2\pi}{2000} = 3.14\ \text{ms}
(b) All the energy starts in the capacitor:
w = \tfrac{1}{2}(10 \times 10^{-6})(5)^2 = 125\ \mu\text{J}
At the peak current all of it is in the inductor:
I_m = V_m\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}} = 5\sqrt{\frac{10 \times 10^{-6}}{25 \times 10^{-3}}} = 5(0.02) = 0.1\ \text{A}
Check: \frac{1}{2}(25 \times 10^{-3})(0.1)^2 = 125\ \mu\text{J} ✓
(c)
v(t) = 5\cos 2000t\ \text{V}, \qquad i(t) = 0.1\sin 2000t\ \text{A}
(d) At v = 3\ \text{V} the capacitor holds \frac{1}{2}(10 \times 10^{-6})(3)^2 = 45\ \mu\text{J}. The rest, 125 - 45 = 80\ \mu\text{J}, is in the inductor:
\tfrac{1}{2}(25 \times 10^{-3})\,i^2 = 80 \times 10^{-6} \quad\Rightarrow\quad i = \sqrt{\frac{2(80 \times 10^{-6})}{25 \times 10^{-3}}} = 0.08\ \text{A}


                  
                  Part (d) didn't need v(t) or i(t) at all. Energy conservation is often the fastest way to relate voltage and current in an LC circuit.
                  
                

Common mistakes

Thinking the current is largest when the capacitor voltage is largest. It’s the opposite: the current peaks when v_C passes through zero
Expecting the capacitor to just discharge to 0 V and stop. The inductor’s current carries it past zero and charges it the other way
Mixing up \omega_0 (rad/s) and f_0 (Hz). They differ by a factor of 2\pi
Forgetting that a real circuit’s resistance makes the oscillation decay, so a pure LC answer that never dies out only applies when R = 0
